title: Create Amazon DynamoDB tables
content:
Create Amazon DynamoDB Tables In this section, we will prepare Amazon DynamoDB tables to store business data for the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform.
To complete this lab, you need to:
Complete section 5.2 - Prerequisite. Complete section 5.3 - Backend Development. Have an AWS account with appropriate DynamoDB permissions. Configure AWS CLI with the sap-dev profile. 1. Design the table structure In Amazon DynamoDB, each table requires a Primary Key to identify individual items.
A Primary Key can consist of:
Partition Key: The primary attribute used to partition and identify data. Sort Key: An attribute used to distinguish multiple items sharing the same Partition Key. The project uses five business data tables:
Table Name Partition Key Sort Key SAP-Activities activity_id None SAP-Registrations activity_id mssv SAP-Attendance activity_id mssv SAP-Evidence activity_id mssv SAP-Participation activity_id mssv The activity_id and mssv keys are represented as Strings to preserve identifier values and leading zeros in student IDs.
Example:
activity_id: ACT#DEMO001 mssv: 0818000001 This design allows the application to retrieve activity information and locate individual student records within an activity.
If you are using tables already created for the project, verify their existing Key Schema before proceeding. Do not recreate or modify the keys of existing tables. The key structure must match the Backend repository implementation.
2. Open the Amazon DynamoDB Console Open the AWS Management Console.
Search for DynamoDB.
Select Amazon DynamoDB.
In the upper-right corner, select the Region:
Asia Pacific (Singapore) ap-southeast-1 In the navigation pane, choose Tables. If the five SAP tables already exist, inspect their status and Key Schema before proceeding to the verification step.
3. Create the SAP-Activities table SAP-Activities stores student activity information.
In the DynamoDB Console, choose Create table.
Enter the Table name:
SAP-Activities Enter the Partition key: activity_id Select String as the data type.
Do not configure a Sort key for this table.
Under Table settings, choose Customize settings if you need to configure the Capacity mode.
Select On-demand for the learning environment if appropriate for your workload and budget.
Keep suitable default encryption settings.
Choose Create table.
After creation, verify that the table status is ACTIVE.
Business attributes stored in the table may include:
activity_id. Activity name. Description. Location. Scheduled time. Activity status. DynamoDB does not require all non-key attributes to be defined when creating a table.
4. Create the SAP-Registrations table This table stores student registration records for individual activities.
Choose Create table.
Enter the Table name:
SAP-Registrations Configure the Partition key: activity_id String Configure the Sort key: mssv String Select an appropriate Capacity mode.
Choose Create table.
This key structure allows multiple students to register for the same activity while distinguishing each student by their student ID.
5. Create the SAP-Attendance table SAP-Attendance stores student Check-in and Check-out records.
Table configuration:
Table name: SAP-Attendance Partition key: activity_id (String) Sort key: mssv (String) Follow the same table creation procedure used for SAP-Registrations.
Items may contain:
Activity ID. Student ID. Check-in timestamp. Check-out timestamp. Attendance status information. The system records attendance through real-time REST APIs rather than importing attendance spreadsheets after an activity.
6. Create the SAP-Evidence table SAP-Evidence stores student participation evidence.
Table configuration:
Table name: SAP-Evidence Partition key: activity_id (String) Sort key: mssv (String) Choose Create table and verify the table status.
Evidence can be exported from Google Forms or Google Sheets as CSV/XLSX files and processed by the Backend.
7. Create the SAP-Participation table SAP-Participation stores reconciliation and participation confirmation results.
Table configuration:
Table name: SAP-Participation Partition key: activity_id (String) Sort key: mssv (String) Relevant business data may include:
Registration status. Attendance status. Evidence status. Reconciliation results. Participation confirmation results. 8. Verify the table list After creating or preparing the tables, return to the DynamoDB Console.
Choose Tables and verify the following resources:
SAP-Activities. SAP-Registrations. SAP-Attendance. SAP-Evidence. SAP-Participation. Each table should have an ACTIVE status.
Verify the table list using AWS CLI:
aws dynamodb list-tables --region ap-southeast-1 --profile sap-dev The output should contain the five business data tables:
{ "TableNames": [ "SAP-Activities", "SAP-Attendance", "SAP-Evidence", "SAP-Participation", "SAP-Registrations" ] } Your AWS account may contain additional tables.
Inspect the SAP-Evidence table:
aws dynamodb describe-table --table-name SAP-Evidence --region ap-southeast-1 --profile sap-dev --query "Table.{Status:TableStatus,KeySchema:KeySchema,Attributes:AttributeDefinitions}" The Key Schema should include:
activity_id: HASH mssv: RANGE HASH represents the Partition Key, and RANGE represents the Sort Key.
Repeat this verification for the remaining tables.
Results After completing this section:
Five DynamoDB tables have been created or verified in the Singapore Region. Partition Keys and Sort Keys have been inspected. The tables are ACTIVE. AWS CLI can access table information. In the next section, we will use boto3 to connect the FastAPI Backend to the DynamoDB tables.
Next: Connect the Backend to Amazon DynamoDB

title: Import Participation Evidence
content:
Import Participation Evidence In this section, we will import student participation evidence into the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform.
Participation evidence may be collected through Google Forms or Google Sheets, depending on the requirements of each activity.
For example, after a seminar or technology event, students may be required to submit a confirmation form, provide participation information, or submit evidence links.
ADMIN users can use these records to verify participation alongside registration and attendance data.
1. Prepare the environment Complete section 5.6 - Registration and Attendance Management.
Prepare the following:
A running FastAPI Backend. A running React/Vite Frontend. An ADMIN Demo account. An activity with existing registration records. Check-in and Check-out data. A CSV/XLSX evidence file. For cloud storage verification, prepare the DynamoDB configuration described in section 5.4.
2. Understand the evidence data source Evidence collection and import workflow:
Student | v Google Forms | v Google Sheets | | Export CSV / XLSX v ADMIN Import Interface | v FastAPI Evidence Processing | v Evidence Records The current implementation uses file-based imports.
Direct integration with the Google Forms API or Google Sheets API is not required.
3. Prepare Google Forms data A Google Forms evidence collection form may include:
Student full name. Student ID. Student class. Activity name. Participation evidence information. Evidence link when required. These are illustrative form fields. Actual data must follow the organizers’ requirements and the application’s Import Template.
Student ID is essential for matching evidence with Registration and Attendance records.
4. Export data from Google Sheets Open the Google Forms used to collect evidence. Select the Responses tab. Open the associated Google Sheets document. Review the collected responses. In Google Sheets, select File → Download. Select Microsoft Excel (.xlsx) or Comma-separated values (.csv). CSV export includes the current worksheet.
Ensure that the selected worksheet contains the intended activity responses.
When Google Forms collects image uploads in Google Drive, exported CSV/XLSX files generally contain information or links associated with the uploaded files. Importing evidence records does not automatically copy the original images to Amazon S3.
5. Prepare a sample evidence file Create:
evidence-demo.csv Example content:
mssv,evidence_url 0818000001,https://example.com/evidence-01 0818000002,https://example.com/evidence-02 0818000003,https://example.com/evidence-03 Where:
mssv: Student ID. evidence_url: Illustrative evidence URL. The example.com URLs are synthetic placeholders, not actual participation evidence images.
Column names and file formats must match the current Backend’s Import Template. If the application provides a downloadable template, use that template.
When preparing Excel files, format Student ID columns as Text to preserve leading zeros.
6. Validate data before importing Before importing, verify:
Student IDs are not missing. Student IDs use supported formats. Required columns are present. Records belong to the correct activity. Duplicate records are identified. Evidence information satisfies the relevant requirements. Example invalid dataset:
mssv,evidence_url 0818000001,https://example.com/evidence-01 0818000002,https://example.com/evidence-02 0818000001,https://example.com/evidence-03 ,https://example.com/evidence-04 This dataset includes a duplicate Student ID and a missing Student ID.
The Backend should handle these cases according to its current Import rules and avoid inconsistent evidence records.
The presence of an evidence URL does not automatically prove that an image has been reviewed or approved.
7. Perform Evidence Import Open the Web Application. Sign in using an ADMIN account. Select the target activity. Open Evidence Import. Select evidence-demo.csv or the corresponding XLSX file. Review the selected activity and file information. Execute the Import operation. The Frontend submits the file to the FastAPI Backend.
The Backend reads the file, validates required data, and stores evidence records according to the current business rules.
If a preview is available, inspect the records before confirming the Import.
8. Verify the Import results After importing:
Open the activity’s evidence list. Inspect the number of records. Verify individual student IDs. Compare the records with the original file. Inspect invalid or duplicate record information if available. Example:
Student ID Evidence 0818000001 Available 0818000002 Available 0818000003 Available 0818000004 Not available This table illustrates a testing scenario.
Having Evidence does not automatically mean that participation has been confirmed.
9. Inspect the Evidence Import REST API Press F12 to open Developer Tools.
Select Network. Select Fetch/XHR. Import a sample evidence file. Inspect the corresponding request. Review the Request URL, HTTP Method, and Response. Use Swagger UI to identify the actual Endpoint and Request Schema:
http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs
Do not replace existing Endpoints when the current Import functionality already works.
10. Verify Evidence in Amazon DynamoDB If the Evidence AWS Pilot is enabled:
Open the Amazon DynamoDB Console. Select Singapore - ap-southeast-1. Select SAP-Evidence. Choose Explore table items. Select Query. Enter the activity_id of the selected activity. Inspect evidence records by Student ID. Verify the table Key Schema according to section 5.4:
Key Type activity_id String mssv String Compare DynamoDB records with the Backend Import results.
In the Demo environment, records may still be processed through local storage when the AWS Pilot is disabled.
11. Summarize test cases Test Expected Result Valid CSV/XLSX Evidence data accepted Missing Student ID Record reported or handled Duplicate Student ID No inconsistent evidence records Incorrect Activity ID No data written to an unrelated activity STUDENT Import Access denied when unauthorized Evidence List Import results displayed DynamoDB Corresponding items when AWS Pilot is enabled Use synthetic or authorized data only. Do not expose personal information, student photographs, private Google Drive links, or Access Tokens in the internship report.
Results After completing this section, we have prepared and imported evidence records from Google Forms/Google Sheets.
Evidence data will be combined with Registration and Attendance to reconcile student participation results.
Next: Reconcile Student Participation Data

title: Import Student Registration Data
content:
Import Student Registration Data In this section, we will import student registration data from CSV/XLSX files into the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform.
Registration data helps organizers identify students registered for each activity and provides a foundation for attendance recording and post-event reconciliation.
1. Prepare the environment Ensure that the following components are available:
FastAPI Backend at http://127.0.0.1:8000. React/Vite Frontend at http://localhost:5173. An ADMIN Demo account. An existing activity in the system. A sample registration file. For AWS storage testing, prepare the DynamoDB integration settings described in section 5.4.
2. Understand the registration data source In practice, students register for university activities through the University Portal.
Organizers can export registration lists as Excel or CSV files and import them into the activity management platform.
Workflow:
University Portal | v Export Registration List | v CSV / XLSX File | v ADMIN Import Interface | v FastAPI Validation | v Registration Records The current implementation uses file-based imports and does not require direct API integration with the University Portal.
3. Prepare a CSV/XLSX file Create a sample CSV file named:
registrations-demo.csv Example content:
mssv,full_name,class_name 0818000001,Student A,DS01 0818000002,Student B,DS01 0818000003,Student C,DS02 0818000004,Student D,DS02 Illustrative fields include:
mssv: Student ID. full_name: Student full name. class_name: Student class. This is synthetic data for the workshop. Column names must match the Import Template supported by the current Backend. If the application provides a downloadable template, use that template.
Microsoft Excel can be used to prepare the file and save it in XLSX or CSV UTF-8 format.
Format student ID columns as Text in Excel to preserve leading zeros.
4. Sign in as ADMIN Open the React/Vite application. Sign in using an ADMIN Demo account. Open Activity Management. Select the activity for which registration data will be imported. Verify the activity name and Activity ID to avoid importing records into the wrong activity.
Example:
Activity Name: AWS Workshop Demo Activity ID: Use the system-generated identifier 5. Perform Registration Import From the activity management interface:
Open the registration import functionality. Select the target activity. Select registrations-demo.csv or the corresponding XLSX file. Review the selected file information. Execute the Import operation. The Frontend sends the file and relevant activity information to FastAPI.
The Backend reads the file, validates its records, and stores valid registration data according to the current business rules.
If a data preview is available, review the records before confirming the Import.
6. Validate input data The following scenarios should be considered:
Missing student IDs. Unsupported student ID formats. Duplicate students within the same registration list. Missing required columns. Unsupported file formats. Invalid Activity IDs. Student data that does not satisfy business requirements. Example test file:
mssv,full_name,class_name 0818000001,Student A,DS01 0818000002,Student B,DS01 0818000001,Student A,DS01 ,Student C,DS02 This file contains four records:
Two valid and distinct student IDs. One duplicate student ID. One record with a missing student ID. The expected behavior is that invalid records are identified and duplicate registrations are not created for the same student and activity.
Depending on the implementation, the Backend may reject the file, skip invalid records, or update existing records. Review the actual Import Response to determine the implemented behavior.
7. Verify the Import result After the Import finishes:
Open the activity’s registration list. Inspect the number of stored registrations. Verify student IDs and student information. Compare the records with the original file. Inspect invalid or duplicate record information if available. Each registration must be associated with the correct Activity ID and Student ID.
Example:
Activity ID: ACT-DEMO-001 Student ID: 0818000001 Registration: Recorded The Activity ID is illustrative. Use the actual identifier generated by the Backend.
8. Inspect the Registration Import REST API Open Developer Tools by pressing F12.
Select the Network tab. Select the Fetch/XHR filter. Import a test file. Select the corresponding HTTP request. Review its HTTP Method, Request URL, and Response. The file is submitted to the Backend through the application’s Import API.
Use Swagger UI to inspect the current Endpoint and Request Schema:
http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs
Do not expose Access Tokens, login credentials, or real student information in Network or Swagger UI screenshots.
9. Verify Registration data in Amazon DynamoDB If the Registration AWS Pilot is enabled:
Open the Amazon DynamoDB Console. Select Singapore - ap-southeast-1. Select SAP-Registrations. Choose Explore table items. Query items by activity_id. Inspect records corresponding to the imported student IDs. The integration uses the following key structure:
Key Type Purpose activity_id String Identifies the activity mssv String Identifies a student within the activity Verify the actual table Key Schema according to section 5.4 before querying.
If AWS Pilot integration is disabled, data may only be processed in the local Demo environment. An empty DynamoDB result does not automatically indicate an Import failure.
10. Summarize test cases Test Case Expected Result Valid CSV file Registration data accepted and processed Valid XLSX file Registration data accepted and processed Missing Student ID Invalid record reported or handled Duplicate Student ID No duplicate registration for the same activity Unsupported file format Appropriate error message STUDENT attempts Import Backend denies unauthorized access Registration list Records match the Import results DynamoDB Integration Corresponding Cloud records when AWS Pilot is enabled Results After completing this section, we have prepared and imported student registration data into the system.
The Backend can receive CSV/XLSX files, validate input data, and store records for activity management.
Registration data provides an important foundation for attendance recording, evidence imports, and participation reconciliation.
Next: Prepare Activity and Attendance

title: Introduction
content:
Introduction to the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform The Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform is a system designed to support the management, tracking, reconciliation, and analysis of student participation data in university activities.
In practice, student activity data is collected from multiple sources, including the University Portal, student identification card QR-based attendance systems, Google Forms, and Google Sheets. After each activity, organizers need to consolidate, validate, and reconcile these datasets to determine the participation results of each student.
Manually processing multiple Excel or CSV files can be time-consuming, introduce duplicate records and missing information, and create additional challenges when managing large-scale student activities.
This workshop introduces how to build a centralized data management platform by combining Web Application development with AWS services. It helps learners understand application development, Cloud data storage integration, data processing, and system deployment.
The system is developed using React/Vite, Python/FastAPI, and SQLite, with Amazon DynamoDB integration. AWS services are also used for Frontend hosting, file storage, Serverless data processing, access management, and execution monitoring.
Introduction to AWS Services Used AWS Amplify: A service that supports Web Application deployment and hosting. In this workshop, AWS Amplify is used to deploy the React/Vite Frontend, allowing ADMIN and STUDENT users to access the system through a Web browser.
Amazon DynamoDB: A fully managed NoSQL database service provided by AWS. DynamoDB is integrated and tested to store business data groups such as Activities, Registrations, Attendance, Evidence, and Participation.
Amazon S3: An object storage service provided by AWS. It is used to store input CSV files and processed JSON results in the Serverless CSV Processing Demo.
AWS Lambda: A Serverless Compute service that allows developers to execute code without directly managing servers. In this workshop, Lambda is used to read CSV files, validate data, detect duplicate records, and generate processing results.
AWS IAM: A service for managing identities and access permissions on AWS. IAM provides Lambda with permissions to access Amazon S3 and write execution logs to Amazon CloudWatch, following the Least Privilege principle.
Amazon CloudWatch: An AWS monitoring and logging service. CloudWatch is used to monitor Lambda execution, review errors, measure execution duration, and inspect operational information.
Workshop Overview In this workshop, you will explore and develop a system consisting of three main components:
1. Web Application
This is the main component of the system, used to manage student activities and participation data.
The Frontend is developed using React/Vite and deployed on AWS Amplify Hosting. The Backend is developed using Python/FastAPI to provide REST APIs and process business logic. Cloudflare Quick Tunnel is used to connect the Frontend with the locally running Backend. SQLite supports data persistence and recovery in the Demo environment. Authentication and Authorization are implemented for the ADMIN and STUDENT user roles. ADMIN users can manage activities, manage student accounts, import registration data, record Check-in/Check-out, import participation evidence, reconcile data, confirm participation results, and export reports.
STUDENT users can sign in, view personal information, browse activities, and track their own participation results within the authorized scope.
2. AWS Cloud Data Storage
Amazon DynamoDB is used to integrate and test cloud-based business data storage.
In this workshop, you will learn how to connect Python/FastAPI to DynamoDB using the AWS SDK for Python (boto3) and perform data reading and writing operations.
The main business data groups include:
Activities: Activity information. Registrations: Student registration records. Attendance: Check-in/Check-out records. Evidence: Student participation evidence. Participation: Participation results. The current Demo combines local persistence using SQLite with DynamoDB integration on AWS. The workshop does not assume that the entire application persistence mechanism has been fully migrated to DynamoDB.
3. AWS Serverless CSV Processing
This is an independent Serverless data processing workflow developed using Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, AWS IAM, and Amazon CloudWatch.
The workflow includes:
Upload a CSV file containing registration data to Amazon S3. Use AWS Lambda to read the CSV data. Validate required data fields. Detect duplicate and invalid records. Aggregate processing results. Store the processed JSON output back in Amazon S3. Use AWS IAM to manage execution permissions. Monitor execution results and logs using Amazon CloudWatch. This workflow helps learners understand how to build an AWS-based Data Processing Pipeline without directly managing servers.
Architecture Overview The following diagram illustrates the architecture of the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform, including the Web Application, Local Demo Environment, AWS Cloud Data Storage, and Serverless CSV Processing Demo.
The system receives data from three primary sources:
University Portal: Provides student registration lists in CSV/XLSX format. Student Card QR / Student ID: Provides student identification information for real-time Check-in/Check-out recording. Google Forms / Google Sheets: Provides participation evidence in CSV/XLSX format. The main business workflow of the system is:
Registration Import → Real-time Attendance → Evidence Import → Reconciliation → Participation Confirmation → Analytics & Export.
Workshop Objectives After completing this workshop, you will be able to:
Understand the overall architecture of a student activity management and analytics system. Develop Backend REST APIs using Python/FastAPI. Develop a Web Application interface using React/Vite. Understand Authentication and ADMIN/STUDENT role-based access control. Import, validate, and process CSV/XLSX data. Understand real-time attendance recording and data reconciliation workflows. Connect a Python application to Amazon DynamoDB. Deploy the Frontend using AWS Amplify Hosting. Build a CSV data processing workflow using Amazon S3 and AWS Lambda. Configure AWS IAM permissions for required resources. Monitor Lambda execution and logs using Amazon CloudWatch. Understand how to select and combine AWS services according to the requirements of a real-world project. Through this workshop, learners will have the opportunity to combine Web Development, Data Processing, Cloud Computing, and AWS knowledge to build a practical student activity management system.
This workshop is designed for educational, internship, and demonstration purposes. Deploying the Backend on stable Cloud infrastructure, fully migrating the persistence mechanism to a Cloud database, and operating the system at Production scale remain future development directions.

title: Prepare Analytics Data and Metrics
content:
Prepare Analytics Data and Metrics In this section, we will prepare business datasets and calculate analytical indicators for the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform.
The objective is to produce accurate and consistent metrics that reflect student activity participation.
1. Prepare the environment Complete the following sections:
5.3 - Backend Development with FastAPI. 5.4 - Amazon DynamoDB Integration. 5.5 - Frontend Development with React/Vite. 5.6 - Registration and Attendance Management. 5.7 - Evidence Processing and Reconciliation. Ensure that the following are available:
FastAPI Backend at http://127.0.0.1:8000. React/Vite Frontend at http://localhost:5173. An ADMIN Demo account. An activity with Registration, Attendance, Evidence, and Participation records. 2. Identify analytics data sources The Analytics Dashboard uses business data processed by the Backend.
Dataset Analytical Purpose Activities Activity information and totals Registrations Student registration counts Attendance Check-in, Check-out, and attendance completion Evidence Evidence availability Participation Confirmed and rejected participation results Each record must be associated with the correct Activity ID and Student ID.
When aggregating multiple activities, distinguish participation records from unique students.
For example, a student participating in three activities can generate three participation records while representing only one unique student.
3. Prepare a sample dataset Reuse the synthetic activity data from section 5.7.
Student ID Registration Check-in Check-out Evidence 0818000001 Yes Yes Yes Yes 0818000002 Yes Yes No Yes 0818000003 Yes No No Yes 0818000004 Yes Yes Yes No Current confirmation results:
Student ID Participation 0818000001 CONFIRMED 0818000002 Not yet confirmed 0818000003 REJECTED 0818000004 Not yet confirmed This dataset contains:
Total registrations: 4. Students with Check-in: 3. Students with Check-out: 2. Students with complete attendance: 2. Students with Evidence: 3. Confirmed participants: 1. Rejected participants: 1. Students awaiting a final decision: 2. These figures are synthetic workshop data.
4. Define analytical metrics Total Registrations The number of valid registration records within the selected activity scope.
Total Registrations = 4 Duplicate file rows should not be counted as separate registrations for the same student and activity.
Total Check-in The number of students with valid Check-in records.
Total Check-in = 3 Total Check-out The number of students with valid Check-out records.
Total Check-out = 2 Complete Attendance The number of students satisfying both Check-in and Check-out requirements.
Complete Attendance = 2 Evidence Submitted The number of students with Evidence records.
Evidence Submitted = 3 Evidence availability does not automatically indicate approved evidence or confirmed participation.
Confirmed Participants The number of students with CONFIRMED participation results.
Confirmed Participants = 1 Rejected Participants The number of students with REJECTED participation results.
Rejected Participants = 1 5. Calculate analytical rates Check-in Rate Check-in Rate = Registered Students with Check-in / Total Registrations x 100 = 3 / 4 x 100 = 75% Attendance Completion Rate Attendance Completion Rate = Registered Students with Complete Attendance / Total Registrations x 100 = 2 / 4 x 100 = 50% Evidence Submission Rate Evidence Submission Rate = Registered Students with Evidence / Total Registrations x 100 = 3 / 4 x 100 = 75% Confirmed Participation Rate Confirmed Participation Rate = Confirmed Registered Students / Total Registrations x 100 = 1 / 4 x 100 = 25% These example rates use registered students as the denominator. The actual Dashboard must follow consistent Backend metric definitions. Handle zero registrations to prevent division-by-zero errors.
6. Illustrate analytics processing using Python Create a separate practice file:
analytics_demo.py Content:
students = [ { "mssv": "0818000001", "check_in": True, "check_out": True, "evidence": True, "participation": "CONFIRMED" }, { "mssv": "0818000002", "check_in": True, "check_out": False, "evidence": True, "participation": None }, { "mssv": "0818000003", "check_in": False, "check_out": False, "evidence": True, "participation": "REJECTED" }, { "mssv": "0818000004", "check_in": True, "check_out": True, "evidence": False, "participation": None } ] total = len(students) check_in = sum( student["check_in"] for student in students ) check_out = sum( student["check_out"] for student in students ) complete_attendance = sum( student["check_in"] and student["check_out"] for student in students ) evidence = sum( student["evidence"] for student in students ) confirmed = sum( student["participation"] == "CONFIRMED" for student in students ) rejected = sum( student["participation"] == "REJECTED" for student in students ) pending = total - confirmed - rejected def rate(count, total): return round(count / total * 100, 2) if total else 0 print("Total registrations:", total) print("Total check-in:", check_in) print("Total check-out:", check_out) print("Complete attendance:", complete_attendance) print("Evidence submitted:", evidence) print("Confirmed participants:", confirmed) print("Rejected participants:", rejected) print("Awaiting decision:", pending) print("Check-in rate:", rate(check_in, total)) print("Attendance completion rate:", rate(complete_attendance, total)) print("Confirmed participation rate:", rate(confirmed, total)) Run:
python analytics_demo.py Expected output:
Total registrations: 4 Total check-in: 3 Total check-out: 2 Complete attendance: 2 Evidence submitted: 3 Confirmed participants: 1 Rejected participants: 1 Awaiting decision: 2 Check-in rate: 75.0 Attendance completion rate: 50.0 Confirmed participation rate: 25.0 analytics_demo.py is a standalone learning example using one record per registered student within one activity. It does not replace the project’s existing Analytics Service.
7. Understand Analytics API data The Backend aggregates business records and returns results for Frontend visualization.
Illustrative JSON response:
{ "total_registrations": 4, "total_check_in": 3, "total_check_out": 2, "complete_attendance": 2, "evidence_submitted": 3, "confirmed_participants": 1, "rejected_participants": 1, "awaiting_decision": 2, "check_in_rate": 75.0, "attendance_completion_rate": 50.0, "participation_rate": 25.0 } These attributes illustrate a possible Analytics API response.
Use the current Backend source code and Swagger UI to determine the actual field names and response structure.
8. Inspect current Analytics data Open Swagger UI:
http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs
Locate the Analytics group or activity statistics APIs.
Authenticate using an ADMIN account. Identify the target Activity ID. Execute the existing API request. Inspect the response. Compare the indicators with Registration, Attendance, and Participation data. If the API aggregates the entire system rather than a single activity, verify its data scope before comparing results.
9. Handle special scenarios Scenario Expected Handling No registrations No division-by-zero error Registration without attendance Check-in count remains zero Check-in without Check-out Not counted as complete attendance Evidence with REJECTED status Not counted as CONFIRMED Student attends multiple activities Distinguish records from unique students Decisions are incomplete Distinguish pending decisions from REJECTED Incorrect Activity ID Do not aggregate unrelated activity data Results After completing this section, we have prepared analytics data and explored the calculation of key Dashboard indicators.
Defining the correct data scope, numerator, and denominator helps ensure that reports accurately reflect activity outcomes.
In the next section, we will display analytical indicators using the React/Vite Frontend.
Next: Build the Analytics Dashboard

title: Prepare Source Code and Deployment Configuration
content:
Prepare Source Code and Deployment Configuration In this section, we will prepare the React/Vite Frontend source code and FastAPI Backend environment for deploying the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform.
The objective is to ensure that the source code builds successfully, is managed through GitHub, and supports the Demo deployment configuration.
1. Prepare the environment Complete workshop sections 5.2 through 5.8.
Required tools and resources:
Visual Studio Code. Git. Node.js and npm. Python and FastAPI. GitHub Account. AWS Account with Amplify Hosting permissions. Cloudflare cloudflared. AWS CLI and sap-dev Profile when testing AWS integrations. 2. Inspect the project source structure Open the project using Visual Studio Code:
C:\Projects\student-activity-platform Main source structure:
student-activity-platform/ ├── backend/ │ ├── app/ │ ├── requirements.txt │ └── ... └── frontend/ ├── src/ │ ├── services/ │ │ └── api.js │ └── ... ├── package.json ├── package-lock.json └── ... The Frontend contains React/Vite source code. The Backend contains APIs, Business Services, and data access mechanisms.
AWS Amplify Hosting only builds the Frontend for the current deployment.
3. Inspect the GitHub Repository The project’s deployment uses:
Repository: fcaj Branch: main Open the fcaj repository on GitHub.
Verify that:
The main branch contains the intended Frontend source. The Frontend directory contains package.json. Build configuration files are up to date. Credentials and sensitive information are not included in the repository. If the project is already connected to GitHub, inspect the repository using:
git status git remote -v git branch --show-current These commands display repository status, configured remotes, and the current branch.
Run them from the appropriate Git Repository directory.
Do not upload AWS credentials, ADMIN passwords, Access Tokens, real student data, or SQLite database files containing personal information to GitHub.
4. Inspect the .gitignore file Open the repository’s .gitignore file.
Verify which files and directories should be excluded from Git.
Example:
node_modules/ dist/ .venv/ __pycache__/ .env .env.local .env.production.local *.db *.sqlite *.sqlite3 These rules are illustrative and should be adapted to the actual repository structure.
Preserve the existing .gitignore when it already provides suitable exclusions.
Remember that .gitignore does not automatically remove files already tracked by Git.
5. Inspect API_BASE_URL configuration Open:
frontend/src/services/api.js The Frontend must use a Backend address appropriate for its environment.
The local development Backend uses port 8000.
The Demo Backend connected through Cloudflare Quick Tunnel uses port 8001.
The project uses the following variable to configure its Backend URL:
VITE_API_BASE_URL Illustrative configuration:
const API_BASE_URL = ( import.meta.env.VITE_API_BASE_URL || "http://127.0.0.1:8000" ).replace(/\/+$/, ""); Explanation:
import.meta.env: Provides access to Vite environment variables. VITE_API_BASE_URL: Specifies the Backend address at build time. Local address: Provides a development fallback. replace(): Removes trailing slashes from the URL. Compare this example with the existing api.js configuration.
Do not introduce another API_BASE_URL declaration if one already exists.
Variables prefixed with VITE_ may be embedded in JavaScript delivered to the browser. Use VITE_API_BASE_URL for the public API address, never for Secret Access Keys, passwords, or Access Tokens.
6. Inspect CORS configuration Open:
backend/app/main.py Review FastAPI’s CORSMiddleware configuration.
The Backend must permit the local Frontend origin and the deployed Amplify Website origin.
The Amplify address used during the previous deployment test was:
https://main.d2p96elhe5x6se.amplifyapp.com Illustrative configuration:
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware app.add_middleware( CORSMiddleware, allow_origins=[ "http://localhost:5173", "http://127.0.0.1:5173", "https://main.d2p96elhe5x6se.amplifyapp.com", ], allow_credentials=True, allow_methods=["*"], allow_headers=["*"], ) For a new Amplify App, use the actual deployed Website origin.
An origin includes the protocol and hostname, not application paths such as /login or /docs.
Do not add duplicate CORSMiddleware when the application already has CORS configuration.
7. Prepare a separate Demo Backend The project uses a Demo Backend on port 8001 with a separate SQLite Demo dataset to avoid interfering with the main development environment.
Environment configuration:
Environment Backend Port Development 8000 Internet-accessible Demo 8001 Different ports do not automatically create separate databases.
Before starting the Demo Backend, verify the persistence configuration to ensure it uses the intended Demo SQLite database.
Do not delete or overwrite the development database.
8. Verify the Frontend build Open the Frontend Terminal:
cd C:\Projects\student-activity-platform\frontend Check the environment:
node --version npm --version If package-lock.json exists:
npm ci Otherwise:
npm install Build the application:
npm run build If PowerShell blocks npm.ps1, use:
npm.cmd run build Vite should generate:
frontend/dist/ This directory contains deployable Frontend assets:
dist/ ├── index.html └── assets/ ├── ... 9. Verify the built application Use Vite Preview to inspect the build:
npm run preview Open the address displayed in the Terminal.
Example:
http://localhost:4173 Verify:
The login page renders correctly. CSS and JavaScript assets load. No critical build errors occur. Navigation works as expected. If testing Backend connectivity through Vite Preview, configure the Backend to allow the actual Preview origin.
This build verifies compilation. The final deployed build will use the Cloudflare Quick Tunnel HTTPS API address.
10. Prepare Amplify build configuration If the Frontend is located in the frontend directory of the GitHub Repository, Amplify must use the correct application location.
The build configuration must:
Install dependencies in the correct Frontend directory. Execute npm run build. Use dist as the build artifacts directory. Provide VITE_API_BASE_URL during the build. Detailed Amplify configuration will be covered in section 5.9.3.
11. Review deployment readiness Component Requirement GitHub Repository Frontend source prepared Branch main Dependencies Installed successfully Frontend Build dist directory generated API Configuration VITE_API_BASE_URL supported CORS Appropriate origins permitted Demo Backend Port 8001 Demo Database Separate SQLite Demo data Credentials No secrets in the repository Results After completing this section, we have prepared source code, verified the Frontend build, and identified the required deployment settings.
The Frontend is ready to receive the Cloudflare Quick Tunnel HTTPS API Endpoint and be deployed using AWS Amplify Hosting.
Next: Connect the Backend using Cloudflare Quick Tunnel

title: Review Resources and Costs
content:
Review Resources and Costs Before performing clean-up, we need to inspect the AWS resources used by the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform.
Resource inventory helps prevent accidental deletion and identify services that may incur charges.
1. Verify AWS Account and Region Sign in to the AWS Management Console. Verify the AWS Account. Select: Asia Pacific (Singapore) ap-southeast-1 Ensure that the Account and Region match the project environment. Standard IAM Roles and Policies are global resources, and AWS Billing operates at the account level. Therefore, resource inventory should not be limited to a single AWS Region.
2. Review AWS Amplify Hosting Open the AWS Amplify Console. Find the project’s Frontend application. Inspect the main branch. Verify Deployment Status. Record the Website URL. The previous Demo used:
https://main.d2p96elhe5x6se.amplifyapp.com Determine whether the Website is still needed for demonstrations or reporting.
3. Review Amazon DynamoDB Open the Amazon DynamoDB Console.
Inspect the following five tables:
SAP-Activities SAP-Registrations SAP-Attendance SAP-Evidence SAP-Participation For each table, record:
Table name. Current status. Billing mode. Storage size. Item count if available. Backup or Point-in-time recovery configuration. These five tables are primary business datasets within the project’s AWS Integration. Retain them if they are needed for workshops, demonstrations, or further testing.
4. Review Amazon S3 Open the Amazon S3 Console.
Select:
sap-data-project-2026-huflit01 Inspect Objects under:
lambda-demo/input/ lambda-demo/processed/ Also review any other Prefixes and Objects.
Do not assume that the Bucket contains only the Lambda Demo files.
Inspect its complete contents before considering deletion.
5. Review AWS Lambda Open the AWS Lambda Console.
Select:
sap-csv-processor-demo Review:
Function State. Runtime. Memory. Timeout. Execution Role. Triggers. Environment variables. Last modified timestamp. Determine whether the Function is still required for the S3 – Lambda – S3 demonstration.
6. Review AWS IAM Open the AWS IAM Console.
Check the Execution Role:
sap-csv-processor-demo-role-9ui2ib5d Check the Policy:
SAP-Lambda-S3-Demo-Access Identify whether the Role or Policy is used by other resources.
Do not delete shared permissions without reviewing dependencies.
7. Review Amazon CloudWatch Open the Amazon CloudWatch Console.
Navigate to Logs → Log groups.
Find:
/aws/lambda/sap-csv-processor-demo Review:
Log Retention. Log Streams. Recent invocations. Log storage. Any recorded errors. The earlier project exercise used a seven-day retention period.
8. Review AWS Billing Open AWS Billing and Cost Management.
Inspect:
Bills. Cost Explorer. Service-level charges. The relevant reporting period. Any currently estimated charges. Review charges associated with:
AWS Amplify Hosting. Amazon DynamoDB. Amazon S3. AWS Lambda. Amazon CloudWatch. Actual costs depend on consumption, configuration, and current pricing.
Do not assume that every service is free.
9. Review AWS Cost Explorer In Billing and Cost Management:
Open Cost Explorer. Choose the desired date range. Group costs by Service. Inspect individual service charges. Record charges requiring follow-up. Cost data may be delayed. A single billing check does not prove that no additional charges will appear.
10. Create a resource inventory Resource Recommendation Reason Amplify Frontend Retain Demonstrations Five DynamoDB Tables Retain AWS Integration data S3 Bucket Retain May contain project data Lambda Function Retain if needed CSV Processing Demo IAM Execution Role Retain while required Function permissions CloudWatch Log Group Retain as appropriate Evidence and debugging Cloudflare Quick Tunnel Stop after Demo Temporary endpoint Local FastAPI Stop when unused Demo Backend This is a recommendation, not confirmation that resources have been cleaned up.
Results After this section, we have identified resources to retain, disposable testing resources, and AWS costs requiring monitoring.
Next: Stop the Demo Environment

title: Set Up Amazon S3 and Prepare Data
content:
Set Up Amazon S3 and Prepare Data In this section, we will use Amazon S3 to store the CSV input file and prepare the output location for JSON results generated by AWS Lambda.
Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) is an AWS object storage service. Data is stored as Objects within Buckets.
1. Open the Amazon S3 Console Open the Amazon S3 Console. Select Buckets. Locate the project’s existing Bucket: sap-data-project-2026-huflit01 Reuse the existing Bucket if it is already available.
2. Create an S3 Bucket if required Choose Create bucket. Select Asia Pacific (Singapore) - ap-southeast-1. Choose General purpose bucket. Enter a Bucket name. Keep Object Ownership set to Bucket owner enforced. Keep Block all public access enabled. Use appropriate default encryption, such as SSE-S3. Choose Create bucket. S3 Bucket names must be unique within the applicable AWS namespace. sap-data-project-2026-huflit01 is the existing project Bucket. If using another AWS account, choose an available Bucket name and update IAM and Lambda configuration accordingly.
The Bucket does not need to be publicly accessible for Lambda to read its Objects.
3. Prepare the storage structure The workshop uses the following Object Keys:
sap-data-project-2026-huflit01/ └── lambda-demo/ ├── input/ │ └── registrations.csv └── processed/ └── registrations-result.json Where:
input/: Stores the original CSV data. processed/: Stores the JSON processing result. Amazon S3 organizes data using Object Keys and Prefixes. Console folders represent these Prefixes.
The processed Prefix does not need to exist before Lambda writes an Object using the corresponding Key.
4. Prepare a CSV file Create registrations.csv with the following synthetic data:
mssv,full_name DEMO001,Student A DEMO002,Student B DEMO001,Student A ,Student C Fields:
mssv: Student identifier. full_name: Student full name. The file contains four data records excluding its header.
Record Expected Classification DEMO001 - Student A Valid DEMO002 - Student B Valid DEMO001 - Student A Duplicate Student C - missing ID Invalid This synthetic dataset reproduces the structure and record counts of the earlier project test. DEMO identifiers validate the Lambda processing logic rather than the full Web Application’s student ID format requirements.
5. Upload the CSV file to S3 Open sap-data-project-2026-huflit01. Create the lambda-demo/input/ Prefix using Create folder if necessary. Open the input Prefix. Choose Upload. Choose Add files. Select registrations.csv. Choose Upload. Verify the Object Key:
lambda-demo/input/registrations.csv S3 URI:
s3://sap-data-project-2026-huflit01/lambda-demo/input/registrations.csv 6. Inspect the uploaded Object Select registrations.csv.
Review:
Bucket name. Object Key. File size. Content type if available. Encryption. Access permissions. Download the file using an authorized account if content verification is required.
Do not make the Bucket public.
7. Verify using AWS CLI With the sap-dev AWS Profile configured, run:
aws s3 ls s3://sap-data-project-2026-huflit01/lambda-demo/input/ --region ap-southeast-1 --profile sap-dev The output should include registrations.csv.
Inspect Object metadata:
aws s3api head-object ` --bucket sap-data-project-2026-huflit01 ` --key lambda-demo/input/registrations.csv ` --region ap-southeast-1 ` --profile sap-dev These commands require appropriate AWS permissions.
8. Prepare the output location Lambda will store its processing result at:
lambda-demo/processed/registrations-result.json S3 URI:
s3://sap-data-project-2026-huflit01/lambda-demo/processed/registrations-result.json Input and output Objects use different Prefixes within the same Bucket.
This separates source data from processed results and supports scoped IAM permissions.
9. Verify security configuration Before proceeding:
Keep Block Public Access enabled. Do not grant public Object access. Use synthetic student data. Do not store AWS credentials in CSV files. Apply the Least Privilege principle. Results After completing this section, we have prepared an Amazon S3 Bucket, created a CSV input file, and uploaded the dataset to AWS.
The registrations.csv Object is ready for Lambda processing.
In the next section, we will configure IAM Execution Role permissions for the required S3 Objects.
Next: Configure IAM Execution Role

title: Set up and configure the FastAPI Backend
content:
Set up and configure the FastAPI Backend In this section, we will prepare the Python environment, install the required dependencies, and start the FastAPI Backend of the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform.
Complete section 5.2 - Prerequisite before proceeding. This workshop uses Windows, PowerShell, and Visual Studio Code as the development environment.
Step 1: Open the project source code Open Visual Studio Code. Select File → Open Folder. Select the project source code directory: C:\Projects\student-activity-platform The main project structure is:
student-activity-platform/ ├── backend/ │ ├── app/ │ │ └── main.py │ └── requirements.txt └── frontend/ backend/: Contains FastAPI source code and business logic components. frontend/: Contains the React/Vite source code. app/main.py: The main Backend entry point. requirements.txt: Contains the required Python dependencies. Step 2: Open the Backend Terminal In Visual Studio Code:
Select Terminal → New Terminal. Use PowerShell. Navigate to the Backend directory: cd C:\Projects\student-activity-platform\backend Verify the Python version:
python --version Step 3: Create a Python Virtual Environment A Python Virtual Environment isolates project dependencies from the system-wide Python environment.
Run the following command:
python -m venv .venv Activate the Virtual Environment:
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 After successful activation, the Terminal will display:
(.venv) PS C:\Projects\student-activity-platform\backend> If the Virtual Environment was already created during the Prerequisite section, simply activate the existing .venv environment.
If PowerShell prevents the activation script from running, use:
Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process -ExecutionPolicy Bypass .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 This Execution Policy setting applies only to the current PowerShell session.
Alternatively, invoke the Virtual Environment’s Python executable directly:
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe --version Step 4: Install Backend dependencies From the backend directory, run:
python -m pip install --upgrade pip python -m pip install -r requirements.txt The dependencies are installed according to the project configuration and include components such as:
FastAPI: REST API development. Uvicorn: ASGI Server for running the Backend. boto3: Connecting to and interacting with AWS services. CSV/XLSX processing libraries. Authentication and data validation libraries. Verify the installed packages:
python -m pip list Step 5: Configure the Demo environment Set the environment variable for the project’s Demo mode:
$env:SAP_DEMO_MODE="1" Verify the environment variable:
$env:SAP_DEMO_MODE Expected output:
1 The Demo version supports local development and testing of the application’s business functions.
SQLite supports local data persistence and application state recovery.
Setting SAP_DEMO_MODE does not automatically migrate all data operations to DynamoDB. AWS integration will be configured and tested separately in section 5.4.
If preparing AWS connectivity for the next section, configure the AWS Profile:
$env:AWS_PROFILE="sap-dev" The profile must already be configured according to section 5.2.
Step 6: Explore the FastAPI Application structure Open:
backend/app/main.py This file initializes the FastAPI Application and connects the Backend components.
When reviewing the source code, pay attention to:
FastAPI Application initialization. API Router registration. CORS configuration for Frontend connectivity. Data initialization and recovery mechanisms. Authentication and Authorization configuration. The system provides API groups for functionality such as:
Authentication. Student Account Management. Activity Management. Registration Import. Check-in / Check-out. Evidence Import. Reconciliation. Participation Confirmation. Analytics and Export. You do not need to recreate main.py when using the existing project source code.
Step 7: Start the FastAPI Backend In the Terminal with the Virtual Environment activated, run:
python -m uvicorn app.main:app --reload Explanation:
app.main: The module containing the FastAPI Application. app: The FastAPI Application object defined in the module. –reload: Automatically reloads the application when source code changes during development. After successful startup, the Terminal should display information similar to:
INFO: Uvicorn running on http://127.0.0.1:8000 INFO: Application startup complete. The Backend is now available at:
http://127.0.0.1:8000 Step 8: Access Swagger UI Open your browser and navigate to:
FastAPI Swagger UI
FastAPI automatically generates Swagger UI documentation based on the APIs defined in the source code.
Swagger UI allows developers to:
Explore available REST APIs. Inspect HTTP Methods and API Endpoints. Review Request Body schemas. Inspect input parameters. Execute API Requests. Verify HTTP Status Codes and Response Bodies. You can also access the ReDoc API documentation at:
http://127.0.0.1:8000/redoc Results After completing this section:
The Python Virtual Environment is ready. Backend dependencies are installed. SAP_DEMO_MODE is configured. The FastAPI Backend can run on port 8000. Swagger UI is available for REST API testing. In the next section, we will test Authentication, Activity Management, and business APIs before integrating Amazon DynamoDB.
Next: Test the Backend and REST APIs

title: Set up and run the React/Vite Frontend
content:
Set Up and Run the React/Vite Frontend In this section, we will prepare the Frontend environment, install Node.js dependencies, and run the Web Application interface of the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform.
Complete section 5.2 - Prerequisite and section 5.3 - Backend Development before proceeding.
1. Open the project source code Open Visual Studio Code. Select File → Open Folder. Open the project directory: C:\Projects\student-activity-platform Main Frontend structure:
student-activity-platform/ ├── backend/ └── frontend/ ├── src/ │ ├── services/ │ │ └── api.js │ └── ... ├── package.json └── ... Important components:
src/: Contains the React application source code. src/services/: Contains Backend communication components. src/services/api.js: Manages application API requests. package.json: Defines dependencies and application scripts. Vite configuration: Manages development and build settings. Other directories follow the current project implementation.
2. Verify Node.js and npm Open the Terminal in Visual Studio Code.
Run:
node --version npm --version Verify the installed Node.js and npm versions.
Use a Node.js version compatible with the project’s package.json and Vite configuration.
If Node.js is not installed, visit:
Node.js Downloads
3. Navigate to the Frontend directory In PowerShell, run:
cd C:\Projects\student-activity-platform\frontend Inspect the directory:
Get-ChildItem Ensure that the current directory contains package.json.
4. Install dependencies Run:
npm install npm reads package.json and installs the required dependencies into the node_modules directory.
If the repository contains package-lock.json and reproducible installation is required, you can use:
npm ci The dependencies support functionality such as:
React interface development. Navigation between pages. HTTP requests to the Backend. Data and Dashboard visualization. Forms and user interactions. Review package.json for the exact dependencies used by the project.
You do not need to create a new React/Vite project using npm create vite when working with the existing project source code.
5. Resolve PowerShell npm execution errors On Windows, PowerShell may display the following error:
npm.ps1 cannot be loaded because running scripts is disabled on this system. You can use npm.cmd instead of npm:
npm.cmd install npm.cmd run dev Alternatively, use Command Prompt in Visual Studio Code.
If permitted by your computer’s security policy, configure the Execution Policy for the current PowerShell session:
Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process -ExecutionPolicy Bypass Then run the npm command again.
6. Start the FastAPI Backend Before starting the Frontend, ensure that the Backend is running.
Open a separate Terminal:
cd C:\Projects\student-activity-platform\backend .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 $env:SAP_DEMO_MODE="1" python -m uvicorn app.main:app --reload Verify the Backend:
http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs
Keep the Backend Terminal running during Frontend testing.
For DynamoDB integration tests, use the AWS configuration prepared in section 5.4.
7. Start the React/Vite Frontend Return to the Frontend Terminal.
Run:
npm run dev After successful startup, the Terminal should display an address similar to:
VITE ready Local: http://localhost:5173/ Open your browser:
http://localhost:5173
If port 5173 is unavailable, use the actual address displayed in the Terminal.
8. Verify the login interface After opening the Frontend, verify that:
The login page is displayed. Interface components are functional. No critical JavaScript errors occur. Login input fields are available. The Frontend can communicate with the Backend. Press F12 to open Developer Tools and inspect the Console and Network tabs.
9. Verify the Frontend build Open another Terminal in the frontend directory:
npm run build After a successful build, Vite generates the following directory:
frontend/dist/ The dist directory contains the built HTML, CSS, and JavaScript resources required for deployment.
Results After completing this section:
Frontend dependencies are installed. FastAPI is available on port 8000. The React/Vite Frontend runs locally. The login interface is accessible. The Frontend can be built for deployment. In the next section, we will explore how the Frontend communicates with Backend REST APIs and configure the application’s API Endpoint.
Next: Connect the Frontend to FastAPI REST APIs

title: AWS Cloud & AI Day Vietnam 2026 – Watch Party
content:
Event Report: AWS Cloud & AI Day Vietnam 2026 – Watch Party Event Objectives Stay informed about recent trends in Cloud Computing and Artificial Intelligence. Explore how AWS helps organizations apply Cloud and AI technologies to real-world challenges. Learn about developments in Generative AI and Agentic AI. Explore approaches for building, deploying, and modernizing applications on AWS. Understand the roles of Data Science, Data Engineering, and Cloud Computing in modern systems. Connect with the technology community and AWS enthusiasts in Southern Vietnam. Apply relevant lessons to my internship project. Speakers Dr. Werner Vogels – Chief Technology Officer (CTO), Amazon.com. Eric Yeo – Country General Manager, Malaysia, Vietnam & Indochina, Amazon Web Services. Other speakers from AWS and technology organizations. Event Highlights Cloud Computing and Artificial Intelligence Trends Cloud Computing and AI are increasingly interconnected in modern application development. AWS provides services for Compute, Storage, Databases, Networking, and AI development. Cloud platforms support scalable and flexible AI deployments while providing tools for cost management. AI is moving beyond experimental models toward integration with real business workflows. Cloud architecture choices should reflect business requirements, data characteristics, and user needs. Agentic AI I explored Agentic AI as an approach to designing AI systems capable of executing multiple steps toward specific goals. AI agents can use tools, APIs, data, and other services to perform more complex tasks. Compared with question-answering alone, Agentic AI emphasizes reasoning, planning, and action. This approach may benefit data management, process automation, and decision-support systems. The session encouraged me to consider future integration between AI, Web applications, and cloud services. Builders x AI The Builders x AI theme focused on developing AI solutions that can be put into practical use. I learned about combining AI with Cloud services to build applications that can be deployed and scaled. An AI product involves more than its model: data, infrastructure, APIs, security, and operations are also essential. The presentations illustrated considerations for taking a technological idea from experimentation toward a more complete product. I recognized that understanding the problem and designing the appropriate system are as important as choosing AI technologies. Data and Analytics Reliable data foundations are essential for analytics and AI applications. Data must be collected, stored, standardized, and processed before it can be used effectively for Analytics or Machine Learning. I gained a clearer understanding of the relationship between Data Science, Data Engineering, Cloud Computing, and AI. Data quality directly affects the accuracy of analytical results. Bringing information from multiple sources into a consistent workflow can reduce manual processing and improve analysis. These lessons relate closely to my student activity management project, where information originates from the University Portal, attendance records, and Google Forms/Google Sheets before reconciliation and analysis.
Application Modernization on AWS AWS provides tools and services that help organizations modernize existing applications. Virtual Machines, Containers, and Serverless deployment models each have different benefits and trade-offs. Serverless architecture can reduce server management effort and scale based on demand. Multiple AWS services can be combined to support practical applications. A system does not have to be migrated to the Cloud all at once; components can be developed, tested, and integrated incrementally. Knowledge and Skills Gained Thinking About Cloud and AI Cloud is more than infrastructure: it can provide a foundation for building, deploying, and operating a complete system. AI requires a broader ecosystem: a machine learning model is only one component of a larger solution. Real-world applications require attention to data, Compute, Storage, Database, APIs, Security, and Deployment. Combining Cloud, Data, and AI creates opportunities for valuable products. Technology choices should follow actual requirements rather than introducing unnecessary architectural complexity. Technical Architecture I strengthened my understanding of Compute, Storage, Database, and REST API responsibilities. I learned about the benefits of Serverless Architecture for event-based or intermittent processing workloads. Frontend, Backend, Database, and Cloud services can play different roles within one application. Security, Access Control, and Monitoring are important parts of system design. A good architecture balances functionality, scalability, cost, and maintainability. Data Science and Data Engineering Effective analytics depends on data collection, cleaning, and processing, not just final visualizations. I developed a better understanding of the data lifecycle, from raw sources to storage, processing, and visualization. Data Pipelines help process information from multiple sources. Analytical metrics are meaningful only when they use accurate data and consistent business rules. The event reinforced my interest in Cloud Computing, Data Engineering, and Cloud & Data Engineering. Applying These Lessons to My Internship Project The event’s lessons connect directly to Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform, the project I developed during my First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) internship learning program.
The project aims to centralize student activity data, reconcile participation records, and provide useful analytics for activity management.
Application Architecture Use React/Vite to develop the Web application interface. Use Python/FastAPI to implement the Backend and REST APIs. Separate Frontend, Backend, Database, and AWS service responsibilities. Implement Authentication and Authorization for two roles: ADMIN and STUDENT. Develop and test the application iteratively, adapting its architecture to project progress. Data Collection and Processing I applied Data Engineering principles to the following workflow:
Import student registration records exported from the University Portal. Record Check-in/Check-out events in real time. Import participation evidence exported from Google Forms or Google Sheets. Standardize student IDs (MSSV) and validate input data. Reconcile Registration, Attendance, and Evidence records. Support ADMIN review and confirmation of participation. Aggregate data for the Analytics Dashboard and report exports. This process helps reduce reliance on manually consolidating multiple Excel files.
AWS Service Integration The event’s Cloud Architecture concepts informed my research and practical experiments with AWS services.
AWS Service Application in the Project AWS Amplify Deploy the React/Vite Frontend Amazon DynamoDB Explore and test Cloud storage of business data Amazon S3 Store sample input CSV files and processed JSON results AWS Lambda Develop and test a Serverless CSV processor AWS IAM Manage resource access and Lambda execution permissions Amazon CloudWatch Review Lambda execution logs, results, and duration The Frontend was deployed using AWS Amplify Hosting. For the demonstration, the FastAPI Backend primarily ran locally and was exposed temporarily through Cloudflare Quick Tunnel.
SQLite provided local Demo persistence, while DynamoDB was used in a separate Cloud practice environment. This does not mean that the complete production Backend and database were migrated to AWS.
Serverless Data Processing A practical application of the Serverless concepts was an independent CSV processing experiment using Amazon S3 and AWS Lambda.
The workflow included:
Reading a sample CSV file from Amazon S3. Validating required data fields. Detecting duplicate records. Identifying invalid records. Summarizing processing results. Writing JSON output back to Amazon S3. Monitoring execution through Amazon CloudWatch. This Serverless CSV Processing experiment was implemented and tested independently from the main Web application’s import functions. It provided a concrete example of Cloud Computing and Data Engineering concepts in practice.
Analytics Dashboard Development The Data and Analytics sessions strengthened my interest in building a management dashboard based on consistent data.
Relevant analytical indicators include:
Total number of activities. Total number of registrations. Check-in and Check-out counts. Number of students with confirmed participation. Activity participation rates. Attendance records with missing information. Missing participation evidence. Students’ activity participation histories. The current Dashboard is implemented within the React/Vite and FastAPI application. In future work, I could explore AWS Glue, Amazon Athena, and Amazon QuickSight to analyze larger volumes of historical data.
Future AI Applications The Generative AI and Agentic AI topics inspired possible future enhancements:
Analyze trends in student activity participation. Recommend activities based on student interests or participation history. Identify potentially anomalous data records. Build an AI assistant for activity information queries. Generate summary reports with AI support. These remain future research directions and are not AI features implemented in the current Demo.
My Experience at the Event Attending AWS Cloud & AI Day Vietnam 2026 – Watch Party was a meaningful part of my internship learning experience. It expanded my perspective on Cloud Computing and AI and showed how AWS concepts could relate to practical engineering projects.
Learning from Experienced Speakers I had the opportunity to follow keynotes and presentations from experienced Cloud and AI professionals. Dr. Werner Vogels, CTO of Amazon.com, was among the prominent speakers featured in the program. I was also interested in Eric Yeo’s insights into AWS and the development of Cloud technology. The presentations broadened my view of modern application development and practical AI adoption. Exploring Cloud and AI Concepts I learned about Agentic AI, Cloud Computing, Data & Analytics, and Modern Applications. I gained a clearer view of how AI technologies are moving toward real use cases. I recognized that complete solutions combine data, infrastructure, Backend services, APIs, and user interfaces. I related the event’s lessons to Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform. The experience encouraged me to continue studying AWS and improving the project’s architecture. Networking and Knowledge Exchange The Watch Party brought together people interested in AWS, Cloud Computing, and AI. I observed how technology communities exchange knowledge, share experiences, and discuss emerging trends. I realized that professional learning also benefits from participation in the wider community, beyond documentation and exercises. This experience motivated me to continue developing my technical skills and career direction. Major Lessons Cloud, Data, and AI are closely connected in modern technology products. A real application must be considered as a complete system rather than a single algorithm or service. AWS knowledge needs to be combined with problem analysis and architectural thinking. High-quality data is fundamental to both Analytics and AI. Security, IAM, Monitoring, and Cost Management are necessary considerations in Cloud deployments. As a Data Science student, I want to strengthen my Cloud Computing and Data Engineering skills to build practical data systems. The event provided useful directions for further development of Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform. Photos from the Event The following photographs document my attendance at AWS Cloud & AI Day Vietnam 2026 – Watch Party.
Conclusion Overall, AWS Cloud & AI Day Vietnam 2026 – Watch Party helped me explore developments in Cloud Computing and Artificial Intelligence while better understanding the role of data, system architecture, and AWS services in practical applications.
The event provided opportunities to connect my Data Science knowledge with Cloud Computing and Data Engineering and apply these ideas to Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform.
It was also an important experience that strengthened my technical thinking and clarified my interest in a future career in Cloud & Data Engineering after completing the First Cloud AI Journey internship program.

title: Blog 1 - What Happens If I Remove Each AWS Service?
content:
I TRIED “REMOVING” EACH AWS SERVICE FROM MY STUDENT ACTIVITY PLATFORM – WHERE WOULD THE SYSTEM BREAK? Understanding AWS Through a Practical Project 1. A Question While Learning AWS When I first started learning AWS, I usually studied each service individually:
Amazon S3 provides data storage. Amazon DynamoDB is a NoSQL database. AWS Lambda runs code without requiring direct server management. AWS IAM manages access permissions. Amazon CloudWatch monitors system resources. AWS Amplify supports Web Application deployment. However, memorizing the definition of each service was not enough to understand how these services work together in a complete system.
While developing the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform during my internship at First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ), I asked myself:
What would happen if I removed each AWS service from my system architecture?
Would the entire application stop working, or would only specific features be affected?
This question became a useful way to understand the responsibilities and dependencies of AWS services instead of simply memorizing their definitions.
2. The Real-world Problem Behind the Project My project focuses on managing and analyzing student participation in university activities.
For a large technology event such as IT Day, organizers need to manage:
Student registration lists from the University Portal. Check-in and Check-out records. Participation evidence from Google Forms or Google Sheets. Reconciliation and participation confirmation results. Post-event statistical reports. When an activity involves more than 1,000 registered students, manually comparing student IDs across multiple Excel files can become time-consuming.
Therefore, I developed a Web Application to centralize these processes.
3. System Architecture The current version of the project uses:
React/Vite for Frontend development. Python/FastAPI for Backend development. SQLite for persistence and recovery in the Demo environment. Amazon DynamoDB for cloud-based business data storage integration and testing. Cloudflare Quick Tunnel to connect the Frontend with the locally running Backend. The project also integrates and experiments with six AWS services:
AWS Amplify. Amazon DynamoDB. Amazon S3. AWS Lambda. AWS IAM. Amazon CloudWatch. The architecture consists of three main components.
Web Application
ADMIN and STUDENT users access the React/Vite interface hosted on AWS Amplify.
The browser sends REST API requests through Cloudflare Quick Tunnel to the FastAPI Backend.
Cloud Data Storage
FastAPI uses SQLite for local persistence while integrating Amazon DynamoDB through the AWS SDK for Python (boto3).
The business data groups integrated or tested with DynamoDB include Activities, Registrations, Attendance, Evidence, and Participation.
Serverless CSV Processing Demo
Amazon S3 stores input CSV files. AWS Lambda reads, validates, and processes the data before writing JSON results back to Amazon S3.
AWS IAM provides execution permissions, while Amazon CloudWatch records Lambda logs and execution information.
4. Removing AWS Amplify: Can Students Still Access the Website? AWS Amplify Hosting is used to deploy the React/Vite Frontend.
When users visit the Website, their browsers load HTML, CSS, and JavaScript resources from the hosting environment.
After loading the interface, the browser sends API requests to the Backend.
If AWS Amplify were removed from the current architecture:
The hosted Website would become unavailable at its current deployment URL. ADMIN and STUDENT users could no longer access the interface through that URL. The FastAPI Backend could continue running. SQLite and DynamoDB resources could still exist. The Lambda CSV Processor could continue operating independently. AWS Amplify provides Frontend deployment and delivery rather than processing the application’s entire business logic.
The Frontend could still be run locally for development and testing.
Lesson learned: Frontend Hosting and Backend Processing are separate responsibilities. A system may lose its public interface while its Backend and data remain available.
5. Removing Amazon DynamoDB: What Happens to Student Data? Amazon DynamoDB is a managed NoSQL database service provided by AWS.
In my project, I integrated and tested the following data groups:
Activities. Registrations. Attendance. Evidence. Participation. These data groups support activity management, attendance tracking, and participation confirmation.
For example, when organizers record a student’s participation, the information is associated with the corresponding student ID and activity.
Student ID: 0818XXXXXX Activity ID: ACT-DEMO-001 Check-in: Recorded Check-out: Recorded If DynamoDB were removed or became inaccessible to the application:
AWS-based read and write operations would fail. Cloud persistence integrations would be interrupted. The application would no longer be able to retrieve cloud records without the required connectivity or permissions. Synchronization between local and AWS environments could be affected. However, because the current Demo version still includes SQLite, local functionality could continue depending on Backend persistence and error-handling behavior.
Removing DynamoDB does not necessarily cause the entire application to stop working.
Lesson learned: A system must clearly define its primary data source, supplementary persistence mechanisms, and failure-handling behavior.
6. Removing Amazon S3: Does Lambda Still Have Data to Process? Amazon S3 is an object storage service used to store data files.
In the Serverless CSV Processing Demo, S3 has two main responsibilities:
Store input CSV files. Store processed JSON results. Consider the following sample registration file:
student_id,full_name 0818000001,Student A 0818000002,Student B 0818000001,Student A ,Student C The file contains four records, including a duplicate record and a record with a missing student ID.
AWS Lambda reads the file, validates each record, and generates a processing result.
If the input S3 storage were removed:
Lambda would no longer have the required CSV input. The object retrieval operation could fail. If the output S3 storage were removed:
Lambda might still read and process the input. However, the result could not be stored in its intended location. This would not necessarily interrupt Registration Import in the Web Application because that feature is handled separately by FastAPI.
Lesson learned: Amazon S3 is more than a file storage service. In Data Pipelines, it can serve as both the input data source and the output destination.
7. Removing AWS Lambda: Who Processes the CSV Data? AWS Lambda allows developers to execute code without directly managing servers.
In my project, Lambda is used to demonstrate a Serverless CSV Processing workflow.
Its responsibilities include:
Read CSV files from Amazon S3. Validate required fields. Detect duplicate records. Detect invalid records. Summarize processing results. Write JSON output back to S3. One CSV Processor test produced the following results:
Metric Result Total Records 4 Valid Records 2 Duplicate Records 1 Invalid Records 1 If AWS Lambda were removed:
The input CSV could remain available in Amazon S3. The file could still be downloaded. However, the Serverless CSV Processing Demo would no longer have a compute component to generate new JSON results. Lambda is not the primary Backend of the current project.
Activity Management, Authentication, Attendance, Reconciliation, and Analytics are handled by FastAPI.
Lesson learned: AWS Lambda provides compute capabilities for independent tasks, particularly data processing workflows that run on demand.
8. Removing AWS IAM: Resources Without Permissions During my AWS studies, I learned that creating a resource does not automatically allow an application to access it.
