AWS IAM manages permissions and access to AWS resources.
For example, the Lambda CSV Processor requires appropriate permissions to:
Read CSV files from S3. Write JSON results to S3. Send execution logs to CloudWatch. If Lambda does not have permission to read an S3 object, the operation may return:
AccessDenied If Lambda can read the input but cannot write the output, the processing result cannot be saved as intended.
Without the necessary logging permissions, troubleshooting information may also become unavailable.
Removing required IAM permissions can therefore interrupt AWS workflows even when all the resources still exist.
IAM permissions should follow the Least Privilege principle, granting only the access required for each component’s responsibilities.
Lesson learned: Cloud Security is not limited to protecting login credentials. It also means controlling which applications can perform specific actions on specific resources.
9. Removing Amazon CloudWatch: Would the System Still Run? Amazon CloudWatch is used to monitor Lambda execution logs and metrics.
When the CSV Processor runs, CloudWatch helps me inspect:
Whether Lambda was invoked. Whether errors occurred. Execution duration. Information recorded in execution logs. Data processing results. Without CloudWatch Logs:
Lambda could still execute if its other requirements and permissions were satisfied. CSV files could still be processed. JSON results could still be written to S3. However, identifying the causes of failures would become more difficult. For example, if Lambda fails to generate a JSON file, logs can help determine whether the cause is a missing input file, invalid data, or incorrect IAM permissions.
Lesson learned: Monitoring does not necessarily produce business results directly, but it provides visibility into system behavior and supports troubleshooting.
10. Summary: Where Would the System Break? AWS Service Responsibility Impact If Removed AWS Amplify Frontend Hosting Website unavailable at the current hosting URL Amazon DynamoDB Cloud Database DynamoDB read/write workflows interrupted Amazon S3 Object Storage Missing input files or unavailable output storage AWS Lambda Serverless Compute CSV Processing Demo cannot execute AWS IAM Access Control Required resource access may be denied Amazon CloudWatch Monitoring Reduced visibility into execution and errors Not every AWS service has the same impact on the overall system.
Some services directly support user-facing functionality, some manage data, and others provide security or monitoring.
This highlights the importance of assigning clear responsibilities to each architectural component.
11. A Learning Exercise for AWS Beginners When studying an AWS architecture, I found it useful to ask four questions:
Where does this service receive its input? What responsibility does it perform? Where does its output go? What happens if it becomes unavailable? For AWS Lambda in my project:
Input: CSV file stored in Amazon S3. Processing: Validate and classify records. Output: JSON file stored in Amazon S3. Failure: New processing results cannot be generated when Lambda does not execute. This approach helps me understand architectures through data flow and service dependencies.
12. Conclusion By analyzing the six AWS services in my Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform, I learned that building a Cloud system is not about combining as many services as possible.
The important considerations are:
Selecting the appropriate service for each responsibility. Understanding data flows. Identifying component dependencies. Applying appropriate access permissions. Monitoring and troubleshooting failures. Considering scalability and operational costs. The process of hypothetically removing individual services helped me understand AWS architectures from a more practical perspective.
Instead of simply memorizing what Amazon S3 or AWS Lambda does, I can now understand why each service is needed and how the system behaves without it.
This provides a valuable foundation for my future development in Cloud Computing and Cloud & Data Engineering.
Note: The service-removal scenarios in this article are hypothetical architecture analyses, not actual deletion of active AWS resources. The architecture and technical content have been updated to reflect the current project scope.
13. References AWS Amplify Hosting Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide Amazon S3 User Guide AWS Lambda Developer Guide AWS IAM User Guide Amazon CloudWatch User Guide AWS Well-Architected Framework 📌 Community Sharing: This technical article has been published in the AWS Study Group VN Facebook community to share practical insights and encourage discussions about AWS Cloud Architecture.

title: Worklog
content:
Worklog Throughout the internship program at First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ), I followed a structured learning, research, and project development plan over 12 weeks, from September 7, 2026, to November 27, 2026.
The internship began with learning the fundamentals of Cloud Computing and AWS, becoming familiar with core AWS services, analyzing project requirements, and designing the system architecture. The subsequent stages focused on Backend development, Frontend development, database implementation, data processing, AWS service integration, system testing, Demo application deployment, and technical documentation.
The main project developed during the internship was:
Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform
The system was designed to support the management, tracking, reconciliation, and analysis of student participation data in university activities. The project focuses on addressing challenges related to consolidating student registration data, attendance records, participation evidence, and activity participation confirmation.
The application was developed using React/Vite for the Frontend, Python/FastAPI for the Backend, and SQLite as the database for the MVP version. The system supports two main user roles, ADMIN and STUDENT, with features for activity management, student account management, registration data import, real-time Check-in/Check-out, evidence import, data reconciliation, participation confirmation, data analytics, and report export.
Throughout the project, I gradually researched, experimented with, and integrated six AWS services within a scope appropriate to the system:
AWS Amplify: Deploying and hosting the Frontend of the Web Application. Amazon DynamoDB: Researching and testing a NoSQL database within the AWS Data Pilot. Amazon S3: Storing data, CSV files, and data processing results. AWS IAM: Managing access permissions and execution permissions for AWS resources. AWS Lambda: Developing a CSV file processing workflow as a Serverless Demo. Amazon CloudWatch: Monitoring execution logs, processing results, and Lambda metrics. In addition to application development, I also studied REST APIs, Authentication, Authorization, Data Processing, Data Analytics, Serverless Architecture, Git/GitHub, software testing, data security, AWS cost management, and application deployment in Cloud environments.
Weekly Work Summary Week 1: Getting familiar with the internship environment, Cloud Computing, AWS Fundamentals, AWS CLI, and Amazon EC2
Week 2: Analyzing the problem, defining requirements, developing the Project Proposal, and designing the system architecture
Week 3: Developing the Backend using Python/FastAPI, SQLite, and core business REST APIs
Week 4: Researching Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon S3, and developing the AWS Data Pilot
Week 5: Developing the Frontend with React/Vite, Authentication, Authorization, and ADMIN/STUDENT role-based access control
Week 6: Implementing Registration Import, Evidence Import, CSV/XLSX processing, and data Export
Week 7: Developing Reconciliation, Participation Status, and the Analytics Dashboard
Week 8: Performing system integration testing, fixing bugs, completing system features, and optimizing the user interface
Week 9: Preparing and deploying the Frontend on AWS Amplify, and connecting the FastAPI Demo through Cloudflare Tunnel
Week 10: Integrating Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, AWS IAM, and Amazon CloudWatch, and consolidating evidence for six AWS services
Week 11: Preparing and presenting the project Demo, collecting Feedback, completing technical documentation, and preparing for project handover
Week 12: Finalizing the internship report, reviewing the Hugo website, archiving the project, reviewing AWS resources, and preparing for project handover
Internship Summary After 12 weeks of internship, my goal is to consolidate and finalize the outcomes achieved throughout the learning, research, and project development process, including:
Develop a solid understanding of Cloud Computing fundamentals, AWS Global Infrastructure, and core AWS services. Understand the process of requirements analysis, system architecture design, and development of a Web-based data management system. Develop the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform using React/Vite, Python/FastAPI, and SQLite. Implement features for activity management, student account management, authentication, authorization, data import, real-time attendance tracking, and participation reconciliation. Gain experience in CSV/XLSX data processing, data aggregation, Analytics Dashboard development, and report export. Research, experiment with, and integrate six AWS services, including AWS Amplify, Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon S3, AWS IAM, AWS Lambda, and Amazon CloudWatch. Understand the differences between traditional Web Application architecture, NoSQL databases, and Serverless data processing models. Improve REST API testing, system integration testing, Debugging, and Troubleshooting skills throughout the software development process. Gain experience in deploying the Frontend to AWS Amplify Hosting and connecting it to the Backend Demo through Cloudflare Tunnel. Improve Git/GitHub usage, source code management, technical documentation, and project presentation skills. Understand the importance of data security, access management, and cost control when working with AWS resources. Finalize the Project Proposal, Architecture Diagram, API Documentation, User Guide, Test Report, Demo Script, and internship report. Summarize the limitations of the MVP version and identify potential directions for future development. Through the internship program at First Cloud AI Journey, I have not only strengthened my academic foundation in Data Science but also expanded my knowledge and practical skills in Cloud Computing, application development, system design, and data processing on AWS.
This internship provides an important foundation for my future career development in Cloud Computing, Data Engineering, and Cloud & Data Engineering.
Note: This Worklog follows the planned 12-week internship schedule. The final outcomes should be updated based on actual project progress, completed documentation, and available supporting evidence at the end of the internship program.

title: Build the Analytics Dashboard
content:
Build the Analytics Dashboard In this section, we will explore analytics visualization using the React/Vite Frontend of the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform.
The Analytics Dashboard helps ADMIN users monitor activities, registrations, attendance, and confirmed participation results.
Dashboard data is aggregated by the FastAPI Backend and delivered through REST APIs.
1. Understand the Dashboard architecture ADMIN | v React / Vite Dashboard | v API Service | | REST API + Access Token v FastAPI Analytics Processing | v Business Data Storage | +-- Activities +-- Registrations +-- Attendance +-- Evidence +-- Participation Processing workflow:
ADMIN opens the Analytics Dashboard. The Frontend requests analytical data. The Backend validates authentication and authorization. The Backend retrieves records within the requested scope. The Backend aggregates and returns results. The Frontend displays indicators, charts, or statistical tables. The Frontend does not connect directly to DynamoDB using AWS credentials.
2. Start the Backend and Frontend Backend Terminal:
cd C:\Projects\student-activity-platform\backend .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 $env:SAP_DEMO_MODE="1" python -m uvicorn app.main:app --reload Frontend Terminal:
cd C:\Projects\student-activity-platform\frontend npm run dev Open:
http://localhost:5173
Do not start additional instances if both services are already running.
3. Open the Analytics Dashboard Sign in using an ADMIN Demo account. Open the Home page or administration menu. Navigate to Analytics or Dashboard. Inspect the available statistical components. Dashboard components may include:
Summary Cards. Activity Statistics. Attendance Overview. Participation Results. Detailed Data Tables. Inspect the current interface to identify which components are implemented.
4. Display summary indicators Summary Cards help users quickly understand important metrics.
Using the sample dataset from section 5.8.1:
Total Registrations: 4 Total Check-in: 3 Complete Attendance: 2 Confirmed Participants: 1 Indicators should be retrieved from the Backend or calculated from API data using consistent business definitions.
Avoid hardcoded statistics in the actual Dashboard.
Illustrative React Component:
function MetricCard({ title, value }) { return ( <div className="metric-card"> <h3>{title}</h3> <strong>{value}</strong> </div> ); } export default MetricCard; The Component receives data through props and can be reused for different metrics.
Example:
function AnalyticsSummary({ metrics }) { return ( <div className="analytics-summary"> <MetricCard title="Total Registrations" value={metrics.total_registrations} /> <MetricCard title="Total Check-in" value={metrics.total_check_in} /> <MetricCard title="Confirmed Participants" value={metrics.confirmed_participants} /> </div> ); } These examples illustrate Component organization. Metric field names must match the actual Backend response.
Preserve existing Dashboard Components when the application already works.
5. Connect the Dashboard to REST APIs Open:
frontend/src/services/api.js Locate the functions responsible for Analytics or activity statistics requests.
Verify:
API_BASE_URL points to the correct Backend. Requests include the appropriate Activity ID or supported parameters. Access Tokens are provided for protected APIs. Responses are processed and passed to Dashboard Components. Connection errors are handled appropriately. Local Backend address:
http://127.0.0.1:8000 When the Frontend is deployed on AWS Amplify, the Backend address is configured using the HTTPS Endpoint provided by Cloudflare Quick Tunnel.
Deployment will be covered in section 5.9.
6. Inspect Analytics API requests Press F12 to open Developer Tools.
Select Network. Select Fetch/XHR. Open the Analytics Dashboard. Identify the statistics request. Inspect its Request URL and HTTP Status Code. Review the Response Body. Compare API response values with the displayed indicators.
If the Dashboard shows four registrations, verify that the API response contains the corresponding data within the same activity scope.
7. Display activity statistics Dashboard functionality may include activity-level statistics.
Illustrative data:
Activity Registrations Check-in Confirmed AWS Workshop 100 85 75 TechConnect 150 130 110 IT Day Demo 200 180 160 These are synthetic visualization examples, not actual event results.
Possible visualization methods include:
Bar Charts for activity comparisons. Summary Tables for detailed records. Percentage Indicators for participation rates. Use the visualization library or Components already available in the project.
If a corresponding chart is unavailable, treat it as a potential extension rather than an implemented feature.
8. Display Participation results Participation results may be grouped into:
CONFIRMED. REJECTED. Records awaiting a final decision. Example:
CONFIRMED: 1 REJECTED: 1 Awaiting decision: 2 Use tables, summary indicators, or distribution charts according to the current interface.
“Awaiting decision” is a descriptive grouping, not a newly defined Backend status.
9. Test data filtering If filtering is available:
Open Analytics. Select an activity. Verify updated indicators. Select another activity. Inspect the new results. Clear filters or return to the overview if supported. Possible filters include:
Activity. Scheduled time. Activity status. Participation result. Only test filters supported by the current Frontend and Backend implementation.
10. Handle data-loading states The Dashboard should handle:
Loading: Waiting for API data. Success: Valid analytics data received. Empty: No records in the selected scope. Error: Request failure or invalid data. Illustrative React Component:
function DashboardContent({ loading, error, metrics }) { if (loading) { return <p>Loading analytics data...</p>; } if (error) { return <p>{error}</p>; } if (!metrics) { return <p>No analytics data available.</p>; } return ( <AnalyticsSummary metrics={metrics} /> ); } This example demonstrates interface state handling rather than a complete Dashboard implementation.
Do not replace failed API results with zero-valued metrics and present them as valid statistics.
11. Verify ADMIN and STUDENT permissions ADMIN users can access administrative analytics within their authorized scope.
STUDENT users can view personal activity participation information through their individual interface.
Verify:
ADMIN can access authorized administrative statistics. STUDENT cannot access other students’ private data. The Backend enforces authorization for protected Analytics APIs. Displayed information remains within the user’s authorized scope. 12. Summarize Dashboard tests Test Case Expected Result Dashboard Loading Data retrieved from Backend Summary Cards Values match API responses Activity Statistics Correct activity scope Participation Statistics CONFIRMED and REJECTED distinguished Activity Filter Correct scope updated when supported Empty Data Appropriate empty state API Error Appropriate error notification ADMIN Authorization Administrative analytics accessible STUDENT Authorization Access restricted to authorized data Conclusion In this section, we explored Analytics Dashboard development using React/Vite and FastAPI REST APIs.
The Dashboard transforms business data into visual information that helps organizers monitor activity results and student engagement.
In the next section, we will export business records as CSV/XLSX reports.
Next: Export CSV/XLSX Reports

title: Configure IAM Execution Role
content:
Configure IAM Execution Role In this section, we will configure AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions so that AWS Lambda can read CSV data from Amazon S3, write JSON results, and send execution logs to Amazon CloudWatch.
IAM manages identities and access to AWS resources.
Instead of storing Access Keys and Secret Access Keys in source code, Lambda uses an IAM Execution Role to obtain temporary credentials during execution.
1. Understand the IAM Execution Role AWS Lambda | | Assume Execution Role v IAM Role | +-- AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole | | | v | CloudWatch Logs | +-- SAP-Lambda-S3-Demo-Access | +--> Read Input CSV | +--> Write Output JSON An Execution Role includes:
Trust Policy: Allows AWS Lambda to assume the Role. Permissions Policy: Defines permitted actions and resources. Required permissions:
Permission Purpose s3:GetObject Read the input CSV s3:PutObject Write the JSON result logs:CreateLogGroup Create Log Groups logs:CreateLogStream Create Log Streams logs:PutLogEvents Write execution logs 2. Open the AWS IAM Console Open the AWS IAM Console. Select Roles. Locate the project’s existing Role: sap-csv-processor-demo-role-9ui2ib5d If the Role already exists, inspect Trust relationships and Permissions.
Do not create another Role unnecessarily.
3. Create an Execution Role if required In IAM, select Roles. Choose Create role. Trusted entity type: AWS service. Use case: Lambda. Choose Next. Attach the AWS managed AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole policy. Choose Next. Enter a Role name. Example:
sap-csv-processor-demo-role Review and choose Create role. A newly created Role name may differ from the automatically generated Role used in the previous project exercise.
4. Inspect the Trust Policy Open the Role and select Trust relationships.
The Lambda Trust Policy uses the following structure:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "lambda.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": "sts:AssumeRole" } ] } Explanation:
Principal: Identifies the trusted service. lambda.amazonaws.com: AWS Lambda Service Principal. sts:AssumeRole: Allows Lambda to assume the Execution Role. The Trust Policy does not itself grant S3 Object permissions.
Those permissions must be defined separately.
5. Create an Amazon S3 access policy In the IAM Console:
Select Policies. Choose Create policy. Switch to the JSON editor. Enter the following Policy. { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "ReadDemoInput", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::sap-data-project-2026-huflit01/lambda-demo/input/registrations.csv" }, { "Sid": "WriteDemoResult", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:PutObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::sap-data-project-2026-huflit01/lambda-demo/processed/registrations-result.json" } ] } Choose Next and enter the Policy name:
SAP-Lambda-S3-Demo-Access Choose Create policy.
This Least Privilege Policy recreates the permissions required for the workshop. If a Policy with the same name already exists, inspect its current permissions before changing it. Avoid duplicates and unintended changes to other applications.
6. Understand the permissions The Policy grants access to two specific S3 Objects.
Read the input file Action: s3:GetObject Resource: arn:aws:s3:::sap-data-project-2026-huflit01/lambda-demo/input/registrations.csv Lambda can read the CSV without receiving delete permissions from this Policy.
Write the processing result Action: s3:PutObject Resource: arn:aws:s3:::sap-data-project-2026-huflit01/lambda-demo/processed/registrations-result.json Lambda can write the JSON result.
The Function does not require s3:ListBucket because the Bucket and Object Keys are known.
Prefix-based wildcard permissions may be considered if multiple input files are required. Expand permissions only when necessary.
7. Attach the Policy to the Execution Role Return to IAM Roles. Select sap-csv-processor-demo-role-9ui2ib5d or the newly created Role. Open Permissions. Choose Add permissions. Choose Attach policies. Search for SAP-Lambda-S3-Demo-Access. Select and attach the Policy. Verify that the Role contains:
AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole. SAP-Lambda-S3-Demo-Access. If S3 uses SSE-KMS rather than SSE-S3, additional KMS permissions may be required according to the Key Policy and Object operations.
This workshop does not require a separate KMS configuration.
8. Verify the Lambda Execution Role If the Function already exists:
Open AWS Lambda Console. Select sap-csv-processor-demo. Select Configuration. Select Permissions. Inspect the Execution role. Ensure that the Function uses the intended Role.
If the Function has not been created, select this Role during section 5.10.3.
9. Understand Least Privilege Least Privilege grants only the permissions necessary for an application to perform its intended task.
For this exercise:
AdministratorAccess is not required. AmazonS3FullAccess is not required. S3 delete permissions are not required. DynamoDB access is not required. Hardcoded AWS Access Keys are not required. Lambda uses its Execution Role to allow boto3 to access AWS resources within its assigned permissions.
10. Troubleshoot access errors Error What to Check AccessDenied reading CSV s3:GetObject and Input ARN AccessDenied writing JSON s3:PutObject and Output ARN Missing CloudWatch Logs CloudWatch Logs permissions Lambda cannot assume Role Trust Policy and Role configuration Policy not found Policy name and AWS Account Permissions still denied Bucket Policy, Permissions Boundary, or SCP Do not resolve AccessDenied errors by granting unnecessary AdministratorAccess.
Results After completing this section, we have configured an IAM Execution Role and Least Privilege S3 permissions for AWS Lambda.
The Function can read registrations.csv, write registrations-result.json, and send execution logs to CloudWatch within its assigned permissions.
Next: Build the AWS Lambda CSV Processor

title: Connect the Backend to Amazon DynamoDB
content:
Connect the Backend to Amazon DynamoDB In this section, we will configure the AWS SDK for Python (boto3) so that the FastAPI Backend can connect to and interact with Amazon DynamoDB.
1. Open the Backend in Visual Studio Code Open the project source code directory:
C:\Projects\student-activity-platform Open PowerShell and navigate to the Backend directory:
cd C:\Projects\student-activity-platform\backend Activate the Python Virtual Environment:
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 If PowerShell blocks script execution:
Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process -ExecutionPolicy Bypass .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 2. Install and verify boto3 boto3 is the AWS SDK for Python. It allows Python applications to interact with AWS services through APIs.
Install boto3:
python -m pip install boto3 Verify the installation:
python -c "import boto3; print(boto3.__version__)" If boto3 has already been installed through requirements.txt, installation is not required again.
3. Configure the AWS Profile The project uses the following AWS Profile:
sap-dev List available profiles:
aws configure list-profiles If sap-dev does not exist, configure the profile according to section 5.2 - Prerequisite.
Set the environment variables:
$env:AWS_PROFILE="sap-dev" $env:AWS_REGION="ap-southeast-1" $env:AWS_DEFAULT_REGION="ap-southeast-1" Verify the AWS Identity:
aws sts get-caller-identity --profile sap-dev Check the configured Region:
aws configure get region --profile sap-dev AWS operations in this section use the Singapore Region.
Do not include AWS Access Keys or Secret Access Keys directly in Backend or Frontend source code. Do not upload credential files to GitHub. Use only authorized accounts and permissions.
4. Understand the DynamoDB connection boto3 supports Sessions and Clients for performing DynamoDB operations.
Illustrative example:
import boto3 session = boto3.Session( profile_name="sap-dev", region_name="ap-southeast-1" ) dynamodb = session.client("dynamodb") response = dynamodb.list_tables() print(response["TableNames"]) Explanation:
boto3.Session: Creates an AWS connection session. profile_name: Uses credentials associated with sap-dev. region_name: Specifies the Region containing the DynamoDB tables. session.client: Initializes the DynamoDB Client. list_tables: Retrieves the table list in the selected Region. The actual project can manage Profile, Region, and table names through environment variables and configuration modules.
Do not replace the entire Backend configuration with the illustrative code above.
5. Prepare DynamoDB permissions for the Backend The Backend requires appropriate permissions to read and write business data.
Common operations include:
dynamodb:DescribeTable. dynamodb:GetItem. dynamodb:PutItem. dynamodb:UpdateItem. dynamodb:Query. dynamodb:Scan. Example IAM Policy:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AccessSAPTables", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "dynamodb:DescribeTable", "dynamodb:GetItem", "dynamodb:PutItem", "dynamodb:UpdateItem", "dynamodb:Query", "dynamodb:Scan" ], "Resource": [ "arn:aws:dynamodb:ap-southeast-1:YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID:table/SAP-Activities", "arn:aws:dynamodb:ap-southeast-1:YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID:table/SAP-Registrations", "arn:aws:dynamodb:ap-southeast-1:YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID:table/SAP-Attendance", "arn:aws:dynamodb:ap-southeast-1:YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID:table/SAP-Evidence", "arn:aws:dynamodb:ap-southeast-1:YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID:table/SAP-Participation" ] }, { "Sid": "ListTables", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "dynamodb:ListTables", "Resource": "*" } ] } Replace YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID with your actual AWS Account ID.
This is an example policy for data integration and verification operations in the workshop, not a complete deployment policy.
If the repository uses BatchWriteItem, DeleteItem, or other operations, grant additional permissions only when required by the actual implementation.
Avoid granting access to unrelated DynamoDB tables.
6. Verify resources using the project script The Backend source code includes:
backend/check_aws_resources.py This script verifies AWS connectivity and the status of project resources.
From the backend directory, run:
$env:AWS_PROFILE="sap-dev" $env:AWS_DEFAULT_REGION="ap-southeast-1" .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe .\check_aws_resources.py The script uses boto3 to inspect AWS resources.
Verify the following tables:
SAP-Activities SAP-Registrations SAP-Attendance SAP-Evidence SAP-Participation The expected result is that the tables are accessible and have an ACTIVE status.
check_aws_resources.py is a read-only verification script. It does not create tables, modify items, or delete DynamoDB data. If the script also checks S3, ensure that the Bucket name and access permissions are configured correctly.
7. Understand Backend data access In the project architecture, FastAPI uses repository components and AWS configuration to perform business data storage operations.
Integration flow:
FastAPI Router | v Business Service | v DynamoDB Repository | | boto3 v Amazon DynamoDB Component responsibilities:
Router: Receives REST API requests. Business Service: Validates and processes business operations. Repository: Encapsulates data access operations. boto3: Sends AWS API requests to DynamoDB. DynamoDB: Stores and retrieves business data. This approach separates business logic from Cloud resource access.
8. Start the Backend Configure the Demo environment:
$env:SAP_DEMO_MODE="1" $env:AWS_PROFILE="sap-dev" $env:AWS_REGION="ap-southeast-1" $env:AWS_DEFAULT_REGION="ap-southeast-1" Review the AWS Pilot settings in the current source code before testing data writes.
Start the Backend:
python -m uvicorn app.main:app --reload Open Swagger UI:
http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs
Configuring an AWS Profile and Region only prepares AWS connectivity. Whether business APIs use DynamoDB depends on the repository and AWS Pilot configuration in the current Backend. SAP_DEMO_MODE=1 does not automatically enable every DynamoDB operation.
Results After completing this section:
boto3 is installed. The sap-dev AWS Profile is configured. The Backend has connection settings for the Singapore Region. check_aws_resources.py can inspect AWS resources. DynamoDB tables are ready for integration testing. In the next section, we will test Backend data reading and writing operations with DynamoDB.
Next: Test data reading and writing

title: Connect the Backend using Cloudflare Quick Tunnel
content:
Connect the Backend using Cloudflare Quick Tunnel In this section, we will use Cloudflare Quick Tunnel to provide an HTTPS Endpoint for the local FastAPI Backend.
The objective is to enable the React/Vite Frontend hosted on AWS Amplify to communicate with the local Backend without deploying it to a separate Cloud server.
1. Understand Cloudflare Quick Tunnel Cloudflare Quick Tunnel establishes a connection from the local computer to Cloudflare’s network.
The local application can then be accessed through a temporary HTTPS URL under the trycloudflare.com domain.
Connection workflow:
React / Vite Frontend | | HTTPS REST API v Cloudflare Public Endpoint | v cloudflared Tunnel | v FastAPI Backend 127.0.0.1:8001 Router Port Forwarding is not required for this Demo workflow.
The Quick Tunnel operates while cloudflared remains running and the Backend is available.
Reference:
Cloudflare Quick Tunnels
2. Prepare the Demo dataset Before exposing the Backend over the Internet:
Use synthetic student data. Prepare ADMIN and STUDENT Demo accounts. Use a separate SQLite Demo database. Verify API access permissions. Ensure that no sensitive information or real student data is exposed. The project uses port 8001 for its Demo Backend, separate from development port 8000.
A Quick Tunnel provides an Internet-accessible address. A random Tunnel URL is not an authentication or authorization mechanism. The Backend must still protect Endpoints and validate Access Tokens.
3. Start the FastAPI Demo Backend Open PowerShell in the Backend directory:
cd C:\Projects\student-activity-platform\backend Activate the Virtual Environment:
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 Configure Demo mode:
$env:SAP_DEMO_MODE="1" Verify the current persistence configuration to ensure a separate Demo SQLite database is used.
Start the Backend:
python -m uvicorn app.main:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8001 Expected output:
INFO: Uvicorn running on http://127.0.0.1:8001 INFO: Application startup complete. Keep the Backend Terminal running.
If AWS integration is required, use the AWS Pilot settings verified in section 5.4. Do not enable unnecessary AWS permissions solely for a Frontend demonstration.
4. Verify the local Backend Open:
FastAPI Health Endpoint
Alternatively, run:
Invoke-RestMethod ` -Uri "http://127.0.0.1:8001/health" The Health Endpoint should return a successful response.
The actual JSON structure depends on the Backend version.
Verify Swagger UI:
http://127.0.0.1:8001/docs Proceed only after confirming local Backend availability.
5. Install cloudflared Open the official documentation:
Install cloudflared
Download and install the Windows version.
Windows Package Manager can also be used:
winget install --id Cloudflare.cloudflared Open a new Terminal and verify:
cloudflared --version If cloudflared is not available in PATH, invoke its executable directly.
The project previously used:
C:\Program Files (x86)\cloudflared\cloudflared.exe Verify the executable:
& "C:\Program Files (x86)\cloudflared\cloudflared.exe" --version Installation paths may vary between computers.
6. Create a Cloudflare Quick Tunnel Open a separate PowerShell Terminal.
Keep the Backend Terminal running.
Execute:
& "C:\Program Files (x86)\cloudflared\cloudflared.exe" tunnel --url http://127.0.0.1:8001 If cloudflared is available in PATH:
cloudflared tunnel --url http://127.0.0.1:8001 After connecting successfully, cloudflared displays a temporary address similar to:
https://random-name.trycloudflare.com Copy the generated URL for the next steps.
During the November 9, 2026 deployment test, the project used:
https://replies-cabinet-recipes-prevent.trycloudflare.com This is a historical test URL rather than a permanent deployment Endpoint.
A new Quick Tunnel can generate a different hostname. Update VITE_API_BASE_URL and rebuild the Frontend whenever the API Tunnel address changes.
7. Verify the HTTPS Health Endpoint Assign the new Tunnel URL to a PowerShell variable:
$tunnelUrl = "https://YOUR-TUNNEL.trycloudflare.com" Replace the placeholder with the actual URL.
Run:
Invoke-RestMethod ` -Uri "$tunnelUrl/health" Alternatively, open:
https://YOUR-TUNNEL.trycloudflare.com/health Expected results:
The HTTPS Endpoint is accessible. Cloudflare forwards the request to FastAPI. The Backend returns a successful Health Response. If the local Health Endpoint works but the Tunnel Endpoint fails, inspect the cloudflared process and Backend address.
8. Verify REST API connectivity Backend API paths remain unchanged when using the Tunnel.
Examples:
POST https://YOUR-TUNNEL.trycloudflare.com/auth/login GET https://YOUR-TUNNEL.trycloudflare.com/auth/me Only the API Base URL changes.
Protected APIs still require appropriate Access Tokens.
If Swagger UI is enabled for the Demo, inspect it at:
https://YOUR-TUNNEL.trycloudflare.com/docs Do not expose sensitive API documentation or testing Endpoints in a Production environment.
9. Verify CORS configuration The Frontend and Backend use different origins.
Example:
Frontend: https://main.d2p96elhe5x6se.amplifyapp.com Backend: https://YOUR-TUNNEL.trycloudflare.com FastAPI CORSMiddleware must allow the Amplify Frontend origin.
Do not substitute the Tunnel URL for the Amplify Website origin.
Cloudflare Tunnel provides HTTPS connectivity but does not replace FastAPI’s CORS configuration.
CORS will be verified again after deploying the Frontend.
10. Keep the Demo environment available Maintain two running processes during the Demo:
Terminal 1: FastAPI Backend - port 8001 Terminal 2: Cloudflare Quick Tunnel If the local computer shuts down, enters Sleep mode, or loses Internet connectivity, the Backend may become unavailable.
Stopping cloudflared makes the Quick Tunnel Endpoint unavailable.
The AWS Amplify Frontend may still load, but Backend-dependent operations will fail.
11. Troubleshoot common issues Issue What to Check cloudflared not recognized PATH or executable location Local Health failure FastAPI Backend and port 8001 Cloudflare HTTP 502 Tunnel connectivity to the local Backend Tunnel URL unavailable cloudflared process or changed hostname HTTP 401 Invalid authentication credentials Browser CORS error Allowed Amplify origin Frontend calls localhost VITE_API_BASE_URL and rebuild 12. Results During the November 9, 2026 deployment test, the project successfully:
Started the FastAPI Demo Backend on port 8001. Created a Cloudflare Quick Tunnel using cloudflared. Verified the HTTPS Health Endpoint. Prepared the public HTTPS API URL for AWS Amplify. These results confirm that the Demo Backend can be reached through HTTPS while the Backend and Tunnel are running.
Cloudflare Quick Tunnel is used for temporary testing and demonstrations. It is not a permanent or highly available Production hosting solution.
Next: Deploy the Frontend with AWS Amplify Hosting

title: Connect the Frontend to FastAPI REST APIs
content:
Connect the Frontend to FastAPI REST APIs In this section, we will configure communication between the React/Vite Frontend and FastAPI Backend of the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform.
The Frontend displays the user interface and receives user interactions. The Backend handles authentication, validation, business logic, and database access.
Both components communicate through REST APIs.
1. Understand Frontend and Backend communication User | v React Component | v API Service (api.js) | | HTTP Request v FastAPI Router | v Business Logic / Repository | v SQLite / DynamoDB Integration | v API Response | v React Component | v Updated User Interface For example, when an ADMIN opens the activity list:
The Frontend requests available activities. The Backend verifies access permissions. The Backend retrieves data from the configured storage mechanism. The Backend returns a JSON response. The Frontend updates the activity list. The Frontend does not need to connect directly to DynamoDB using AWS credentials.
2. Verify the Backend and Frontend Ensure that the Backend is running at:
http://127.0.0.1:8000 Ensure that the Frontend is running at:
http://localhost:5173 Use two separate Terminals in Visual Studio Code.
Backend Terminal:
cd C:\Projects\student-activity-platform\backend .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 $env:SAP_DEMO_MODE="1" python -m uvicorn app.main:app --reload Frontend Terminal:
cd C:\Projects\student-activity-platform\frontend npm run dev 3. Inspect the API Service file In Visual Studio Code, open:
frontend/src/services/api.js The api.js file manages API requests from the Frontend to the Backend.
Locate the API_BASE_URL configuration.
The local Backend address used in the project is:
const API_BASE_URL = "http://127.0.0.1:8000"; If the current source code uses environment variables to configure the API address, preserve that mechanism and verify its value.
Do not declare another API_BASE_URL if it already exists.
This code illustrates the local API Base URL. Do not replace the entire api.js file because it also contains business APIs, authentication logic, and error handling.
4. Understand REST API requests The system provides APIs such as:
API Method Purpose /auth/login POST User login /auth/me GET Retrieve current user information /auth/logout POST User logout /admin/students GET Retrieve student accounts /activities/{activity_id}/check-in POST Record Check-in /activities/{activity_id}/check-out POST Record Check-out Other APIs related to Activity Management, Registration, Evidence, Participation, Analytics, and Export should be reviewed using the current Backend’s Swagger UI.
The following example retrieves current user information:
async function getCurrentUser() { const token = localStorage.getItem("sap_access_token"); if (!token) { throw new Error("No access token found"); } const response = await fetch( "http://127.0.0.1:8000/auth/me", { method: "GET", headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}`, }, } ); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error(`API error: ${response.status}`); } return await response.json(); } Explanation:
fetch(): Sends an HTTP request. Authorization: Provides the Access Token for a protected API. response.ok: Checks whether the request was successful. response.json(): Converts the Response into JavaScript data. This example demonstrates REST API communication. Existing project components should continue using the shared API Service rather than introducing duplicated request mechanisms.
5. Understand CORS The local Frontend and Backend operate on different origins:
Frontend: http://localhost:5173 Backend: http://127.0.0.1:8000 Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) allows the Backend to specify which origins can access its APIs through a browser.
Open:
backend/app/main.py Review the CORSMiddleware configuration.
Illustrative example:
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware app.add_middleware( CORSMiddleware, allow_origins=[ "http://localhost:5173", "http://127.0.0.1:5173", ], allow_credentials=True, allow_methods=["*"], allow_headers=["*"], ) Use this example only if it matches the current application configuration.
If CORSMiddleware is already configured, do not add a duplicate middleware.
When deploying the Frontend using AWS Amplify, add the actual HTTPS Website origin to the allowed origins.
CORS does not replace Authentication or Authorization. The Backend must still validate Access Tokens and user permissions for protected APIs.
6. Inspect API requests in the browser Open the Frontend at http://localhost:5173. Press F12 to open Developer Tools. Select the Network tab. Select the Fetch/XHR filter. Sign in using a Demo account. Observe the API request sent to the Backend. Inspect the login request:
Request URL. Request Method. HTTP Status Code. Request Payload. Response Body. After successful login, open the activity list or personal profile page.
Inspect the corresponding API requests sent to FastAPI.
When capturing Network or Swagger UI screenshots for the internship report, hide Access Tokens, passwords, and personal information.
7. Handle API responses The Frontend must handle responses returned by the Backend.
HTTP Status Code Meaning 200 Successful request 201 Resource created successfully 400 Invalid request 401 Authentication required or invalid Access Token 403 Insufficient permissions 404 Resource not found 409 Data or business operation conflict 422 Invalid input data 500 Internal Server error Actual status codes depend on each API Endpoint.
When an API returns an error, the Frontend should display an appropriate message.
Examples include:
Invalid login credentials: Display a login failure message. Expired Token: Request authentication again according to the application’s session handling. Insufficient permissions: Display an access restriction message. Backend unavailable: Display a connection error. 8. Test business APIs After establishing connectivity, sign in using an ADMIN Demo account and perform the following operations:
Open the activity list. Create a test activity. Open the student account management page. Review personal profile information. Use Developer Tools to inspect the corresponding HTTP requests and responses.
Registration Import, Attendance, and Evidence Import will be covered in detail in the following workshop sections.
9. Troubleshoot common connectivity issues Error What to check Failed to fetch Backend availability, API URL, and CORS ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED Uvicorn running on port 8000 CORS error Allowed Frontend origins in CORSMiddleware HTTP 401 Access Token and login session HTTP 403 ADMIN/STUDENT Role HTTP 404 API path in Swagger UI HTTP 422 Request Body and API Schema HTTP 500 Backend logs and data configuration Results After completing this section:
The Frontend is configured to communicate with FastAPI. API_BASE_URL is correctly configured. REST API requests and responses can be inspected in the browser. CORS is configured for the local environment. Learners understand common connectivity and API errors. In the next section, we will explore Authentication, Access Token management, and ADMIN/STUDENT authorization.
Next: ADMIN/STUDENT authentication and authorization

title: Prepare Activity and Attendance
content:
Prepare Activity and Attendance Before recording Check-in and Check-out, we need to prepare the activity, student data, and applicable business conditions.
In the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform, attendance is recorded for a specific activity. Each attendance record must be associated with the correct Activity ID and Student ID.
1. Prepare a Demo activity Open the Web Application. Sign in using an ADMIN account. Navigate to Activity Management. Select the activity used for registration imports in section 5.6.1. If no suitable activity exists, create a new activity.
Illustrative information:
Activity Name: AWS Workshop Demo Location: University Hall Description: Attendance Recording Workshop Complete the required fields in the application form.
Record the Activity ID for subsequent tests.
2. Configure the activity schedule The activity schedule directly affects Check-in and Check-out eligibility.
Illustrative example:
Start Time: 08:00 End Time: 11:30 Timezone: Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh During the workshop, select a date and time appropriate for the actual testing session.
To test Check-in immediately, prepare an activity whose Check-in window includes the current time.
The 08:00 and 11:30 timestamps are illustrative. Do not use an activity whose permitted attendance window has expired and expect attendance requests to succeed.
3. Verify the activity status The activity must be in a state permitted by the business rules before attendance can be recorded.
For example, a newly created activity may have DRAFT status.
ADMIN should review the supported activity state transitions and move the activity into an appropriate attendance-enabled state.
Do not modify database status values directly to bypass Backend business rules.
4. Understand Check-in time rules The project’s Backend uses the following time zone:
Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh UTC+07:00 The attendance configuration previously used in the project includes:
Early Check-in: 30 minutes before the activity start time. Late Check-in: 20 minutes after the activity start time. For an activity starting at 08:00, the illustrative Check-in window is:
07:30 - Check-in window opens 08:00 - Activity starts 08:20 - Check-in window closes Test scenarios:
Time Expected Result 07:15 Before the Check-in window 07:45 Within the Check-in window 08:00 Within the Check-in window 08:10 Within the Check-in window 08:30 After the Check-in window These scenarios assume that all other business conditions are satisfied.
Before performing the lab, verify the current Attendance Service configuration to ensure the time rules have not changed.
5. Understand Check-out rules Check-out records when a student completes or leaves an activity according to the applicable business rules.
Verify the following conditions:
The activity exists and is in an appropriate state. The student has a Check-in record if required. The Check-out time satisfies the current rules. The operation does not create duplicate Check-out records. The user is authorized to record attendance. Do not assume that Check-out uses the same 30-minute early and 20-minute late intervals as Check-in.
Review the Check-out rules in the current source code and actual API responses.
6. Verify registered students Open the registration list for the selected activity.
Inspect the synthetic student IDs:
0818000001 0818000002 0818000003 0818000004 Ensure that the test students satisfy the registration and attendance requirements.
Prepare an unknown student ID to test invalid student scenarios.
7. Prepare a QR scanner In the project’s intended business workflow, organizers use student card QR codes to receive student identification information.
A compatible scanner may operate as a keyboard-input device, entering the student ID into the attendance interface.
Workflow:
Student Card QR | v QR Scanner | v Student ID Input | v Attendance Interface If a scanner is unavailable, enter student IDs manually to test the REST API workflow.
Inspect the actual QR payload. If it contains additional information, the system must extract the correct student identifier.
Do not assume that every student card QR code contains only a plain-text student ID.
Manual student ID input is suitable for testing when scanner hardware is unavailable. Camera-based QR scanning or dedicated scanner integration should only be reported as tested after verification with the actual hardware.
8. Prepare ADMIN permissions Ensure that the user recording attendance has the ADMIN role.
The current system uses two roles:
ADMIN. STUDENT. ADMIN users are responsible for administrative attendance operations.
The Backend must validate access permissions before recording or updating Attendance data.
Do not grant administrative access by modifying Frontend role information.
9. Open the attendance interface In the Web Application:
Select the Demo activity. Open attendance management. Verify the Activity ID and activity name. Inspect the student ID input area. Select the intended Check-in or Check-out operation. 10. Verify attendance readiness Component Requirement Activity Created successfully Activity Status Attendance operations permitted Schedule Appropriate for the actual test time Registration Student list prepared Student ID Valid synthetic student data ADMIN Account Authorized to record attendance Backend Running Frontend Connected to the REST API Scanner / Manual Input Student ID input available Results After completing this section, we have prepared the activity, student registration records, administrative permissions, and time conditions required for attendance recording.
In the next section, we will perform Check-in and Check-out through the Web interface and inspect REST API results, including invalid business scenarios.
Next: Record Check-in and Check-out

title: Prerequisite
content:
Prerequisites Before starting the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform workshop, we need to prepare the local development environment, AWS account, resource access permissions, and required tools for developing, deploying, and testing the application.
In this workshop, we will use:
Python/FastAPI for Backend development. React/Vite for Frontend development. SQLite for local Demo persistence. Amazon DynamoDB for Cloud data storage integration. AWS Amplify for Frontend deployment. Amazon S3 and AWS Lambda for CSV data processing. AWS IAM for access management. Amazon CloudWatch for execution monitoring. Cloudflare Quick Tunnel to connect the Frontend with the local Backend. 1. Prepare an AWS Account First, you need an AWS account to use the services included in this workshop.
Access the AWS Management Console.
Sign in to your AWS account. Use an IAM User or IAM Role with appropriate permissions. Avoid using the AWS Root account for daily application development. Verify the AWS Region before creating resources. Review AWS Billing to monitor potential charges during the workshop. In this workshop, we will use the AWS Region appropriate for the actual project deployment environment.
Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, and Amazon CloudWatch resources should be configured in the appropriate Region to support integration and testing.
Use the same AWS Region selected for the project. Resource names and configuration values may need to be adjusted according to your AWS account.
2. Prepare IAM Permissions AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) is used to manage identities and control access to AWS resources.
In this workshop, we distinguish between two permission groups:
Permissions required by workshop participants to create, configure, test, and clean up resources. Execution permissions required by AWS Lambda and the Backend to access AWS resources. 2.1. Workshop Participant Permissions The IAM identity used for the workshop requires appropriate permissions to perform the following operations:
Service Required Operations Amazon DynamoDB Create tables, inspect tables, read and write items Amazon S3 Create buckets, upload, download, and manage objects AWS Lambda Create functions, update code, configure, and test functions AWS IAM Create or use execution roles, configure policies, and pass roles Amazon CloudWatch View log groups, log streams, metrics, and configure log retention AWS Amplify Create applications, connect repositories, configure builds, and deploy When using an AWS account provided by an internship program or organization, verify the permissions already assigned to your identity before proceeding.
Avoid assigning AdministratorAccess or permissions outside the required workshop scope.
2.2. IAM Role for AWS Lambda The AWS Lambda CSV Processor requires permissions to:
Read input CSV files from Amazon S3. Write processed JSON results back to Amazon S3. Send execution logs to Amazon CloudWatch. Open the AWS Management Console.
Search for IAM. Select Roles. Choose Create role. Under Trusted entity type, select AWS service. Under Use case, select Lambda. Choose Next. Attach the AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole policy for CloudWatch logging. Enter a role name, for example: SAP-Lambda-CSV-Processor-Role Choose Create role. Next, add an Inline Policy that allows Lambda to read and write objects within the S3 storage locations used in the workshop.
Example IAM Permission Policy:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "ReadInputCSV", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "s3:GetObject" ], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::YOUR-SAP-BUCKET/input/*" }, { "Sid": "WriteOutputJSON", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "s3:PutObject" ], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::YOUR-SAP-BUCKET/output/*" } ] } Where:
YOUR-SAP-BUCKET: The actual S3 Bucket used in the workshop. input/: The prefix containing input CSV files. output/: The prefix containing processed JSON results. Replace YOUR-SAP-BUCKET and the prefixes with your actual resource configuration.
This IAM Policy is intended only for the Lambda CSV Processor. It is not a complete deployment policy for the IAM user performing the workshop. Adjust the Resource ARNs if your actual bucket or prefixes differ from the example.
3. Install the Development Environment In this workshop, we will develop and test the application locally before integrating AWS services.
3.1. Visual Studio Code Visual Studio Code is used for Backend and Frontend development.
Download and install:
Visual Studio Code
Recommended extensions include:
Python. Pylance. ESLint. Prettier. AWS Toolkit. 3.2. Python Python is used to develop the FastAPI Backend and AWS Lambda CSV Processor.
Download Python:
Python Downloads
After installation, open PowerShell and verify:
python --version pip --version Use a Python version compatible with the project source code and dependencies.
3.3. Node.js and npm Node.js and npm are used to develop and run the React/Vite Frontend.
Download Node.js:
Node.js Downloads
Use a Node.js LTS version compatible with Vite and the project’s package.json configuration.
Verify the installation:
node --version npm --version 3.4. Git Git is used for source code management and connecting the repository to AWS Amplify Hosting.
Download Git:
Git Downloads
Verify the installation:
git --version A GitHub account is also required to store the source code and support Frontend deployment.
3.5. AWS CLI The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) allows AWS operations to be performed directly from the Terminal.
Installation guide:
AWS CLI Installation Guide
Verify the installation:
aws --version 4. Configure AWS CLI and AWS Profile The project uses an AWS Profile to connect the Python Backend with AWS resources through boto3.
The workshop uses the following profile name:
sap-dev 4.1. Configure AWS Credentials If you use an IAM User with Access Keys provided for the learning environment, open PowerShell and run:
aws configure --profile sap-dev Enter the requested configuration values:
AWS Access Key ID: <Your Access Key ID> AWS Secret Access Key: <Your Secret Access Key> Default region name: <Your AWS Region> Default output format: json If your account uses AWS IAM Identity Center, configure the profile using:
aws configure sso --profile sap-dev aws sso login --profile sap-dev Choose the authentication method appropriate for your AWS account.
4.2. Verify AWS Connectivity After configuration, verify the profile:
aws sts get-caller-identity --profile sap-dev If the configuration is successful, AWS CLI will return information about the AWS Account and IAM Identity currently in use.
Verify the configured Region:
aws configure get region --profile sap-dev You can also verify DynamoDB and S3 access if the necessary permissions have been granted:
aws dynamodb list-tables --profile sap-dev aws s3 ls --profile sap-dev Do not expose AWS Access Keys, Secret Access Keys, Session Tokens, or authentication credentials in GitHub repositories, Frontend source code, or internship report screenshots.
5. Prepare the Project Source Code In this workshop, we use the source code of the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform.
The main project directory structure is:
student-activity-platform/ ├── backend/ └── frontend/ The source code can be stored on GitHub or in a local development directory.
If the source code is available on GitHub, run:
cd C:\Projects git clone <YOUR_GITHUB_REPOSITORY_URL> cd student-activity-platform Replace YOUR_GITHUB_REPOSITORY_URL with your actual project repository URL.
If the source code is already available on your computer, simply open the project directory in VS Code.
6. Prepare the FastAPI Backend 6.1. Create a Python Virtual Environment Open a Terminal in the Backend directory:
cd C:\Projects\student-activity-platform\backend Create a Python Virtual Environment:
python -m venv .venv Activate the Virtual Environment in PowerShell:
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 If PowerShell blocks script execution, use:
Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process -ExecutionPolicy Bypass .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 This configuration applies only to the current PowerShell session.
6.2. Install Dependencies Install the Backend dependencies using requirements.txt:
python -m pip install --upgrade pip pip install -r requirements.txt The main dependencies used in the project include:
FastAPI. Uvicorn. boto3. CSV/XLSX processing libraries. Authentication and Authorization libraries specified in the project’s requirements.txt. 6.3. Start the Backend Configure the project’s Demo environment:
$env:SAP_DEMO_MODE="1" Configure the AWS Profile when testing AWS integration:
$env:AWS_PROFILE="sap-dev" Start FastAPI:
python -m uvicorn app.main:app --reload After the Backend starts successfully, access:
http://127.0.0.1:8000 Check the REST API documentation:
http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs Swagger UI can be used to test APIs related to Authentication, Activities, Registration, Attendance, Evidence, and Participation.
7. Prepare the React/Vite Frontend Open a new Terminal and navigate to the Frontend directory:
cd C:\Projects\student-activity-platform\frontend Install Node.js dependencies:
npm install Start the Frontend:
npm run dev Vite typically provides the following local URL:
http://localhost:5173 If port 5173 is already in use, check the URL displayed in the Terminal.
The Frontend must connect to the FastAPI Backend at:
http://127.0.0.1:8000 Verify the API_BASE_URL configuration in the Frontend source code.
Ensure that:
The Backend is running. The Frontend is running. The Frontend can communicate with the Backend. Backend CORS settings allow the Frontend origin. The application login page is accessible. ADMIN and STUDENT test accounts are available. 8. Prepare Amazon DynamoDB Resources Amazon DynamoDB will be used to integrate and test business data storage on AWS.
The project includes the following DynamoDB tables:
Table Name Purpose SAP-Activities Store activity information SAP-Registrations Store student registration records SAP-Attendance Store Check-in/Check-out records SAP-Evidence Store participation evidence SAP-Participation Store participation results Access the Amazon DynamoDB Console.
Verify the AWS Region. Select Tables. Review the tables already created in the project environment. If performing the workshop in a new AWS account, the tables will be created according to the Partition Key and Sort Key definitions required by the source code in the Amazon DynamoDB Integration section.
Do not change the table Key Schema without checking the Backend implementation, as this may cause read and write operations to fail.
Verify available tables using AWS CLI:
aws dynamodb list-tables --profile sap-dev SQLite remains part of local persistence and recovery in the Demo environment. DynamoDB represents the tested AWS data storage integration. This workshop does not assume that the entire Backend has been fully migrated to DynamoDB.
9. Prepare Amazon S3 and AWS Lambda 9.1. Amazon S3 Access the Amazon S3 Console.
Prepare an S3 Bucket for the Serverless CSV Processing Demo.
Illustrative storage structure:
YOUR-SAP-BUCKET/ ├── input/ │ └── registrations.csv └── output/ └── registrations-result.json Where:
input/: Contains CSV files to be processed. output/: Contains JSON results generated by Lambda. Use the Bucket and Object Keys required by the actual Lambda configuration.
When creating a Bucket:
Choose a valid and globally unique Bucket name. Select the appropriate AWS Region. Keep Block Public Access enabled. Use appropriate default encryption. Do not upload real student information without authorization. 9.2. AWS Lambda Access the AWS Lambda Console.
Prepare the following information for the Lambda Function:
Function name: SAP-CSV-Processor (illustrative name). Runtime: A Python runtime compatible with the Lambda source code. Execution Role: SAP-Lambda-CSV-Processor-Role or the actual configured role. Input: CSV Object stored in S3. Output: JSON Object stored in S3. The Lambda Function will be configured and tested in detail in the Serverless CSV Processing section.
9.3. Amazon CloudWatch Amazon CloudWatch will be used to inspect logs after Lambda execution.
Prepare the following:
Lambda has logging permissions through its Execution Role. A Log Group corresponding to the Lambda Function. An appropriate Log Retention period for the learning environment. For the Demo environment, a seven-day retention period can be configured to support monitoring and testing.
10. Prepare Cloudflare Quick Tunnel In the current project implementation, the FastAPI Backend runs on a local computer. Cloudflare Quick Tunnel provides a temporary HTTPS Endpoint so the Frontend hosted on AWS Amplify can send REST API requests to the Backend.
Download and install cloudflared:
Cloudflare Tunnel Downloads
Verify the installation:
cloudflared --version Ensure that the FastAPI Backend is running at:
http://127.0.0.1:8000 Start a Quick Tunnel:
cloudflared tunnel --url http://127.0.0.1:8000 Cloudflare will provide a temporary HTTPS URL similar to:
https://<random-name>.trycloudflare.com This URL will be used when configuring the API Endpoint for the Frontend deployed on AWS Amplify.
Cloudflare Quick Tunnel is intended for development and demonstration purposes. The URL may change whenever the tunnel is restarted. Do not use Quick Tunnel as a Production Backend solution. Do not expose real personal data, default credentials, or unprotected administrative APIs through a public endpoint.
11. Prepare AWS Amplify Hosting AWS Amplify is used to deploy the React/Vite Frontend.
Before deployment, prepare:
A GitHub Repository containing the Frontend source code. A deployment branch. The package.json file and Vite configuration. The API Endpoint configuration for the deployment environment. A running FastAPI Backend and Cloudflare Tunnel for the Demo. Verify that the Frontend builds successfully:
cd C:\Projects\student-activity-platform\frontend npm run build After a successful build, Vite typically generates:
dist/ Access the AWS Amplify Console.
Connecting the GitHub Repository, configuring Build Settings, and deploying the Website will be covered in the Application Deployment section.
12. Prepare Sample Data To test Registration Import, Attendance, Evidence Import, Reconciliation, and Analytics, we need to prepare sample datasets.
The following data is synthetic and intended only for learning purposes.
12.1. Registration Data Example student registration file:
student_id,full_name,class_name 0818000001,Student A,DS01 0818000002,Student B,DS01 0818000003,Student C,DS02 12.2. Attendance Data Prepare sample student IDs for testing Check-in and Check-out in the Web Application:
Student ID: 0818000001 Student ID: 0818000002 Student ID: 0818000003 Attendance records are captured in real time through REST APIs rather than imported from Check-in/Check-out files after an activity.
12.3. Evidence Data Example participation evidence file:
student_id,evidence_url 0818000001,https://example.com/evidence-01 0818000002,https://example.com/evidence-02 Column names and file formats must be adjusted to match the actual project’s Import Templates.
12.4. Lambda CSV Processing Data Prepare a CSV file containing four records:
student_id,full_name 0818000001,Student A 0818000002,Student B 0818000001,Student A ,Student C This file is used to test duplicate detection and required-field validation in the Lambda CSV Processor.
Expected processing results:
Metric Count Total Records 4 Valid Records 2 Duplicate Records 1 Invalid Records 1 13. Verify Workshop Readiness After completing the preparation steps, verify the following components:
Component Requirement AWS Account Accessible with appropriate permissions Python Installed and working Node.js/npm Installed and working Git Source code is accessible AWS CLI The sap-dev profile is configured FastAPI Backend can run on port 8000 React/Vite Frontend runs locally and builds successfully SQLite Ready for local Demo persistence DynamoDB Access permissions and business tables are prepared Amazon S3 Workshop storage is ready to be created or reused AWS Lambda Runtime and Execution Role are prepared Amazon CloudWatch Execution logs can be accessed Cloudflare Tunnel A temporary HTTPS Endpoint can be generated AWS Amplify GitHub Repository is available for deployment Sample Data Registration, Attendance, and Evidence samples are available Once these requirements are satisfied, the environment is ready for Backend development, AWS integration, Frontend deployment, and application testing.
Conclusion In this section, we prepared the development environment and prerequisites required for the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform workshop.
The architecture combines React/Vite, FastAPI, SQLite, and AWS services selected according to their respective responsibilities.
In the next section, we will begin developing and configuring the FastAPI Backend, which provides the foundation for activity management, attendance recording, data processing, and Amazon DynamoDB integration.

title: Reconcile Student Participation Data
content:
Reconcile Student Participation Data In this section, we will reconcile Registration, Attendance, and Evidence records in the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform.
Data Reconciliation is the process of comparing information from multiple sources to verify consistency, identify missing data, and support student participation decisions.
This functionality reduces manual verification workloads after university activities.
1. Understand the reconciliation problem Assume four students register for an activity.
Registration records imported from the University Portal:
Student ID Full Name 0818000001 Student A 0818000002 Student B 0818000003 Student C 0818000004 Student D Real-time attendance records:
Student ID Check-in Check-out 0818000001 08:05 11:30 0818000002 08:10 Not recorded 0818000004 08:15 11:35 Evidence records imported from Google Forms:
Student ID Evidence 0818000001 Available 0818000002 Available 0818000003 Available Reviewing each file independently makes it difficult to identify complete participation records efficiently.
Reconciliation combines information from all three sources.
These records are synthetic workshop data.
2. Identify data matching keys The system uses two important identifiers:
activity_id: Identifies the activity. mssv: Identifies the student. A student can participate in multiple activities.
Matching records using only Student ID across the entire system may incorrectly associate data from different activities.
Example:
Activity ID: ACT-DEMO-001 Student ID: 0818000001 Registration, Attendance, and Evidence records must be matched within the correct Activity ID.
3. Understand the reconciliation workflow Registration | v Normalize Student ID | +----------------+ | Attendance ----------> Match by Activity ID + MSSV | Evidence ------------>| v Reconciliation Result | v ADMIN Review The Backend performs the following operations:
Retrieve registration records. Retrieve Check-in and Check-out information. Retrieve evidence records. Standardize and match student IDs. Identify available and missing information. Consolidate results for administrative review. The project’s current reconciliation workflow is implemented using Python/FastAPI.
AWS Glue and Amazon Athena are not required for this functionality.
4. Prepare reconciliation data Before proceeding:
Complete Registration Import in section 5.6.1. Complete Check-in and Check-out in section 5.6.3. Complete Evidence Import in section 5.7.1. Use the same Demo activity for all three data sources. Verify Activity ID and Student ID before continuing.
5. Open the reconciliation interface Open the Web Application. Sign in using an ADMIN account. Navigate to Activity Management. Select the Demo activity. Open Reconciliation. Review the activity and its source datasets.
If a dataset is missing, determine whether this represents a valid business scenario or an input problem.
6. Perform reconciliation Execute the reconciliation or data consolidation operation provided by the current interface.
The Frontend sends the request to the Backend.
The Backend retrieves relevant datasets and processes results according to the current business rules.
Example results:
Student ID Registration Check-in Check-out Evidence 0818000001 Yes Yes Yes Yes 0818000002 Yes Yes No Yes 0818000003 Yes No No Yes 0818000004 Yes Yes Yes No This consolidated view helps ADMIN users identify records requiring additional review.
7. Analyze business scenarios Scenario 1: Complete records Student 0818000001 has Registration, Check-in, Check-out, and Evidence records.
Result:
All input data is available in this example. The record may be eligible for confirmation if the activity requirements are satisfied. Scenario 2: Missing Check-out Student 0818000002 has Check-in and Evidence but no Check-out.
Result:
Attendance data is incomplete. ADMIN should review the record according to activity rules. Scenario 3: Evidence without attendance Student 0818000003 has Registration and Evidence but no Attendance records.
Result:
Evidence alone does not establish that the student attended the activity. The record requires evaluation according to missing-attendance rules. During an earlier AWS Pilot test, some project records contained NO_ATTENDANCE even though evidence_status was YES.
Scenario 4: Missing evidence Student 0818000004 has Registration and complete attendance but no Evidence.
Result:
Attendance information is complete. ADMIN should determine whether evidence is required for the activity. These scenarios illustrate reconciliation logic. Exact status values and eligibility rules must follow the current Reconciliation Service implementation. Do not introduce new Backend statuses based only on these examples.
8. Illustrate reconciliation using Python The following example demonstrates key-based data matching.
registrations = [ {"activity_id": "ACT-DEMO-001", "mssv": "0818000001"}, {"activity_id": "ACT-DEMO-001", "mssv": "0818000002"}, {"activity_id": "ACT-DEMO-001", "mssv": "0818000003"}, {"activity_id": "ACT-DEMO-001", "mssv": "0818000004"}, ] attendance = { ("ACT-DEMO-001", "0818000001"): { "check_in": "08:05", "check_out": "11:30" }, ("ACT-DEMO-001", "0818000002"): { "check_in": "08:10", "check_out": None }, ("ACT-DEMO-001", "0818000004"): { "check_in": "08:15", "check_out": "11:35" } } evidence = { ("ACT-DEMO-001", "0818000001"), ("ACT-DEMO-001", "0818000002"), ("ACT-DEMO-001", "0818000003") } results = [] for student in registrations: key = ( student["activity_id"], student["mssv"] ) record = attendance.get(key, {}) result = { "activity_id": student["activity_id"], "mssv": student["mssv"], "registered": True, "checked_in": bool(record.get("check_in")), "checked_out": bool(record.get("check_out")), "has_evidence": key in evidence } results.append(result) for result in results: print(result) This example uses dictionaries and sets to retrieve records by Activity ID and Student ID.
It is a standalone learning example rather than the complete project’s Reconciliation Service.
The algorithm uses Registration as its primary dataset. If the business requirements include identifying students with Attendance or Evidence but no Registration, additional checks must inspect keys that appear only in the other datasets.
9. Inspect reconciliation results After reconciliation:
Review the student list. Verify Registration status. Verify Check-in and Check-out. Inspect Evidence availability. Review the displayed business evaluation results. Identify records requiring administrative review. Use status filters or Student ID search if supported by the current interface.
Appearing in a reconciliation result does not automatically establish final participation confirmation.
10. Inspect the REST API Open Developer Tools and select Network.
Perform the reconciliation operation again.
Inspect:
The Endpoint called by the Frontend. Activity ID in the Request. HTTP Status Code. Consolidated Response data. Student-level status information. Use Swagger UI to identify the actual Reconciliation or Participation Endpoint.
11. Handle inconsistent data Scenario Recommended Action Missing leading zeros Verify String/Text formatting Incorrect Activity ID Verify the selected activity Duplicate Registration Review Import rules Missing Evidence Inspect Evidence Import results Missing Attendance Review Check-in/Check-out records Inconsistent source data Compare individual records Outdated results Review API responses and rerun supported reconciliation Do not arbitrarily modify attendance or evidence records to make participation appear valid.
Changes must be based on accurate information and authorized operations.
12. Summarize test cases Test Case Expected Result Complete source records Complete reconciliation information Missing Check-out Incomplete attendance detected No Attendance Missing attendance detected Missing Evidence Missing evidence identified Incorrect Activity ID No cross-activity mismatching STUDENT calls admin API Access denied when unauthorized Reconciliation rerun Results reflect updated data according to current rules Conclusion In this section, we combined Registration, Attendance, and Evidence to generate student-level reconciliation results.
This workflow transforms separate datasets into meaningful information for activity management.
ADMIN users will review the reconciliation results before performing final participation confirmation.
Next: Confirm Participation Results

title: Stop the Demo Environment
content:
Stop the Demo Environment In this section, we will stop local processes after completing the application demonstration.
The deployment uses AWS Amplify Hosting for the Frontend and Cloudflare Quick Tunnel to connect to the FastAPI Backend.
Stopping local services is different from deleting AWS Hosting resources.
1. Review running components The Demo environment uses:
Frontend: AWS Amplify Hosting Backend: 127.0.0.1:8001 Cloudflare: Quick Tunnel Database: SQLite Demo Main Terminal sessions:
Terminal 1: FastAPI Backend Terminal 2: Cloudflare Quick Tunnel 2. Verify data before shutdown Before stopping services:
Sign in as ADMIN. Review the Demo activity. Record Activity IDs needed later. Verify saved data. Capture required screenshots. If SQLite backup is needed, identify the configured database file.
Do not copy an actively written database without using a consistent backup method.
3. Stop Cloudflare Quick Tunnel Open the cloudflared Terminal.
Example command:
cloudflared tunnel --url http://127.0.0.1:8001 Press:
Ctrl + C The cloudflared process receives the stop request.
After stopping the Tunnel, its trycloudflare.com URL no longer forwards requests to the local Backend.
Do not treat the previous temporary hostname as a permanent API Endpoint.
4. Stop FastAPI Open the Uvicorn Terminal.
Previously used command:
python -m uvicorn app.main:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8001 Press Ctrl + C.
Verify that the process has terminated.
Stopping FastAPI does not require deleting the Backend source code or Virtual Environment.
5. Verify port 8001 Open PowerShell:
Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 8001 -State Listen -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue No result indicates that no TCP listener is found on port 8001 at the time of inspection.
Alternatively:
Test-NetConnection 127.0.0.1 -Port 8001 After shutdown, TcpTestSucceeded would normally be False.
6. Verify the Amplify Website Open the previously deployed Website:
https://main.d2p96elhe5x6se.amplifyapp.com If the Amplify App remains deployed, Frontend assets can still be served by AWS.
However, Backend-dependent features will fail when the Tunnel is stopped.
Architecture:
AWS Amplify Frontend | v Cloudflare Quick Tunnel | v Local FastAPI Backend Cloud-hosted Frontend availability does not mean that the Backend is hosted in the Cloud.
7. Stop the local Frontend If the Vite Development Server is running:
npm run dev Press Ctrl + C in its Terminal.
Stopping Vite does not affect the separate Amplify-hosted Frontend.
8. Preserve SQLite data After the Backend has fully stopped:
Identify the correct Demo SQLite file. Create a backup if future work requires it. Preserve the Backend source code. Retain configuration required to restart the Demo. Do not delete SQLite data unless its retention and backup requirements are understood.
9. Understand stopping versus deletion Operation Effect Stop FastAPI Local Backend becomes unavailable Stop cloudflared Tunnel forwarding stops Stop Vite Local development server stops Keep Amplify App Website remains hosted Delete Amplify App Application hosting is removed Delete SQLite Demo data may be lost Results After completing this section, the local Demo environment has been shut down in a controlled manner.
Source code, necessary databases, and AWS resources remain intact unless separately managed.
