Next: Clean Up AWS Test Resources

title: Test the Backend and REST APIs
content:
Test the Backend and REST APIs In this section, we will use Swagger UI to test the main APIs of the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform.
The objective is to verify Backend functionality, user authentication, authorization, and business operations before integrating Amazon DynamoDB.
Step 1: Verify Backend availability Ensure that the FastAPI Backend is running:
python -m uvicorn app.main:app --reload Access:
Swagger UI
Review the available API groups.
Step 2: Test Authentication In Swagger UI, locate:
POST /auth/login Expand the Endpoint. Choose Try it out. Enter the ADMIN Demo account information according to the displayed Request Body. Choose Execute. If the credentials are valid, the Backend returns a successful login response and Access Token information according to the API response schema.
Expected result:
HTTP 200 OK Use Demo accounts only. Do not expose real passwords or Access Tokens in internship report screenshots.
Step 3: Verify the current user information Locate the Endpoint:
GET /auth/me Use the Access Token received from the login operation.
If Swagger UI provides an Authorize button, select it and enter the Token according to the API authentication configuration.
Alternatively, send the request using PowerShell:
$token = "YOUR_DEMO_ACCESS_TOKEN" Invoke-RestMethod ` -Method Get ` -Uri "http://127.0.0.1:8000/auth/me" ` -Headers @{ Authorization = "Bearer $token" } Replace YOUR_DEMO_ACCESS_TOKEN with a valid Access Token.
Review the Response to verify the current user and assigned Role.
Step 4: Test Student Account Management Using an ADMIN account, locate the Endpoint:
GET /admin/students Execute the Request using the ADMIN Access Token.
Expected results:
The Backend authorizes the request. Student account information is returned according to the API schema. ADMIN users can access the authorized account management operations. Next, sign in with a STUDENT account and attempt to access the same Endpoint.
Expected results:
The STUDENT account cannot access administrative student account management functionality. The Backend returns an authorization error, typically HTTP 403 Forbidden when a valid Token lacks the required permissions. Step 5: Test Activity Management In Swagger UI, locate the Activity Management API group.
Use the Endpoints provided by the current project source code to:
Create a Demo activity. Retrieve the activity list. Retrieve activity details. Update activity information. Example activity data:
Activity Name: AWS Workshop Demo Location: University Hall Description: Student activity management test When creating the activity, provide the required fields displayed in the Swagger UI Request Body.
Expected results:
The activity is created successfully. The activity appears in the activity list. An Activity ID is available for subsequent tests. Step 6: Test Attendance APIs The system records Check-in and Check-out in real time.
Attendance Endpoints:
POST /activities/{activity_id}/check-in POST /activities/{activity_id}/check-out Prepare the following:
An existing Demo activity. A valid Demo student. An ADMIN account or an account authorized to record attendance. An activity in a state and time window that permits attendance. A student registration record if required by the business rules. In Swagger UI:
Expand the Check-in Endpoint. Choose Try it out. Enter the Activity ID. Enter the student information according to the Request Body. Choose Execute. Review the Response. Repeat the procedure using the Check-out Endpoint.
Expected results:
Check-in is associated with the correct activity and student. Check-out is recorded after Check-in when the business requirements are satisfied. Duplicate or invalid operations are handled appropriately. Requests outside the permitted attendance window are handled according to the business rules. Attendance APIs operate in real time. Use an activity with an appropriate attendance window instead of an activity that has already ended.
Step 7: Verify SQLite persistence The Demo version uses SQLite to support local data persistence and application state recovery.
To verify this behavior:
Create a Demo activity through the API. Record its Activity ID. Stop the Backend using Ctrl + C. Restart the Backend: python -m uvicorn app.main:app --reload Open Swagger UI. Retrieve the activity using the relevant API and verify the recorded Activity ID. The expected result is that data covered by the persistence mechanism remains recoverable after restarting the application.
If the data cannot be recovered, review the Demo configuration and persistence implementation in the source code.
Step 8: Summarize the test results Test Expected Result FastAPI Startup Backend available on port 8000 Swagger UI REST API documentation displayed Authentication Successful login with valid credentials Current User Current user information returned ADMIN Authorization Administrative functionality accessible STUDENT Authorization Administrative functionality restricted Activity Management Activities can be created and retrieved Check-in / Check-out Valid real-time attendance recording SQLite Persistence Data covered by persistence can be recovered The results above represent testing criteria. Workshop participants should verify the actual results and capture corresponding screenshots.
Conclusion After completing this section, the FastAPI Backend is prepared and its primary business functions can be tested.
The Backend is ready for React/Vite Frontend connectivity and Amazon DynamoDB integration for cloud-based business data storage.
In the next section, we will create and configure DynamoDB tables and verify data reading and writing operations using the AWS SDK for Python.
Next: Amazon DynamoDB Integration

title: AWS First Cloud AI Journey Community Day 2026
content:
AWS First Cloud AI Journey Community Day 2026 1. Event Introduction AWS First Cloud AI Journey Community Day 2026 is a community event associated with First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ). It provides students and technology enthusiasts with opportunities to learn, exchange ideas, and explore developments in cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and software development.
The sessions covered AWS Cloud, serverless architecture, Amazon SQS, internship experiences, and the importance of consistent open-source contributions.
For me, this event was an opportunity to broaden my technical perspective and relate industry discussions to my Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform internship project.
2. Event Information Item Details Event AWS First Cloud AI Journey Community Day 2026 Date Saturday, October 31, 2026 Time 09:00–12:00 Venue Bitexco Financial Tower Address 02 Hai Trieu Street, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam Format In-person Participation Student / Attendee 3. Participation Objectives Keep up with AWS services and cloud application development practices. Learn how serverless systems are designed and deployed. Understand AWS Lambda and Amazon SQS in modern architectures. Learn from AWS internship and project development experiences. Identify skills relevant to cloud computing and data engineering. Understand how open-source communities support continuous learning. 4. Sessions Attended The program included six main topics:
Lessons Learned from Building Software Factories Education AWS Lambda Web Functions: Rethinking Serverless Web Architecture Amazon SQS: Building Asynchronous Systems My 3-Month AWS Internship Journey Start & Maintain Consistency with Open Source Contributing 5. Technical Knowledge Gained 5.1. Lessons Learned from Building Software Factories This session emphasized that software engineering involves more than writing individual features. Good solutions require clear architecture, repeatable development practices, testing, deployment, code quality, and maintainability.
Connection to my project: My platform is divided into a React/Vite frontend, a Python/FastAPI backend, a SQLite database for the local demonstration, and a distinct AWS experimental scope. Separation of responsibilities makes the project easier to test, maintain, and extend.
5.2. Education – Preparing for Technology Careers The Education session highlighted the importance of programming skills, problem-solving, technical documentation, and active independent learning. As a Data Science student, I found that studying cloud computing complements my knowledge of databases, data processing, and analytics.
5.3. AWS Lambda Web Functions: Rethinking Serverless Web Architecture The discussion introduced HTTP workloads on serverless functions, scaling, performance, operational costs, and trade-offs compared with server-based or container-based applications.
Connection to my project: I developed and tested an independent AWS Lambda CSV Processing Demo. The experiment was performed as follows:
Upload a sample CSV file to Amazon S3. Invoke Lambda through a Test Event. Read and validate registration data. Distinguish valid, duplicate, and invalid records. Save the processing result as JSON in Amazon S3. Inspect execution logs using Amazon CloudWatch. This experiment is separate from the primary FastAPI backend and does not represent a fully automated S3-triggered production data pipeline.
5.4. Amazon SQS: Building Asynchronous Systems The Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) session explained how message queues decouple components and support asynchronous background tasks. I learned that queues may help systems tolerate peaks in workloads and avoid blocking user-facing requests.
Future consideration: SQS could potentially be used to process large registration files asynchronously or to decouple ingestion and processing. SQS is not implemented in the current project.
5.5. My 3-Month AWS Internship Journey The internship sharing session reinforced the value of hands-on practice, systematic troubleshooting, technical documentation, time management, and regularly reviewing progress. These lessons are reflected in my worklog and workshop materials.
5.6. Start & Maintain Consistency with Open Source Contributing This session demonstrated how open-source participation can improve code-reading skills, collaboration, Git/GitHub usage, and long-term technical learning. I was particularly interested in how consistent documentation and version control help maintain software projects.
6. Lessons Learned and Project Applications After attending the event, I became more aware of the need to select cloud components based on the actual problem rather than on service popularity.
The current project includes:
Frontend: React/Vite, deployed to AWS Amplify Hosting. Backend: FastAPI running on a local demo computer, accessible through Cloudflare Quick Tunnel. Data persistence: SQLite in the demo environment, with separate DynamoDB integration and testing. Core business functions: registration import, real-time check-in/check-out, evidence import, reconciliation, participation confirmation, analytics, and export. Independent serverless experiment: Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, AWS IAM, and CloudWatch. The event also encouraged further research into asynchronous tasks, data pipelines, observability, cost optimization, and open-source collaboration.
7. Personal Reflection AWS First Cloud AI Journey Community Day 2026 provided valuable perspectives on practical cloud systems and the skills needed for a technology career.
I particularly appreciated the combination of architecture, implementation, internship experience, and open-source learning. The discussions motivated me to continue improving my knowledge of cloud computing and data engineering.
8. Event Participation Photos The following are photographs documenting my attendance at the actual event:
Photo 1 – Event participation Photo 2 – Event activities Photo 3 – Community event moments Photo 4 – Additional event evidence 9. Conclusion The event strengthened my understanding of serverless architecture, asynchronous processing, practical software engineering, and the importance of maintaining a learning community. The lessons gained will support future improvements to the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform and my professional development in cloud and data engineering.

title: Blog 2 - Secure File Uploads to Amazon S3 with Pre-signed URLs
content:
UPLOADING CSV/XLSX FILES TO AWS WITHOUT EXPOSING S3 CREDENTIALS: HOW DO PRE-SIGNED URLS WORK? Learning How to Build a Secure File Upload Workflow on AWS 1. Starting with a Familiar Problem While developing the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform, I needed to support data import from CSV and Excel files.
These files may include:
Student registration lists from the University Portal. Participation evidence from Google Forms. Student records requiring reconciliation. Files used for reporting and analytics. In the current implementation, Registration and Evidence files are submitted to FastAPI for validation and processing.
However, while studying how the system could be expanded on AWS, I asked myself:
How can users upload files directly to Amazon S3 without knowing the AWS Access Key and Secret Access Key?
One solution I discovered was Amazon S3 Pre-signed URLs.
2. Why Should AWS Credentials Not Be Stored in the Frontend? Suppose I develop a React application that uploads files directly to Amazon S3.
An insecure approach would be to include AWS Access Keys and Secret Access Keys in the Frontend source code.
React Frontend | | AWS Credentials v Amazon S3 JavaScript running in a browser can be inspected by users.
If credentials are embedded in Frontend code, they may be discovered through browser Developer Tools or built JavaScript files.
This creates risks such as:
Unauthorized AWS resource access. Reading data outside the intended scope. Unwanted uploads or deletions. Unexpected AWS costs. Exposure of student information. Environment variables embedded in a Frontend build are not secure secret storage if their values become part of the delivered JavaScript.
Therefore, a Web Application should not expose long-term AWS credentials directly to the browser.
3. What Is a Pre-signed URL? A Pre-signed URL is a URL signed using AWS credentials that allows its holder to perform a specific operation on an S3 resource for a limited period.
Examples include:
Uploading an object using HTTP PUT. Downloading an object using HTTP GET. The Backend generates a signed URL and returns it to the user.
The user does not need an AWS Access Key or Secret Access Key to perform the authorized operation.
A Pre-signed URL contains information related to:
The S3 Bucket. The Object Key. The HTTP Method. The expiration time. The AWS signature. The URL is generated using the permissions of the signing IAM Principal.
If that Principal does not have permission to upload the specified object, the URL cannot grant access beyond those permissions.
The S3 Bucket does not need to be public.
4. How Does a Pre-signed URL Work? Assume an ADMIN user needs to upload a student registration file.
The proposed workflow is:
ADMIN / React Frontend | | 1. Request Upload URL v FastAPI Backend | | 2. Generate Pre-signed URL v AWS SDK / IAM Permissions | | 3. Return Signed URL v ADMIN / React Frontend | | 4. HTTP PUT File v Amazon S3 The implementation steps are:
The ADMIN signs in to the Web Application. The ADMIN selects a CSV or XLSX file. The Frontend requests an upload URL from FastAPI. The Backend validates the Access Token and ADMIN permissions. The Backend validates file information and the associated activity. The Backend generates a Pre-signed URL using boto3. The Frontend receives the signed URL. The browser uploads the file directly to Amazon S3. The system verifies the upload before beginning data processing. The file does not need to pass through FastAPI during the entire upload process.
The Backend focuses on authentication, business validation, and issuing appropriate upload URLs.
5. Generating a Pre-signed URL with Python The following example demonstrates Python and boto3:
import boto3 from uuid import uuid4 s3 = boto3.client("s3") bucket_name = "your-private-demo-bucket" object_key = f"uploads/{uuid4()}.csv" upload_url = s3.generate_presigned_url( ClientMethod="put_object", Params={ "Bucket": bucket_name, "Key": object_key, "ContentType": "text/csv" }, ExpiresIn=300 ) print(upload_url) Explanation:
put_object: The S3 upload operation. Bucket: The destination S3 Bucket. Key: The object’s storage path. ContentType: The content type used during upload. ExpiresIn: The URL validity period in seconds. In this example, the URL is configured to expire after 300 seconds.
The Backend must have valid AWS credentials and s3:PutObject permission for the specified resource.
When temporary credentials are used, the signed URL may expire earlier if the underlying credentials expire.
Note: This example is intended for learning. Production applications should not unnecessarily print or log signed URLs because anyone holding the URL may use its granted access while it remains valid.
6. Uploading a File from React After receiving the signed URL, the Frontend can upload the file using the Fetch API.
async function uploadFile(file, uploadUrl) { const response = await fetch(uploadUrl, { method: "PUT", headers: { "Content-Type": "text/csv", }, body: file, }); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error("Upload failed"); } return true; } The Content-Type should match the value used when generating the URL.
For XLSX files, the appropriate content type can be used:
application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet If the Frontend and S3 use different origins, the Bucket must have an appropriate CORS configuration allowing upload requests from the application’s origin.
CORS does not replace IAM or authentication. It controls cross-origin requests permitted by web browsers.
7. What IAM Permissions Are Required? The Backend should only receive the permissions necessary for its responsibilities.
An illustrative IAM Policy is shown below:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:PutObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::your-private-demo-bucket/uploads/*" } ] } This policy allows uploads within the uploads/ prefix of the specified Bucket.
It does not automatically grant permissions to read, delete, or administer the entire Bucket.
This demonstrates the Least Privilege principle:
The Backend receives only the required upload permissions. Users receive a URL for a specific object. The S3 Bucket can remain private. 8. Important Security Considerations Pre-signed URLs are useful, but they do not automatically solve every security problem.
Expiration
Use short validity periods appropriate for the upload requirements.
Access Control
Generate URLs only after validating the user’s identity and authorization for the relevant activity.
Object Keys
The Backend should generate controlled Object Keys rather than accepting unrestricted storage paths from users.
Example structure:
uploads/ ACT-DEMO-001/ registration/ unique-file-id.csv File Validation
File extensions and Content-Type values are not sufficient to guarantee valid files.
The system must still validate content, structure, file size, and data after upload.
Pre-signed POST with a content-length-range condition can be considered when an upload size restriction must be enforced through a policy.
URL Protection
A Pre-signed URL may be reused during its validity period. It is not automatically a one-time credential.
Avoid public sharing and unnecessary logging of signed URLs.
Personal Data
Use synthetic data or properly authorized information. Do not expose student records through publicly accessible storage.
9. Combining Pre-signed URLs with AWS Lambda After a file is successfully uploaded to Amazon S3, an automated processing workflow could be implemented in the future.
React Frontend | | Pre-signed Upload v Amazon S3 Input | | S3 Event Notification v AWS Lambda | | Validate & Process v Amazon S3 Output AWS Lambda could:
Read CSV files from S3. Validate student IDs. Detect duplicate records. Identify invalid data. Generate JSON results. S3 Event Notifications can be configured to invoke Lambda when new objects arrive in the input prefix.
If Lambda writes results to the same Bucket, the trigger should not also match the output prefix, as this could create unintended recursive invocations.
10. Connection to My Internship Project In the current Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform:
Registration and Evidence imports are handled by FastAPI. The Frontend is deployed using AWS Amplify. DynamoDB is integrated and tested for AWS-based data storage. Amazon S3 and AWS Lambda are used in an independent Serverless CSV Processing Demo. AWS IAM provides required resource permissions. Pre-signed URLs represent a potential enhancement to the file upload architecture.
With this integration, ADMIN users could upload files directly to S3 while FastAPI manages authorization and business information.
This could reduce file transfer workloads on the Backend and support a more flexible Data Pipeline.
However, this article does not claim that Pre-signed URLs or automated S3 Event Notifications have been fully integrated into the current Website.
11. Conclusion Through studying Amazon S3 Pre-signed URLs, I learned that Cloud file uploads involve more than storage. They also require authentication, authorization, and security.
My main takeaways include:
Never expose secret AWS credentials in the Frontend. Use the Backend to validate permissions and generate signed URLs. Restrict access to specific Object Keys and operations. Configure appropriate expiration periods. Validate uploaded data. Combine S3 and Lambda for Serverless processing when appropriate. This knowledge is useful for Web Applications that handle documents, images, CSV files, or Excel files.
It also provides a foundation for my future studies in Cloud Security, Data Engineering, and AWS-based data processing architectures.
12. References Amazon S3 – Sharing objects with presigned URLs Uploading objects with presigned URLs Boto3 – generate_presigned_url Amazon S3 CORS Amazon S3 Event Notifications AWS IAM User Guide

title: Worklog Week 2
content:
Week 2 Objectives: Define the internship project topic and implementation scope. Analyze the practical challenges of managing, tracking, and evaluating student participation in university activities. Identify the main user roles and access control requirements. Investigate the data sources used for student activity management. Establish the business workflow from registration and attendance to evidence collection, reconciliation, and participation confirmation. Identify AWS services appropriate for the project requirements and cost constraints. Design a high-level architecture that distinguishes local development components from potential AWS integrations. Prepare a preliminary data model and synthetic datasets for subsequent development and testing. Establish the overall project objectives and MVP scope. - Identify core modules: Activity Management, Registration, Attendance, Evidence, Reconciliation, Analytics, and Export. - Outline the main functional and non-functional requirements. 14/09/2026 14/09/2026 Project proposal and https://cloudjourney.awsstudygroup.com/ Tuesday - Design the registration and attendance workflow. - Establish Registration Preview and Import as the main mechanisms for importing external registration records. - Analyze the process of scanning QR codes on student identification cards for Check-in/Check-out. - Define the requirement for APIs to receive attendance events and immediately record timestamps. - Determine how the system verifies whether a student has registered for an activity. - Specify expected behavior for duplicate Check-ins, invalid Check-outs, and missing attendance events. - Analyze how Evidence contributes to participation verification and reconciliation. 16/09/2026 16/09/2026 Business requirements and Project Proposal Thursday - Design the high-level system architecture. - Select React and Vite for Frontend development. - Select Python and FastAPI for the Backend REST API. - Investigate SQLite for local development and demonstration environments. - Research Amazon DynamoDB for experimental cloud-based business data storage. - Explore Amazon S3 for file storage and data processing outputs. - Study AWS Amplify for Frontend hosting. - Investigate AWS IAM, Lambda, and CloudWatch for access control, serverless processing, and monitoring. - Distinguish the proposed architecture from services that would be implemented in later weeks. 17/09/2026 17/09/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/ https://vite.dev/ Friday - Outline the REST API endpoints required for development. - Define the workflow Registration → Attendance → Evidence → Reconciliation → Analytics/Export. - Prepare synthetic test scenarios involving valid registrations, duplicate records, missing Check-ins, missing Check-outs, and missing Evidence. - Summarize the analysis results, update the Project Proposal, and prepare for Backend development in Week 3. 18/09/2026 18/09/2026 Project Proposal, AWS Documentation, and architecture notes Week 2 Achievements: Defined the project topic and development direction:
Selected Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform as the internship project. Established the goal of developing a web-based system for managing activities, tracking participation, reconciling data, and analyzing student engagement. Defined an MVP focused on essential business functions before expanding AWS integrations. Analyzed the practical problem:
Registration, attendance, and evidence records may originate from different independent systems. Manual data consolidation can introduce missing records, duplicates, and inaccurate participation results. A centralized workflow is needed to validate, reconcile, and confirm participation outcomes. Reconciled data should support statistical analysis and reporting. Defined two main user roles:
ADMIN:
Manage activities and publication status. Manage student accounts. Import Registration and Evidence datasets. Perform or manage attendance operations. Reconcile and confirm participation results. Access Analytics and export reports. STUDENT:
Sign in and manage a personal profile. View permitted activities and their details. Check personal participation history and results. Access relevant notifications. Identified the primary data sources:
Registration: Student registration data exported from the university system and imported through CSV/XLSX. Attendance: Check-in/Check-out events sent directly to the API when an organizer scans a code or enters a Student ID. Evidence: Participation evidence exported from Google Forms/Google Sheets as CSV/XLSX. Activity: Activity information created and maintained within the application. Established preliminary business rules:
Registration records must be validated before import. Students must have valid registrations before their attendance is accepted under the defined workflow. Check-in and Check-out are designed as real-time API events rather than primarily being imported from Excel files. Duplicate or invalid attendance operations must be detected. Evidence is used alongside Registration and Attendance during reconciliation. Missing or inconsistent records must be flagged for ADMIN review. Final participation results must be confirmed before reporting. Designed the overall data processing workflow:
Activity Management → Registration Import → Real-time Attendance → Evidence Import → Reconciliation → Participation Result → Analytics & Export
The workflow includes:
ADMIN creates and manages activities. Registration datasets are validated and imported. Attendance is recorded immediately when the relevant action occurs. Evidence records are imported and validated. Backend services reconcile the data sources. Final results are aggregated for analysis and reporting. Proposed the technology architecture:
React + Vite: Web user interface. FastAPI + Python: REST API and business logic. SQLite: Data persistence for local development and demonstration. AWS Amplify: Planned cloud hosting for the Frontend. Amazon DynamoDB: Planned pilot integration for business data. Amazon S3: Planned storage for posters, datasets, and processed results. AWS IAM: Research into secure service-to-service permissions. AWS Lambda: Research into serverless data processing. Amazon CloudWatch: Research into monitoring and execution logs. These components represented the proposed architecture and development plan for Week 2, not a claim that all AWS services had already been deployed.
Distinguished research options from actual implementation:
Amazon Cognito and Amazon API Gateway were considered as alternatives within a fully serverless architecture. AWS Glue, Amazon Athena, and Amazon QuickSight were explored as possible future analytics enhancements. These services were not treated as implemented components. Initial Backend development with FastAPI was prioritized before cloud integration. Prepared the initial data model:
Activities. Students. Registrations. Attendance. Evidence. Participation. Users. Identified the basic relationships between Activity ID, Student ID, Registration, Attendance, and participation results.
Prepared synthetic testing scenarios:
Valid registration and complete attendance. Student not present in the registration list. Duplicate Student IDs. Missing Check-in. Missing Check-out. Missing Evidence. Registration without attendance. Records requiring manual review. Established the next development steps:
Outlined the required modules and REST API endpoints. Selected a local-first development strategy followed by targeted AWS integration. Prioritized synthetic datasets to protect student information and reduce cloud costs. Prepared the basic requirements for Backend development in Week 3. Challenges and Lessons Learned: Multiple data sources: Registration, Attendance, and Evidence have different structures, making data validation and reconciliation essential. Real-time attendance design: It is important to distinguish immediate Check-in/Check-out API events from batch data imports. AWS architecture selection: A fully serverless design introduces multiple services and additional complexity, making it unsuitable to deploy all components at the start of the project. Cost management: A local-first development approach with synthetic data helps minimize AWS expenses during development. Role-based access control: ADMIN and STUDENT responsibilities must be defined early to avoid extensive modifications during Backend and Frontend development. Plan for Next Week: Initialize the Python and FastAPI Backend project. Design REST API endpoints and business data models. Develop basic Activity Management functionality. Implement Registration Import and Evidence Import processing. Build Check-in/Check-out APIs using synthetic data. Develop reconciliation logic for missing, duplicate, and inconsistent records. Test core business workflows locally before integrating AWS services.

title: Proposal
content:
This proposal describes the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform, a student activity management, reconciliation, and reporting project developed during First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ). It distinguishes the implemented application and experimental AWS components from future extensions.
Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform A Platform for Student Activity Management, Participation Reconciliation, and Engagement Analytics 1. Executive Summary The platform is designed to help event organizers manage activities, record attendance, reconcile participation data, and analyze student engagement in university activities.
The project is relevant to workshops, seminars, academic competitions, extracurricular programs, and large annual events such as IT Day. A typical activity may involve around 100–200 students; larger events can exceed 1,000 participants. These figures describe potential business needs, not verified load-testing results.
Student registration, attendance, and participation evidence often originate from separate systems. Registration lists come from a University Portal, check-in/check-out is associated with student-card QR codes or IDs, and supporting evidence can come from Google Forms or Sheets. Consolidating such records by hand is slow and error-prone.
The implemented MVP includes:
React/Vite for the frontend. Python/FastAPI for authentication, REST APIs, and business rules. SQLite for local demo persistence and recovery. AWS Amplify Hosting for the frontend deployment. Cloudflare Quick Tunnel connecting a hosted frontend with a locally running FastAPI backend during demonstration. Amazon DynamoDB as a tested AWS cloud-data integration, without claiming a complete migration away from SQLite. An independent Amazon S3 + AWS Lambda CSV Processing Demo, with AWS IAM permissions and CloudWatch logging. The application has two business roles: ADMIN and STUDENT. The goal is to improve data consistency, reduce repetitive Excel work, and enable organizers to review participation and analytics in one place.
2. Problem Statement 2.1. Existing Process Organizers publish an activity. Students register through the University Portal. Organizers export registration lists to CSV or Excel. Student-card QR codes or student IDs are used for attendance. Students submit participation evidence using Google Forms where applicable. Organizers check students out and reconcile the available records. The final participant list is submitted through the university’s existing administrative process. Fragmented files can contain invalid or duplicate student IDs, missing check-in/check-out records, and incomplete evidence. Manual verification becomes increasingly difficult as participation grows.
2.2. Proposed Solution The project consolidates the relevant workflows in a Web Application. It does not claim direct API integration with the University Portal or Google Sheets.
Source Collection method in the current MVP University Portal ADMIN exports and imports CSV/XLSX registration lists. Student Card QR / Student ID ADMIN records Check-in/Check-out immediately through FastAPI, using ID entry or a scanner acting as keyboard input. Google Forms / Google Sheets ADMIN exports and imports evidence files in CSV/XLSX format. The backend validates required fields, student IDs, and duplicates. Registration, Attendance, and Evidence are associated with the corresponding Activity ID to support reconciliation.
Important: Check-in and Check-out are designed to be written when a student arrives or leaves; they are not primarily recorded by importing attendance spreadsheets after the event. Complete camera-based QR scanning on physical devices still requires further verification.
2.3. Objectives Centralize student activity and participation data. Reduce manual CSV/Excel reconciliation. Support real-time Check-in and Check-out. Validate imported registration and evidence data. Reconcile records using Activity ID and Student ID. Let ADMIN review and confirm participation outcomes. Provide an Analytics Dashboard and report export. Build practical experience with Web APIs, data processing, security, and AWS. Test business data integration with DynamoDB and independent CSV processing with S3/Lambda. 2.4. Project Scope Implemented or tested within the MVP: Authentication, ADMIN/STUDENT authorization, activity and student-account management, personal profile, registration/evidence import, attendance APIs, reconciliation, participation confirmation, analytics/export, AWS Amplify frontend deployment, FastAPI demo through Cloudflare Tunnel, SQLite persistence, DynamoDB experiments, and the S3/Lambda/IAM/CloudWatch CSV test.
Outside the current scope or not fully verified: Direct University Portal/Google Sheets API integrations, a verified camera QR scanner on real devices, automatic university conduct-point credits, an always-on AWS-hosted FastAPI production backend, migration of every API to DynamoDB, automated S3-to-Lambda event triggering, Cognito, API Gateway, Glue, Athena, QuickSight, and production-scale load testing.
2.5. Target Users Role Access and responsibilities ADMIN Manage activities and student accounts; import data; record attendance; reconcile and confirm participation; view analytics and export results. STUDENT Sign in, view authorized personal information and activities, change password, and track personal participation results. Event organizers operate under ADMIN. STAFF is not a separate business role in the current application.
3. Solution Architecture 3.1. Actual Architecture Overview This actual project architecture diagram shows the main application, the tested DynamoDB storage integration, and the independently executed serverless CSV processing experiment. It does not claim that the backend is deployed on AWS or that an S3 event trigger has been configured.
Web Application and local demo: Users access React/Vite through AWS Amplify Hosting. Their browsers send API requests through Cloudflare Quick Tunnel to a locally running FastAPI backend, with an access token on protected endpoints. The backend handles business logic and SQLite local persistence.
AWS cloud-data experiment: FastAPI has been integrated or tested with DynamoDB through boto3 for Activities, Registrations, Attendance, Evidence, and Participation. Successful table or item tests do not mean all application storage was migrated from SQLite.
Independent serverless experiment: Amazon S3 stores CSV input, AWS Lambda validates records and writes JSON output, AWS IAM authorizes resource access, and CloudWatch provides execution logs and metrics. The Lambda function was invoked manually through a Test Event.
3.2. Application Connectivity AWS Amplify serves the web interface; it is not the application’s API Gateway or backend proxy. The user browser makes the actual FastAPI requests through Cloudflare Quick Tunnel. SQLite remains part of the local demo, while DynamoDB integration is treated as a separate tested capability.
For evidence, refer to the actual architecture diagram above and the frontend/backend screenshots in Workshop 5.3–5.9.
3.3. Technology Stack Component Technology Responsibility Frontend React/Vite ADMIN/STUDENT interface and analytics. Backend Python/FastAPI REST APIs, authentication, authorization, and business logic. Local persistence SQLite Demo persistence and recovery. Tested cloud database Amazon DynamoDB Cloud-data integration tests. Frontend hosting AWS Amplify Frontend build and hosting. Network connectivity Cloudflare Quick Tunnel Temporary HTTPS access to local FastAPI. Object storage Amazon S3 Sample CSV input and processed JSON output. Serverless processing AWS Lambda Independent CSV processing demonstration. Resource permissions AWS IAM Execution role and service permissions. Monitoring Amazon CloudWatch Lambda logs and metrics. Version control Git/GitHub Project source and change history. Documentation Hugo/Markdown Internship workshop and report. 3.4. Data Design Group Main information Users / Students Account, student ID, profile, role, status. Activities Activity ID, name, schedule, location, status. Registrations Registration by student and activity. Attendance Check-in, check-out, timestamps. Evidence Participation evidence by student and activity. Participation Reconciliation result and confirmation status. Reconciliation uses Student ID together with Activity ID to avoid mixing records from different events.
3.5. Implemented Business Features – Screenshots Instead of a hypothetical flowchart, the following screenshots demonstrate real interfaces and results implemented in the project.
3.6. Security and Monitoring FastAPI uses token-based authentication and ADMIN/STUDENT authorization for application access. AWS IAM controls AWS resource permissions and does not replace application sign-in. The project emphasizes validation, least-privilege AWS permissions, secret protection, and synthetic or anonymized demo data.
CloudWatch logging applies to the independent Lambda demo. No API Gateway logging, CloudWatch alarm configuration, or FastAPI log integration is claimed without implementation evidence. The demo log retention setting was seven days.
4. Technical Implementation 4.1. Main Features Feature Implemented responsibility Authentication Sign-in/out, token validation, password changes. Authorization ADMIN/STUDENT role restrictions in frontend and backend. Activity management Activity creation, display, updates, and status. Student-account administration ADMIN list, lock/unlock, reset passwords, synchronize accounts. Personal profile Authorized profile view and updates. Registration import CSV/XLSX validation and import. Attendance Real-time check-in and check-out with duplicate/time checks. Evidence import Import and validate participation evidence. Reconciliation Associate registration, attendance, and evidence. Participation confirmation ADMIN review and decision. Analytics Summary indicators and activity statistics. Export Supported report and data export formats. Students cannot access administrative account management, data imports, or participation confirmation. Business time logic uses Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh.
4.2. Reconciliation Rules Registration Check-in Check-out Evidence Example result Yes Yes Yes Yes Complete data. Yes Yes No Yes Missing Check-out. Yes No Yes Yes Missing Check-in. Yes No No No Registered without participation records. Yes Yes Yes No Missing evidence. Yes No No Yes Evidence present, attendance missing. No Yes Yes Yes Registration needs review. Missing information does not automatically prove non-participation. ADMIN applies activity-specific business rules when confirming or rejecting records.
4.3. Actual Serverless CSV Processing Test The real experiment was performed on Amazon S3 and AWS Lambda using an IAM execution role and CloudWatch logs. The Lambda console test returned the following recorded results:
Test metric Observed result Total records 4 Valid records 2 Duplicate records 1 Invalid records 1 Response status code 200 Output object registrations-result.json This experiment is separate from the web application’s CSV/XLSX import implementation. S3 Event Notifications were not configured as an automatic trigger during the recorded test.
4.4. Non-functional Requirements Usability: Clear role-based user interface and understandable errors. Security: Backend permission checks, protected credentials, appropriate personal-data handling. Reliability: Validation, duplicate checks, and relevant backup practices. Maintainability: Separate modules and repositories, documentation, version control. Performance: Adequate for demos; production-scale load testing remains necessary. 4.5. Test Strategy Test cases cover valid and invalid sign-in, locked accounts, unauthorized ADMIN API access, malformed CSV/XLSX files, duplicate student IDs, invalid check-in/check-out records, missing evidence, reconciliation, confirmation, analytics, and export. AWS-related checks include DynamoDB read/write tests and Lambda processing with S3 and CloudWatch. A proper Test Report should distinguish expected from observed results.
5. Roadmap and Implementation Milestones The twelve-week internship plan runs from September 7 to November 27, 2026. Future milestones should not be described as completed before evidence exists.
Week Main activity 1 Cloud Computing, AWS Fundamentals, AWS CLI, Amazon EC2. 2 Requirements and architecture proposal. 3 FastAPI, SQLite, and core REST APIs. 4 DynamoDB/S3 research and cloud-data experiments. 5 React/Vite, authentication, role-based controls. 6 Registration and evidence CSV/XLSX import. 7 Reconciliation and analytics. 8 Integration tests and improvements. 9 Amplify hosting, FastAPI demo, Cloudflare Tunnel. 10 S3, Lambda, IAM, CloudWatch experiments. 11 Demo preparation and technical documentation. 12 Report finalization, website review, archiving and handover preparation. Future enhancements: Stable cloud backend deployment, production data architecture, QR scanner verification, direct university-system APIs, S3/Lambda event-driven automation, advanced analytics, monitoring, CI/CD, and load/security testing.
6. Budget Estimation AWS Service Cost drivers Amplify Build, hosting, storage, transfer. DynamoDB Storage and database requests/capacity. S3 Object storage, requests, transfer. Lambda Invocations, memory, duration. CloudWatch Log ingestion/storage and metrics. IAM No direct charges for roles or policies. The MVP minimizes cost through local demo hosting, limited test data, and cleanup of unnecessary resources. Actual charges depend on the region, workload and account terms; the project does not assume zero AWS expenditure. Use AWS Pricing Calculator and Billing data for estimates.
7. Risk Assessment Risk Potential impact Mitigation Invalid files / duplicate IDs Medium–High Input validation and duplicate detection. Missing attendance or evidence High Reconciliation and manual ADMIN review. Unauthorized access High Token validation and backend role checks. Local FastAPI outage High Pre-demo verification and local restart plan. Temporary Cloudflare URL changes High Update frontend API URL and retest. SQLite and DynamoDB mismatch High Identify source of truth and synchronization boundaries. Lambda/IAM failure Medium–High Verify role permissions, S3 objects and logs. Personal-data/secret exposure High Synthetic data, anonymization, least privilege. Unexpected AWS costs Medium Billing review and resource cleanup. Production scaling limits High Load testing before operational deployment. When necessary, organizers can correct and re-import files or use the existing spreadsheet procedure. Backup assumptions should reflect the persistence mechanism actually in use.
8. Expected Outcomes 8.1. Improved Operations The system is intended to reduce repetitive manual comparison of student IDs and provide a centralized view of Registration, Attendance, Evidence, Reconciliation, and Participation. STUDENT can access only their authorized records.
8.2. Analytics and Export The dashboard supports indicators for activities, registrations, attendance, confirmed participation, rates and missing data. As an illustrative example only, 1,050 confirmations out of 1,200 registrations would yield 87.5%; these are not actual event measurements.
8.3. AWS Outcomes Actual evidence documents AWS Amplify hosting, DynamoDB tests, S3 input/output, Lambda CSV processing, IAM permissions and CloudWatch monitoring. Undeployed technologies are not presented as completed services.
8.4. Deliverables Frontend/Backend source code and GitHub repository. Web Application demo with synthetic data. Architecture diagram, proposal and documentation. API guide, test report, and demo materials. AWS screenshots, worklog and Hugo workshop website. 8.5. Limitations and Future Work FastAPI currently depends on a local computer and the temporary Cloudflare Tunnel. SQLite remains part of the demo; not every data-access API has been verified as fully migrated to DynamoDB. Lambda processing is a separate experiment. Full camera QR scanning, direct university API integration, production backend hosting, and large-scale performance testing remain future work.
Note: This proposal reflects documented implementation and experimental evidence. Any incomplete final internship milestones must be checked before being reported as finished.

title: ADMIN/STUDENT Authentication and Authorization
content:
ADMIN/STUDENT Authentication and Authorization In this section, we will explore how the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform manages user authentication, login sessions, and access permissions.
The system uses two main roles:
ADMIN: Administrators and activity organizers. STUDENT: Students who access activities and their participation results. Authentication and Authorization are handled by the FastAPI Backend. The Frontend uses authentication results to display the appropriate interface.
The current Demo does not use Amazon Cognito.
1. Understand Authentication and Authorization Authentication
Authentication verifies a user’s identity.
For example, a user enters a username and password. The Backend validates the credentials and returns an Access Token when the credentials are valid.
Authorization
Authorization determines whether a user is permitted to perform a specific operation.
For example:
ADMIN users can manage student accounts. STUDENT users cannot access other students’ account management information. Authentication identifies the user, while Authorization determines what the user can do.
2. Understand the login workflow ADMIN / STUDENT | | Username + Password v React Login Interface | | POST /auth/login v FastAPI Authentication | | Validate Credentials v Access Token + User Information | v Frontend Session Storage | v Role-based User Interface The login workflow includes:
The user opens the login page. The user enters a username and password. The Frontend sends a request to POST /auth/login. The Backend validates the credentials and account status. The Backend returns authentication information after successful login. The Frontend stores the login session. The Frontend displays functionality appropriate for the user’s Role. 3. Review Authentication APIs Open Swagger UI:
http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs
Relevant Authentication APIs include:
Endpoint Method Purpose /auth/login POST User login /auth/me GET Retrieve current user information /auth/logout POST User logout /auth/change-password POST Change password Profile and avatar functionality uses the corresponding APIs in the Backend’s Authentication/Profile group.
Review each API’s HTTP Method and Request Schema in Swagger UI before sending a request.
4. Understand Access Token management The project’s Frontend uses two localStorage keys for authentication sessions:
sap_access_token sap_current_user Where:
sap_access_token: Stores the Access Token received from the Backend. sap_current_user: Stores information about the current user. An illustrative session storage function:
function saveSession(token, user) { localStorage.setItem("sap_access_token", token); localStorage.setItem( "sap_current_user", JSON.stringify(user) ); window.dispatchEvent( new Event("sap-auth-change") ); } The sap-auth-change event helps interface components detect authentication state changes.
The project uses subscribeAuthChange to observe authentication changes and update related session information and interface components.
This example demonstrates the underlying mechanism. Preserve the existing authentication functions when working with the project source code.
5. Inspect the browser login session Open the Frontend. Sign in using an ADMIN Demo account. Press F12. Select the Application tab. Open Local Storage. Select the http://localhost:5173 origin. Verify that the following keys exist:
sap_access_token sap_current_user The complete Token value does not need to be displayed in the internship report.
localStorage is the session storage mechanism used in the current Demo. JavaScript running on the same origin can access these values, so XSS prevention is important. Never store passwords or AWS credentials in localStorage. A Production architecture may consider more secure session mechanisms, such as HttpOnly Cookies with appropriate CSRF protection.
6. Verify current user information After login, the Backend provides:
GET /auth/me The Frontend can use this API to verify the current authentication session.
Workflow:
Stored Access Token | v GET /auth/me | v FastAPI Token Validation | v Current User Information | v Update Frontend Session Review the returned user information and Role.
The Role provided by the Backend determines which operations the user is authorized to perform.
Changing the Role in localStorage must not grant additional Backend permissions.
7. ADMIN and STUDENT authorization The system uses only two main roles.
Feature ADMIN STUDENT Sign in Yes Yes View personal profile Yes Yes View authorized activities Yes Yes Create and manage activities Yes No Manage student accounts Yes No Import registration records Yes No Administrative attendance recording Yes No Import evidence files Yes No Reconcile participation data Yes No Confirm participation results Yes No View personal participation results As authorized Yes View administrative reports Yes No Actual access must follow the application’s business rules and Backend API authorization.
STAFF is not an independent user Role in the current implementation.
8. Test the ADMIN interface Sign in using an ADMIN Demo account.
Inspect the administrative functionality available on the Home page or Sidebar.
ADMIN users can access:
Activity Management. Student Account Management. Registration Import. Attendance Management. Evidence Import. Reconciliation and Participation Confirmation. Analytics and Export. Open Student Account Management.
Administrative operations include:
View student accounts. Lock and unlock accounts. Reset passwords. Synchronize student accounts. Use a dedicated synthetic student account when testing account locking or password resets.
9. Test the STUDENT interface Sign out of the ADMIN account.
Sign in using a STUDENT Demo account.
Verify that:
The student Home page is displayed. Authorized personal functionality is accessible. Students can view activity information and their own participation results. Student Account Management is not displayed. ADMIN-only features are not displayed. Hiding administrative features improves the user interface, but it is not the only security mechanism.
10. Verify Backend authorization Use a STUDENT Access Token to test the administrative API:
GET /admin/students Send the request through Swagger UI or an API Client.
Expected result:
HTTP 403 Forbidden If the Token is invalid or authentication is missing, the Backend may return HTTP 401.
Next, test the same Endpoint using an ADMIN account.
Expected result:
HTTP 200 OK The Frontend displays functionality according to user roles. FastAPI enforces actual resource access permissions. Administrative APIs must verify ADMIN permissions through Backend Authorization.
11. Test the personal profile Sign in using a Demo account.
Open the personal profile page.
Verify the functionality available in the current Frontend:
View user information. Update permitted profile fields. Change the avatar if the feature is enabled. Change the password. Profile-related APIs are managed by the Backend, including the /auth/profile and /auth/avatar API groups.
Perform operations according to the current interface and API Schema.
12. Test logout Select Logout in the user interface.
The Frontend should handle the authentication session according to the existing implementation, including clearing local authentication information and updating the interface state.
Illustrative example:
function clearLocalSession() { localStorage.removeItem("sap_access_token"); localStorage.removeItem("sap_current_user"); window.dispatchEvent( new Event("sap-auth-change") ); } If the application calls POST /auth/logout, also verify the Backend response.
After logout:
The login interface is displayed. Protected functionality is no longer available through the previous Frontend session. Local authentication information has been removed. 13. Summarize authentication test results Test Expected Result ADMIN Login Successful login STUDENT Login Successful login Invalid Credentials Login failure message Access Token Managed within the authentication session ADMIN Interface Administrative functionality displayed STUDENT Interface Only authorized functionality displayed Protected API Access Token validation Admin API with STUDENT Token Access denied Personal Profile Current user information displayed Logout Local login session cleared Conclusion In this section, we explored Authentication and Authorization in the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform.
The React/Vite Frontend uses Access Tokens and user information to manage authentication state and display the appropriate interface. FastAPI verifies user identity and enforces resource access permissions.
Clear separation between ADMIN and STUDENT permissions helps protect student data and ensures administrative operations remain within their authorized scope.
Next: Test the interface and system functionality

title: Backend Development with FastAPI
content:
Backend Development with FastAPI In this section, we will develop and configure the Backend for the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform using Python and FastAPI.
FastAPI is a modern Python Web Framework that supports high-performance REST API development, input validation, and automatic API documentation through Swagger UI.
The Backend is responsible for the main business functions of the system:
User authentication and Access Token management. ADMIN and STUDENT role-based authorization. Student activity management. Student account management. Registration and evidence imports from CSV/XLSX files. Real-time Check-in and Check-out recording. Data reconciliation and participation confirmation. Data aggregation for Analytics Dashboard and Export. In the Demo version, the Backend uses SQLite for local data persistence and recovery. Amazon DynamoDB integration and testing will be covered in the following workshop section.
The React/Vite Frontend communicates with the Backend through REST APIs.
Contents Set up and configure the FastAPI Backend Test the Backend and REST APIs After completing this section, you will have a working local Backend environment ready for Frontend connectivity and AWS service integration.

title: Build the AWS Lambda CSV Processor
content:
Build the AWS Lambda CSV Processor In this section, we will develop an AWS Lambda Function to process student registration data stored in Amazon S3.
AWS Lambda enables code execution without directly managing servers.
The Function uses Python and boto3 to interact with Amazon S3.
1. Understand the processing workflow Lambda Test Event | v Lambda Handler | v Get CSV Object from S3 | v Decode UTF-8 Content | v Read CSV Records | +-- Missing Student ID | -> Invalid | +-- Repeated Student ID | -> Duplicate | +-- Valid Unique Student ID -> Valid | v Generate JSON Summary | v Put JSON Object to S3 | v Return Execution Result This exercise focuses on input validation and summary report generation.
Lambda does not directly update FastAPI Registration records or write business data to DynamoDB.
2. Open the AWS Lambda Console Open the AWS Lambda Console. Select Asia Pacific (Singapore) - ap-southeast-1. Select Functions. Locate: sap-csv-processor-demo Reuse the existing Function if available.
3. Create a Lambda Function if required Choose Create function. Choose Author from scratch. Enter the Function name: sap-csv-processor-demo Select an AWS-supported Python Runtime, such as Python 3.12. Architecture: x86_64. Under Execution role, select Use an existing role. Select the Role configured in section 5.10.2. Choose Create function. A Function URL is not required.
A VPC connection is not required for this exercise.
The Python Runtime above is a workshop reproduction choice, not a verified historical Runtime version.
4. Configure Lambda resources Open the Function.
Select Configuration. Select General configuration. Choose Edit. Configure: Memory: 128 MB Timeout: 10 seconds Choose Save. These settings match the project’s previous CSV Processor exercise.
The small test dataset does not require a large memory allocation.
5. Configure environment variables In the Lambda Console:
Select Configuration. Select Environment variables. Choose Edit. Add: Key Value S3_BUCKET sap-data-project-2026-huflit01 INPUT_KEY lambda-demo/input/registrations.csv OUTPUT_KEY lambda-demo/processed/registrations-result.json These variables configure the Bucket and Object Keys in the reconstructed workshop implementation.
Do not store AWS Access Keys, Secret Access Keys, or passwords in these variables.
6. Implement Lambda source code Select the Code tab.
Open lambda_function.py.
Use the following code to reproduce the exercise.
import os import csv import io import json import logging import boto3 logger = logging.getLogger() logger.setLevel(logging.INFO) s3 = boto3.client("s3") def lambda_handler(event, context): bucket = os.environ.get( "S3_BUCKET", "sap-data-project-2026-huflit01" ) input_key = os.environ.get( "INPUT_KEY", "lambda-demo/input/registrations.csv" ) output_key = os.environ.get( "OUTPUT_KEY", "lambda-demo/processed/registrations-result.json" ) try: # Step 1: Read the input CSV from S3 response = s3.get_object( Bucket=bucket, Key=input_key ) content = response["Body"].read().decode("utf-8-sig") # Step 2: Parse CSV records reader = csv.DictReader( io.StringIO(content) ) required_columns = {"mssv", "full_name"} if not required_columns.issubset( set(reader.fieldnames or []) ): raise ValueError( "CSV must contain mssv and full_name columns" ) seen_students = set() total = 0 valid = 0 duplicates = 0 invalid = 0 # Step 3: Validate each record for row in reader: total += 1 mssv = (row.get("mssv") or "").strip() full_name = ( row.get("full_name") or "" ).strip() if not mssv or not full_name: invalid += 1 continue if mssv in seen_students: duplicates += 1 continue seen_students.add(mssv) valid += 1 # Step 4: Generate JSON summary result = { "total": total, "valid": valid, "duplicates": duplicates, "invalid": invalid } # Step 5: Save the result to S3 s3.put_object( Bucket=bucket, Key=output_key, Body=json.dumps(result).encode("utf-8"), ContentType="application/json" ) # Step 6: Record processing information logger.info( "SAP S3 demo processed: %s", json.dumps(result) ) return { "statusCode": 200, "body": json.dumps(result) } except Exception: logger.exception( "SAP CSV processing failed" ) raise Choose Deploy to save and deploy the source code.
This workshop implementation recreates the project’s previously recorded CSV processing results. It is not a verbatim copy of the historical Lambda source code. Preserve the original working source before replacing it or use a separate test Function.
7. Understand the source code Initialize the Amazon S3 Client s3 = boto3.client("s3") boto3 is the AWS SDK for Python.
Lambda uses temporary credentials from its Execution Role rather than hardcoded AWS credentials.
Read the CSV file response = s3.get_object( Bucket=bucket, Key=input_key ) get_object() retrieves the CSV Object from Amazon S3.
content = response["Body"].read().decode("utf-8-sig") utf-8-sig supports UTF-8 files with or without a Byte Order Mark.
Parse CSV records reader = csv.DictReader( io.StringIO(content) ) DictReader converts CSV rows into Dictionaries using column headers.
The Function validates the mssv and full_name columns before processing records.
Validate records if not mssv or not full_name: invalid += 1 continue Records with missing required information are classified as invalid.
if mssv in seen_students: duplicates += 1 continue Repeated student IDs are classified as duplicates when a valid record with that ID has already been processed.
seen_students.add(mssv) valid += 1 Valid unique records are counted and their identifiers are tracked.
This validation applies to the current CSV file, not the university’s actual student database.
Generate and store JSON result = { "total": total, "valid": valid, "duplicates": duplicates, "invalid": invalid } The Function generates a summary Dictionary.
s3.put_object( Bucket=bucket, Key=output_key, Body=json.dumps(result).encode("utf-8"), ContentType="application/json" ) put_object() stores the JSON result in Amazon S3.
Subsequent successful invocations write a new result to the same configured Object Key.
8. Verify the Handler Inspect Runtime settings.
Handler: lambda_function.lambda_handler Where:
lambda_function: Python module name. lambda_handler: Function invoked by AWS Lambda. Update the Handler if the module or Function name changes.
9. Create a Lambda Test Event Select Test.
Choose Create new event. Enter the Event name: SAPCSVProcessingTest Use: {} Save the Test Event. The reconstructed Function reads Bucket and Object Keys from environment variables, so an empty JSON Event is sufficient.
This is the Test Event for the workshop implementation, not a verified copy of the historical Test Event.
10. Verify execution readiness Component Requirement Region ap-southeast-1 Function sap-csv-processor-demo Memory 128 MB Timeout 10 seconds Handler lambda_function.lambda_handler Execution Role S3 and CloudWatch Logs permissions Input registrations.csv exists in S3 Output Correct JSON Object Key Source Code Deployed successfully Test Event Created Results After completing this section, we have developed a Lambda Function that reads, validates, and processes CSV data from Amazon S3.
The Function classifies records as valid, duplicate, or invalid and stores a JSON summary.
In the next section, we will invoke the Function and inspect the results in Amazon S3 and CloudWatch Logs.
Next: Test and Monitor with CloudWatch

title: Clean Up AWS Test Resources
content:
Clean Up AWS Test Resources In this section, we will review how to manage and clean up AWS test resources after completing the Workshop.
The objective is to avoid unnecessary costs while preserving resources required by the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform.
The deletion procedures below are conditional guidance. Do not delete resources that are still used by the application or do not have an appropriate backup.
1. Classify resources Resources can be divided into three groups.
Group 1: Retain
Amplify App used for Frontend demonstrations. Five SAP DynamoDB Tables. Project S3 Bucket. Required backups and evidence. Group 2: Potentially disposable
Temporary CSV files no longer required. Temporary JSON processing outputs. Independent test Lambda Functions. Execution Roles and Policies used exclusively by deleted Functions. CloudWatch Log Groups no longer needed. Group 3: Require further review
Deployed Amplify Apps and branches. DynamoDB Tables with business data. S3 Buckets containing multiple Prefixes. IAM Roles shared by several services. 2. Review DynamoDB backups Open the Amazon DynamoDB Console.
Select ap-southeast-1. Choose the table to review. Open Backups. Inspect On-demand Backup or Point-in-time Recovery settings. Create an appropriate backup if the data must be retained. DynamoDB supports On-demand Backup and Point-in-time Recovery.
Restoring a backup creates a new table rather than overwriting an existing table.
Backup storage may incur charges.
3. Retain the five DynamoDB Tables Project tables:
SAP-Activities SAP-Registrations SAP-Attendance SAP-Evidence SAP-Participation Current workshop recommendation:
Action: RETAIN Reasons:
Support AWS Integration evidence. May be required for future tests. May contain Demo or business records. Form part of the existing project architecture. Consider deleting only independent test tables that no longer have dependencies and contain no data requiring retention.
4. Review Amazon S3 Objects Open the Amazon S3 Console.
Select:
sap-data-project-2026-huflit01 Review:
lambda-demo/input/registrations.csv lambda-demo/processed/registrations-result.json Retain these Objects if they are needed for screenshots or continued Lambda testing.
If they are confirmed to be disposable:
Save copies if required. Verify the Object Keys. Inspect Bucket Versioning. Select only the intended test Objects. Use Delete in the S3 Console. Verify the result. For versioned S3 Buckets, ordinary deletion may create a Delete Marker rather than permanently remove existing Object Versions. Inspect Versions and storage costs during clean-up.
5. Retain the project S3 Bucket Project Bucket:
sap-data-project-2026-huflit01 Recommendation:
Action: RETAIN Do not delete the entire Bucket solely to remove two Lambda Demo Objects.
The Bucket may contain data required by other project components.
Deleting the Bucket releases its name and does not guarantee that the same name will be available later.
6. Manage AWS Lambda Open the AWS Lambda Console.
Select:
sap-csv-processor-demo If the Function is required for section 5.10 demonstrations:
Action: RETAIN If an independent test Function is no longer required:
Verify the Function name. Inspect Triggers and dependencies. Save the source code and configuration if needed. Select the appropriate Function. Choose Actions → Delete. Review the confirmation dialog. Do not delete a Function that is still required or has not been backed up.
7. Review IAM Roles and Policies Existing resources:
Role: sap-csv-processor-demo-role-9ui2ib5d Policy: SAP-Lambda-S3-Demo-Access Retain the Execution Role and required Policies while Lambda uses them.
If a separate disposable Function has been deleted:
Verify whether its Role is used by other Functions. Inspect other Policy attachments. Remove only permissions that are no longer required. Verify that remaining applications still have the correct access. Do not delete Roles or Policies shared with other resources.
8. Manage CloudWatch Logs Open the Amazon CloudWatch Console.
Inspect:
/aws/lambda/sap-csv-processor-demo If execution evidence is still required, retain the Log Group with its configured retention:
7 days If a Log Group belongs exclusively to a deleted test Function and its logs are no longer required:
Confirm that the logs are not needed for troubleshooting or reporting. Select the appropriate Log Group. Choose Actions. Choose Delete log group(s). Review the confirmation dialog. Deleting a Lambda Function does not automatically mean its CloudWatch Logs have been deleted.
9. Manage AWS Amplify Hosting Open the AWS Amplify Console.
Review the project’s Frontend application.
If the Website is still needed:
Action: RETAIN If Hosting is no longer required and the application has been approved for removal, use the Amplify Console’s Delete app function.
Before deletion:
Review the App and Branch. Preserve required Build Settings. Record necessary non-sensitive Environment variables. Verify that GitHub retains the source code. Confirm that the Website is no longer required. Do not delete the Amplify App while its Website URL is still needed for demonstrations or reporting.
10. Review costs after clean-up Open AWS Billing and Cost Management.
Review:
Service-level charges. Remaining storage resources. Pending billing updates. Stopped or deleted services. Resources requiring continued monitoring. Billing and Cost Explorer data may be delayed.
Do not assume that charges immediately become zero after stopping or deleting a resource.
11. Summarize the clean-up plan Resource Recommended Action Amplify Frontend RETAIN SAP-Activities RETAIN SAP-Registrations RETAIN SAP-Attendance RETAIN SAP-Evidence RETAIN SAP-Participation RETAIN Project S3 Bucket RETAIN Lambda CSV Processor RETAIN if needed IAM Execution Role RETAIN while required CloudWatch Logs RETAIN as needed Cloudflare Quick Tunnel STOP FastAPI Demo STOP Results After completing this section, we have reviewed AWS resource lifecycle management.
Resources required for demonstrations and future testing are prioritized for retention, while independent test resources can be cleaned up after appropriate verification.
Next: Verify Clean-up and Review Workshop

title: Confirm Participation Results
content:
Confirm Participation Results In this section, we will confirm student participation based on previously reconciled data.
After combining Registration, Attendance, and Evidence, ADMIN users review the applicable business requirements to determine whether each student’s participation should be approved.
Confirmation results are stored as Participation records and used for Analytics Dashboard, student activity history, and report exports.
1. Distinguish Reconciliation and Participation Reconciliation
The process of comparing records from:
Registration. Attendance. Evidence. Reconciliation identifies complete and incomplete data.
Participation Confirmation
The process of determining a final participation outcome according to business requirements and ADMIN decisions.
The project’s final participation statuses include:
CONFIRMED: Student participation is approved. REJECTED: Student participation is not approved. Before a final decision, a record may remain unconfirmed according to the current implementation.
A reconciliation result does not automatically indicate confirmed Participation. Verify the actual confirmation status stored by the Backend.
2. Prepare the environment and data Complete:
Section 5.6 - Registration and Attendance Management. Section 5.7.1 - Import Participation Evidence. Section 5.7.2 - Reconcile Student Participation Data. Ensure that the following are available:
FastAPI Backend. React/Vite Frontend. An ADMIN Demo account. An activity with reconciliation results. Use the same Activity ID from previous exercises.
3. Understand the confirmation workflow Reconciliation Result | v ADMIN Review | v Validate Activity Requirements | v Participation Decision | +-- CONFIRMED | +-- REJECTED | v FastAPI Participation Processing | v Store Participation Result | v Analytics / Student History / Export The Backend validates ADMIN permissions, activity information, student information, and business conditions before saving the confirmation result.
4. Open the participation confirmation interface Open the Web Application. Sign in using an ADMIN account. Select the reconciled activity. Open Reconciliation or Participation. Inspect student records and reconciliation results. Review:
Student ID. Full name if displayed. Registration status. Check-in information. Check-out information. Evidence status. Reconciliation result. Current confirmation status. 5. Review participation requirements Use the synthetic dataset from section 5.7.2:
Student ID Check-in Check-out Evidence 0818000001 Yes Yes Yes 0818000002 Yes No Yes 0818000003 No No Yes 0818000004 Yes Yes No For this illustrative exercise, assume the activity requires registration, complete Check-in/Check-out, and valid evidence.
Under this assumption:
Student 0818000001 has complete data for confirmation review. Student 0818000002 requires missing Check-out review. Student 0818000003 has no Attendance records. Student 0818000004 requires evidence review. These are assumed workshop requirements. Actual confirmation decisions must follow the activity’s configured business rules.
6. Perform a CONFIRMED decision Select the Demo student with complete records:
Student ID: 0818000001 Perform the following:
Open the student’s reconciliation details. Review Registration, Attendance, and Evidence. Select the participation confirmation operation. Verify the information before saving. Confirm the operation. The Frontend submits the confirmation request to FastAPI.
The Backend validates permissions and business conditions, then saves the result if the operation is valid.
Expected result:
Student ID: 0818000001 Participation Status: CONFIRMED Reload the records to verify the stored status.
7. Perform a REJECTED decision Select the Demo student who does not satisfy the illustrative requirements:
Student ID: 0818000003 This student has Evidence but no Check-in or Check-out records.
Perform the following:
Review the reconciliation result. Identify the reason for ineligibility. Select the rejection operation. Provide a reason if supported by the interface and API. Save the result. Expected result:
Student ID: 0818000003 Participation Status: REJECTED Earlier AWS Pilot tests included records containing NO_ATTENDANCE, REJECTED, and evidence_status: YES.
This illustrates that having evidence does not automatically satisfy attendance requirements.
8. Review incomplete records Not every incomplete record should be rejected immediately.
Examples include:
Missing Check-out information requiring investigation. Evidence not yet submitted at the reconciliation time. Registration data not yet fully updated. Imported evidence awaiting review. ADMIN users should evaluate records according to activity requirements before making decisions.
If source data is legitimately updated, perform reconciliation again using the application’s supported workflow.
If a final participation decision needs modification, use the supported Backend operation rather than directly editing SQLite or DynamoDB records.
9. Inspect the confirmation REST API Press F12 to open Developer Tools.
Select Network. Select Fetch/XHR. Confirm a Demo participation record. Inspect the corresponding request. Verify Activity ID, Student ID, and confirmation status. Inspect the HTTP Status Code and Response. Open Swagger UI to identify the actual confirmation Endpoint in the Participation group:
http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs
Illustrative business data:
{ "activity_id": "ACT-DEMO-001", "mssv": "0818000001", "participation_status": "CONFIRMED" } This is an illustrative data model. Do not use it as an actual Request Body without verifying the current API Schema.
10. Verify confirmation authorization The system uses two roles:
ADMIN. STUDENT. ADMIN users review and confirm participation results.
STUDENT users can access their own participation information within their authorized scope.
Test:
Sign in using a STUDENT Demo account. Verify that administrative confirmation controls are unavailable. Use a STUDENT Access Token to test the confirmation Endpoint identified in Swagger UI. Verify that the Backend rejects unauthorized operations. The expected result is HTTP 403 Forbidden for an authenticated account without sufficient permissions.
11. Verify confirmed results Return to the activity’s Participation list.
Verify that:
CONFIRMED is stored for the correct student. REJECTED is stored for the correct student. Other student records remain unchanged. Activity ID remains correct. Attendance and Evidence source records remain accurate. Example:
Student ID Participation Status 0818000001 CONFIRMED 0818000003 REJECTED Do not assume that other students have been confirmed without corresponding decisions.
12. Summarize test cases Test Case Expected Result Confirm an eligible record CONFIRMED stored Reject an ineligible record REJECTED stored Incorrect Activity ID No unrelated activity updated Invalid Student ID No incorrect student updated STUDENT attempts confirmation Access denied when unauthorized Reload page Saved results displayed Updated source data Handled through the current reconciliation workflow Conclusion In this section, we practiced confirming and rejecting participation results using ADMIN permissions.
Participation represents a business outcome based on reconciled data rather than merely registration or attendance status.
These results will support student activity history, Analytics Dashboard, and Export.
Participation confirmation in the project does not automatically update official student conduct scores in the university’s University Portal.
Next: Verify Participation Results

title: Deploy the Frontend with AWS Amplify Hosting
content:
Deploy the Frontend with AWS Amplify Hosting In this section, we will deploy the React/Vite interface of the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform using AWS Amplify Hosting.
AWS Amplify retrieves the Frontend source code from GitHub, installs dependencies, builds the application, and provides an Internet-accessible HTTPS Website.
1. Prepare for deployment Complete:
Section 5.9.1 - Prepare Source Code and Deployment Configuration. Section 5.9.2 - Connect the Backend using Cloudflare Quick Tunnel. Required components:
