GitHub Repository fcaj. Branch main. React/Vite Frontend that builds successfully. FastAPI Demo Backend running on port 8001. Cloudflare Quick Tunnel HTTPS URL. AWS Account with Amplify Hosting permissions. Verify the Tunnel Health Endpoint before deployment.
2. Open the AWS Amplify Console Open the AWS Management Console.
Search for AWS Amplify.
Open the AWS Amplify Console.
Select the Region containing the project’s Amplify App.
For a new application, choose Create new app.
If the Amplify App already exists, open it and inspect the main branch. Do not create another application solely to update the Backend API URL.
3. Connect the GitHub Repository When creating a new Amplify App:
Select GitHub as the Git Provider. Choose Next. Authenticate the GitHub connection. Grant access to the required repository. Select fcaj. Select the main branch. Grant access only to the required repository when possible.
4. Identify the Frontend directory Inspect the GitHub source code to identify the directory containing the React/Vite package.json file.
Example structure:
fcaj/ ├── backend/ ├── frontend/ │ ├── src/ │ └── package.json └── ... In this example, the application root is:
frontend If the project is nested:
fcaj/ └── student-activity-platform/ └── frontend/ └── package.json The application root becomes:
student-activity-platform/frontend These structures are illustrative. Use the actual Frontend location in the current GitHub Repository.
If the My app is a monorepo option is available, select it and specify the appropriate application path.
5. Configure Amplify Build Settings Amplify requires instructions for dependency installation, application builds, and locating deployment artifacts.
If frontend is located directly in the repository root, an illustrative monorepo build configuration is:
version: 1 applications: - appRoot: frontend frontend: phases: preBuild: commands: - npm ci build: commands: - npm run build artifacts: baseDirectory: dist files: - '**/*' Explanation:
appRoot: Identifies the React/Vite application directory. preBuild: Installs dependencies. build: Builds the Frontend. baseDirectory: Identifies the output directory. files: Specifies deployment artifacts. With this configuration, build commands run from appRoot.
If package-lock.json is unavailable, prepare a lockfile or use npm install as appropriate.
For a nested Frontend, replace appRoot with the actual directory.
For monorepo applications, verify that AMPLIFY_MONOREPO_APP_ROOT matches appRoot.
This is an illustrative React/Vite build configuration, not a verified copy of the original amplify.yml used during the previous deployment. Preserve existing working build settings and review the required configuration.
Reference:
Configuring monorepo build settings
6. Configure VITE_API_BASE_URL This step enables the Amplify-hosted Frontend to communicate with FastAPI.
In the Amplify Console:
Open the Frontend application. Select Hosting from the navigation pane. Select Environment variables. Choose Manage variables. Add or update: Variable: VITE_API_BASE_URL Value:
https://YOUR-TUNNEL.trycloudflare.com Replace the example with the active Cloudflare Quick Tunnel URL.
During the November 9, 2026 test, the project used:
VITE_API_BASE_URL= https://replies-cabinet-recipes-prevent.trycloudflare.com This is a historical deployment value.
For a new workshop execution, use the active URL from section 5.9.2.
Do not append /health or /docs to the Base URL.
Do not store AWS credentials, account passwords, or Access Tokens in VITE_-prefixed variables. These values may be embedded in publicly delivered JavaScript.
7. Deploy the Frontend For a new Amplify App:
Review the Repository and Branch. Review Build Settings. Review Environment variables. Choose Save and deploy. For an existing application:
Save the updated environment variable. Open the main branch. Redeploy the branch using the Amplify Console. Amplify prepares the build environment, retrieves source code, installs dependencies, builds the application, and deploys Frontend assets.
Inspect the Build Logs to monitor these operations.
8. Verify Deployment status After deployment:
The main branch has a successful deployment status. Build Logs contain no critical errors. The dist directory has been used for deployment. A Website URL is available. The project previously used:
https://main.d2p96elhe5x6se.amplifyapp.com This is the Website URL used during the historical deployment test. A new Amplify App will provide its own Website URL.
9. Configure React SPA routing If the React application uses client-side routing, verify direct access and page refresh behavior for application routes.
Illustrative routes:
/login /activities /profile Use the actual routes defined in the application.
If the Home page loads but direct navigation to an application route fails, inspect Rewrites and redirects in Amplify Hosting.
An SPA rewrite can route application paths to index.html.
Illustrative configuration:
[ { "source": "</^[^.]+$/>", "target": "/index.html", "status": "200" } ] This example handles SPA routes without periods and avoids rewriting ordinary assets with file extensions.
Preserve suitable existing rewrite rules rather than introducing duplicates.
Reference:
Redirects and rewrites in Amplify Hosting
10. Verify the Website and API connectivity Open the Amplify Website.
Verify:
The login page is displayed. CSS and JavaScript assets load correctly. No critical Frontend resource errors occur. The Frontend uses the Cloudflare HTTPS API Endpoint. Press F12 to open Developer Tools.
Select Network and perform a login operation.
The Request URL should point to:
https://YOUR-TUNNEL.trycloudflare.com/auth/login Instead of:
http://127.0.0.1:8000/auth/login If the Frontend still calls localhost, verify:
VITE_API_BASE_URL has been saved correctly. api.js reads the environment variable. Amplify has rebuilt the Frontend. The browser is not using an outdated build. 11. Verify CORS after deployment FastAPI must allow the Amplify Website origin.
The previous deployment used:
https://main.d2p96elhe5x6se.amplifyapp.com For a new Amplify App, configure its actual Website origin.
Restart FastAPI if the CORS configuration changes.
Inspect Network requests to confirm browser API access.
12. Update the application when the Tunnel changes When cloudflared starts again and generates a new URL:
Copy the new URL. Verify its /health Endpoint. Open Amplify Environment variables. Update VITE_API_BASE_URL. Save the configuration. Redeploy the main branch. Open the Website and inspect API requests. Vite reads VITE_-prefixed variables during the build process.
Saving a new environment variable does not update JavaScript that has already been deployed.
Rebuild and redeploy the Frontend to apply the new URL.
13. Troubleshoot common issues Issue What to Check Build failure Node.js, package.json, and Build Logs package.json not found appRoot or build directory dist not found Build command and artifacts Blank Website JavaScript, CSS, and build configuration Route refresh failure SPA Rewrites and redirects Failed to fetch Tunnel, Backend, and CORS Requests target localhost VITE_API_BASE_URL and Redeploy Outdated API URL Environment variables and deployed build HTTP 502 Backend port 8001 and cloudflared Results During the November 9, 2026 deployment test, the project successfully:
Deployed the React/Vite Frontend using AWS Amplify Hosting. Used the fcaj repository and main branch. Configured VITE_API_BASE_URL. Redeployed the Frontend with the HTTPS Backend URL. Verified requests from Amplify to FastAPI through Cloudflare Quick Tunnel. AWS Amplify provides Cloud hosting for the Web interface, while the Demo Backend remains hosted on the local computer.
Next: Verify the Deployed Application

title: Export CSV/XLSX Reports
content:
Export CSV/XLSX Reports In this section, we will explore report export functionality in the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform.
After completing registration, attendance recording, evidence imports, and participation confirmation, organizers need consolidated results for administration and reporting.
Export functionality converts business data into files that can be opened using Microsoft Excel or other data processing tools.
1. Understand the purpose of Export Exported records can support:
Registration list verification. Check-in and Check-out summaries. Evidence tracking. Reconciliation review. Confirmed participant lists. Activity result archiving. Administrative reporting. Exported results reflect the selected data scope at the time the report is generated.
Exporting a report does not automatically update official student conduct scores or university records in the University Portal.
2. Distinguish CSV and XLSX Criteria CSV XLSX Format Delimited text Excel Workbook Compatibility Excel, Python, and other tools Excel and compatible applications Cell formatting Not supported Supported Multiple worksheets No Yes Purpose Data exchange and processing Structured reporting Select the file format supported by the current application.
Do not rename a CSV file with an XLSX extension because the two formats use different file structures.
3. Understand the Export architecture ADMIN | v React / Vite Frontend | | Export Request v FastAPI Backend | v Authentication & Authorization | v Retrieve Business Records | v Generate Report Data | v Return CSV / XLSX File | v Browser Download The Backend validates permissions, retrieves records, and generates report content.
The Frontend receives the response and supports the browser download process.
If an existing Export operation generates the file directly in the Frontend from API data, review its actual implementation.
4. Prepare report data Reuse the Demo activity from sections 5.6 and 5.7.
Illustrative records:
Student ID Check-in Check-out Evidence Participation 0818000001 08:05 11:30 Yes CONFIRMED 0818000002 08:10 Not recorded Yes Not yet confirmed 0818000003 Not recorded Not recorded Yes REJECTED 0818000004 08:15 11:35 No Not yet confirmed These are synthetic examples.
Use the actual Activity ID and business records stored by the Backend when performing the Export exercise.
5. Access the Export function Open the Web Application. Sign in using an ADMIN account. Select the target activity. Open data management, reconciliation, or participation results. Locate Export or Download Report. Verify the selected activity and report scope.
If filters are available, determine whether the Export includes all records or only filtered records.
6. Export a CSV report If CSV Export is available:
Select the activity. Select the report type. Choose Export CSV. Verify the downloaded file. Open it using Excel or a text editor. Example filename:
participation-report.csv Illustrative content:
activity_id,mssv,full_name,check_in,check_out,evidence_status,participation_status ACT-DEMO-001,0818000001,Student A,08:05,11:30,YES,CONFIRMED ACT-DEMO-001,0818000002,Student B,08:10,,YES, ACT-DEMO-001,0818000003,Student C,,,YES,REJECTED ACT-DEMO-001,0818000004,Student D,08:15,11:35,NO, The filename, column names, and timestamp format are illustrative.
Use the actual report structure supported by the application.
7. Open CSV using Microsoft Excel To preserve leading zeros in student IDs:
Open Microsoft Excel. Select Data. Select From Text/CSV. Select the exported file. Inspect the File Origin and encoding. Select Transform Data if data types need adjustment. Set the Student ID column to Text. Load the data into the worksheet. CSV files do not store cell data types. Opening a CSV directly in Excel may convert student IDs into numbers and remove leading zeros. Verify identifier formatting when reviewing reports.
8. Export an XLSX report If Excel Export is supported:
Select the target activity. Choose Export XLSX or Export Excel. Download the file. Open it using Microsoft Excel. Inspect worksheets and report content. Example filename:
participation-report.xlsx Verify relevant information:
Activity name. Activity ID. Student ID. Student full name. Registration information. Check-in and Check-out timestamps. Evidence status. Participation confirmation result. Actual columns depend on the supported report type.
If the report is generated using Python, use the Excel processing libraries declared in the project’s requirements.txt.
9. Illustrate report generation using Python Create a separate practice file:
export_report_demo.py Content:
import csv records = [ { "activity_id": "ACT-DEMO-001", "mssv": "0818000001", "full_name": "Student A", "check_in": "08:05", "check_out": "11:30", "evidence_status": "YES", "participation_status": "CONFIRMED" }, { "activity_id": "ACT-DEMO-001", "mssv": "0818000003", "full_name": "Student C", "check_in": "", "check_out": "", "evidence_status": "YES", "participation_status": "REJECTED" } ] fields = [ "activity_id", "mssv", "full_name", "check_in", "check_out", "evidence_status", "participation_status" ] def safe_csv_value(value): if isinstance(value, str): if value.startswith(( "=", "+", "-", "@", "\t", "\r", "\n" )): return "'" + value return value with open( "participation-report.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8-sig" ) as file: writer = csv.DictWriter( file, fieldnames=fields ) writer.writeheader() for record in records: writer.writerow({ key: safe_csv_value(value) for key, value in record.items() }) print("Report exported successfully") Run:
python export_report_demo.py Expected output:
Report exported successfully The participation-report.csv file is created in the current directory.
Explanation:
csv.DictWriter: Writes dictionary data into CSV. writeheader(): Generates column headers. writerow(): Writes individual records. utf-8-sig: Helps Excel recognize UTF-8 encoding. safe_csv_value(): Illustrates a basic mitigation for CSV Formula Injection in text fields. This is a standalone learning script using two synthetic records. It does not connect to the Backend, access DynamoDB, or replace the project’s Export functionality.
10. Inspect the Export API Open Developer Tools.
Select Network. Perform an Export operation. Identify the corresponding request. Inspect the Request URL and HTTP Method. Verify the HTTP Status Code. Inspect Response Headers. Common Content-Type values:
CSV: text/csv XLSX: application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet The Backend may include a Content-Disposition header to suggest the downloaded filename.
Review the actual Endpoint and response using the API Service and Swagger UI.
If the file is generated entirely in the Frontend using previously retrieved data, there may be no separate file download request.
11. Verify report access permissions Test the ADMIN and STUDENT roles.
ADMIN:
Export administrative reports within authorized permissions. Access records belonging to authorized activities. STUDENT:
Cannot export other students’ private information without permission. Can only access personal reporting functionality if supported. The Backend must enforce authorization for protected Export APIs.
Reports may contain student IDs, names, and participation information. Do not upload real student data to public GitHub repositories or internship report websites. Use synthetic records or redact identifying information.
12. Distinguish Export from Serverless CSV Processing The project contains two different workflows:
Application Export: Generate reports from application business data. Serverless CSV Processing Demo: Read CSV files from Amazon S3, process them using AWS Lambda, and write JSON results back to S3. The Web Application Export workflow does not automatically use AWS Lambda.
Downloading a CSV/XLSX report does not establish that the file has been stored in Amazon S3.
Serverless CSV Processing will be covered separately in section 5.10.
Results After completing this section, we have explored the process of exporting business data as CSV/XLSX reports.
These reports support activity result verification, data archiving, and administrative reporting.
In the next section, we will compare the Dashboard, REST API responses, and exported reports to verify data accuracy.
Next: Verify Analytics and Reports

title: Record Check-in and Check-out
content:
Record Check-in and Check-out In this section, we will practice real-time student attendance recording in the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform.
Check-in records a student’s arrival at an activity.
Check-out records when the student completes or leaves the activity according to the applicable business rules.
Both operations are performed through the Web interface and FastAPI REST APIs.
1. Understand the attendance workflow ADMIN / Organizer | v Scan Student Card QR or Enter Student ID | v React / Vite Frontend | | POST Check-in / Check-out v FastAPI Backend | v Validate Business Rules | v Store Attendance Record | v Return API Response | v Display Attendance Result The Backend validates:
Authentication and user permissions. Activity ID. Student ID. Activity status. Registration requirements where applicable. Attendance time windows. Existing attendance records. After the required conditions are satisfied, the Backend records Attendance data and returns the result.
2. Prepare the workshop environment Complete sections 5.6.1 and 5.6.2 before proceeding.
Open the Backend Terminal:
cd C:\Projects\student-activity-platform\backend .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 $env:SAP_DEMO_MODE="1" python -m uvicorn app.main:app --reload Open the Frontend Terminal:
cd C:\Projects\student-activity-platform\frontend npm run dev Access:
http://localhost:5173
If both services are already running, do not start additional instances.
3. Sign in and select an activity Sign in using an ADMIN Demo account. Open Activity Management. Select the prepared activity. Open the attendance interface. Verify the activity name, status, and schedule. Ensure that the current time is within the permitted Check-in window.
4. Perform Check-in through the interface Step 1: Receive the student ID Select a student from the sample registration list:
Student ID: 0818000001 The organizer can:
Scan the student card QR code using compatible hardware. Enter the student ID manually in the attendance interface. Step 2: Submit the Check-in request Select the Check-in operation.
The Frontend sends a request to:
POST /activities/{activity_id}/check-in Where:
activity_id: Identifier of the selected activity. Request Body: Student information according to the API Schema. Authorization: ADMIN Access Token. The Backend validates the request and business conditions before storing the record.
Step 3: Verify the result After successful processing, the interface should display the appropriate Check-in result.
Illustrative example:
Student ID: 0818000001 Activity: AWS Workshop Demo Operation: Check-in Result: Success The actual timestamp is recorded according to the Backend implementation.
Entering a student ID alone does not confirm successful attendance. Wait for the Backend result.
5. Test the Check-in API using Swagger UI Open:
http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs
Sign in through POST /auth/login if an Access Token is not available. Configure authentication according to Swagger UI. Locate POST /activities/{activity_id}/check-in. Choose Try it out. Enter the Activity ID. Enter student information according to the actual Request Body. Choose Execute. Inspect the HTTP Status Code and Response Body. Illustrative Request Body:
{ "mssv": "0818000002" } Verify the actual field names and required attributes in the current Swagger UI.
Use a different student from the previous Check-in test when testing a new successful attendance operation.
Repeating Check-in for a student who already has a Check-in record may produce a duplicate-operation response. This tests business validation rather than API connectivity.
6. Test invalid Check-in scenarios Use synthetic data to verify Backend business validation.
Scenario 1: Duplicate Check-in Submit Check-in again for a student who has already checked in.
Expected results:
The Backend identifies the existing record. No additional independent Check-in record is created for the same student and activity. The interface displays an appropriate result or notification. Scenario 2: Invalid student ID Enter an unknown student ID or an unsupported student ID format.
Expected results:
The Backend rejects or handles the request according to the current rules. Attendance is not incorrectly recorded for another student. Scenario 3: Outside the Check-in window Use an activity whose Check-in window has not opened or has already closed.
Expected results:
The Backend validates the current time. The request is not recorded contrary to the attendance rules. Scenario 4: Insufficient permissions Use a STUDENT account to call an administrative attendance API.
Expected results:
The Backend denies the request when the user lacks permission. No unauthorized Attendance Record is created. 7. Perform Check-out through the interface After a student has checked in and satisfies the Check-out requirements:
Open the attendance interface. Select the correct activity. Select the Check-out operation. Scan the QR code or enter the student ID. Submit the Check-out request. Example:
Student ID: 0818000001 The Frontend sends a request to:
POST /activities/{activity_id}/check-out The Backend validates the Check-out requirements and updates the corresponding Attendance Record.
Expected result:
Student ID: 0818000001 Activity: AWS Workshop Demo Operation: Check-out Result: Success A successful Check-out requires an appropriate activity state and time window. Do not assume that Check-out is always permitted immediately after Check-in.
8. Test the Check-out API Open Swagger UI.
Locate:
POST /activities/{activity_id}/check-out Perform the following:
Provide the ADMIN Access Token. Enter the Activity ID. Enter the ID of a student who has checked in. Review the required Request Body fields. Execute the request. Inspect the Response. Use a student who has not previously checked out when testing the first Check-out operation.
9. Test invalid Check-out scenarios Test Case Expected Result Valid Check-out Attendance Record updated Missing Check-in Handled according to business rules Duplicate Check-out No duplicate Check-out record Outside permitted time Handled according to time rules Incorrect Activity ID No update to an unrelated activity Invalid Student ID No incorrect attendance record STUDENT calls admin API Access denied when unauthorized 10. Inspect Attendance data in the interface After Check-in and Check-out, open the activity’s attendance list.
Illustrative data:
Student ID Check-in Check-out 0818000001 08:05 11:30 0818000002 08:10 Not recorded 0818000003 Not recorded Not recorded The timestamps are illustrative. Actual workshop results must come from records stored by the Backend.
The attendance list helps organizers identify:
Students who have checked in. Students who have checked out. Students without attendance records. Students with missing Check-out records. 11. Inspect HTTP requests and responses Open Developer Tools and select the Network tab.
Inspect Check-in and Check-out requests:
Request URL. HTTP Method. Request Payload. HTTP Status Code. Response Body. Possible Attendance API response codes include:
HTTP Status Code Meaning 200 Successful request processing 401 Authentication required 403 Insufficient permissions 404 Resource not found 409 State or business operation conflict 422 Invalid input or business conditions The exact response codes should be verified against the Backend Attendance Service error mapping.
12. Handle connectivity interruptions In the Demo environment, FastAPI runs locally.
If the Backend becomes unavailable or the Frontend loses connectivity:
The attendance request may not reach the Backend. A student should not be marked as successfully recorded without a confirmed response. ADMIN should verify connectivity and the record status before retrying. If a response is lost, the Backend may already have saved the attendance record. Inspect the attendance list before submitting another request.
The current system should not be assumed to provide offline attendance recording or automatic synchronization queues after connectivity is restored.
Results After completing this section, we have practiced real-time attendance recording from the Frontend to FastAPI.
Each Check-in and Check-out operation is processed using the Activity ID, Student ID, user permissions, and applicable business conditions.
Attendance records provide the foundation for subsequent data verification, reconciliation, and participation confirmation.
Next: Verify Attendance Data

title: Test DynamoDB data reading and writing
content:
Test DynamoDB Data Reading and Writing In this section, we will test connectivity, data retrieval, and business data storage between the FastAPI Backend and Amazon DynamoDB.
The objective is to verify Backend business operations and confirm that data covered by the AWS Pilot integration can be stored on AWS.
1. Prepare the testing environment Open PowerShell in the Backend directory:
cd C:\Projects\student-activity-platform\backend .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 Configure AWS:
$env:AWS_PROFILE="sap-dev" $env:AWS_REGION="ap-southeast-1" $env:AWS_DEFAULT_REGION="ap-southeast-1" Verify resources:
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe .\check_aws_resources.py Ensure that all five DynamoDB tables have an ACTIVE status.
2. Test data retrieval using boto3 We will use the DynamoDB Resource interface to retrieve data from SAP-Activities.
Create a Python test file in the backend directory:
test_dynamodb_read.py Add the following content:
import boto3 from pprint import pprint session = boto3.Session( profile_name="sap-dev", region_name="ap-southeast-1" ) dynamodb = session.resource("dynamodb") table = dynamodb.Table("SAP-Activities") response = table.scan(Limit=5) print("DynamoDB connection successful") print("Returned items:", response.get("Count", 0)) for item in response.get("Items", []): pprint(item) Run the script:
python test_dynamodb_read.py Expected results:
Successful DynamoDB connectivity. Data can be retrieved from SAP-Activities. Existing items are displayed if the table contains data. If the table is empty, the returned item count may be zero. This does not indicate a connection failure.
Scan is used here to inspect a small set of records. In real applications, use GetItem or Query when the data keys are known to avoid unnecessary table scans. Limit controls the number of items evaluated in one request, not the total number of items in the table.
3. Test activity creation through the Backend Start FastAPI:
$env:SAP_DEMO_MODE="1" python -m uvicorn app.main:app --reload Before starting the Backend, review the Activities AWS Pilot or repository configuration in the current source code to ensure that activity creation uses DynamoDB.
Open Swagger UI:
http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs
Step 1: Sign in as ADMIN Locate POST /auth/login. Choose Try it out. Enter the ADMIN Demo account credentials. Choose Execute. Retrieve the returned Access Token. Use the Access Token to authenticate administrative requests according to the Backend configuration.
Step 2: Create a test activity Locate the activity creation API in the Activities group.
The Endpoint is typically:
POST /activities Enter test data according to the Request Body displayed in Swagger UI.
Example information:
Activity Name: AWS DynamoDB Integration Test Location: University Hall Description: Testing cloud data storage Provide the required time, status, and other fields according to the actual API Schema.
Choose Execute.
Expected results:
The Backend creates the activity successfully. The Response contains the new Activity ID. If the Activities AWS Pilot is correctly enabled, the item appears in SAP-Activities. Record the actual Activity ID for the next step.
4. Verify the activity using GetItem DynamoDB GetItem retrieves an item when its complete Primary Key is provided.
An Activity ID used in a previous project integration test was:
ACT#AWSTEST-9198ABC48900 For a new workshop execution, use the Activity ID returned by your API rather than relying on an existing test record.
Create the following test file:
test_dynamodb_activity.py Content:
import boto3 from pprint import pprint session = boto3.Session( profile_name="sap-dev", region_name="ap-southeast-1" ) dynamodb = session.resource("dynamodb") table = dynamodb.Table("SAP-Activities") activity_id = input("Enter Activity ID: ").strip() response = table.get_item( Key={ "activity_id": activity_id }, ConsistentRead=True ) item = response.get("Item") if item: print("Activity found in DynamoDB") pprint(item) else: print("Activity not found in DynamoDB") Run:
python test_dynamodb_activity.py Enter the Activity ID created through the Backend.
Finding the item confirms that the Activity exists in DynamoDB.
If no item is found, check:
Whether the Activity ID is correct. Whether the Region and AWS Profile are correct. Whether AWS integration is enabled for Activities. Whether the repository is using SQLite or DynamoDB. Whether the Backend logs contain IAM or connectivity errors. 5. Test Registration, Attendance, and Evidence Use a Demo activity and synthetic student accounts to perform the following operations.
Registration Import student registrations using the CSV/XLSX Template. Verify Registration data through the Backend. Inspect corresponding records in SAP-Registrations when its AWS Pilot is enabled. Attendance Record Check-in and Check-out through the attendance APIs. Use an activity within a valid attendance state and time window. Verify corresponding data in SAP-Attendance. Attendance Endpoints:
POST /activities/{activity_id}/check-in POST /activities/{activity_id}/check-out Evidence Import participation evidence from CSV/XLSX files. Validate student IDs and evidence information. Inspect corresponding items in SAP-Evidence. Each business data group may have its own AWS Pilot configuration. Verify and enable the appropriate settings before performing each integration test.
6. Query data by Activity ID The Registration, Attendance, Evidence, and Participation tables use activity_id as the Partition Key and mssv as the Sort Key.
Query can retrieve records associated with the same activity.
Create:
test_dynamodb_query.py Add the following content:
import boto3 from boto3.dynamodb.conditions import Key from pprint import pprint session = boto3.Session( profile_name="sap-dev", region_name="ap-southeast-1" ) dynamodb = session.resource("dynamodb") activity_id = input("Enter Activity ID: ").strip() tables = [ "SAP-Registrations", "SAP-Attendance", "SAP-Evidence", "SAP-Participation" ] for table_name in tables: table = dynamodb.Table(table_name) items = [] params = { "KeyConditionExpression": Key("activity_id").eq(activity_id), "ConsistentRead": True } while True: response = table.query(**params) items.extend(response.get("Items", [])) last_key = response.get("LastEvaluatedKey") if not last_key: break params["ExclusiveStartKey"] = last_key print("\nTable:", table_name) print("Total items:", len(items)) for item in items: pprint(item) Run:
python test_dynamodb_query.py Enter the Activity ID to inspect.
The script queries the four tables and displays records associated with the specified activity.
7. Test Participation After preparing Registration, Attendance, and Evidence data:
Perform the reconciliation operation through the Backend. Inspect complete and incomplete participation records. Confirm participation using ADMIN permissions. Verify SAP-Participation records when the corresponding AWS Pilot is enabled. Relevant statuses may include:
CONFIRMED: Participation has been confirmed. REJECTED: Participation has not been approved. Actual results depend on the input data, business rules, and ADMIN decisions.
8. Summarize the test results Test Expected Result AWS Connectivity Successful AWS connection Scan Activity data can be retrieved Create Activity The Backend creates an activity GetItem The activity is found in DynamoDB Registration Registration records appear when the Pilot is enabled Attendance Attendance is recorded according to business rules Evidence Evidence is stored by Activity ID and Student ID Participation Reconciliation and confirmation results are stored when the Pilot is enabled Query Records can be retrieved by Activity ID These results represent workshop testing criteria.
Participants should compare API Responses with DynamoDB items to confirm actual Cloud data storage.
Conclusion In this section, we explored DynamoDB connectivity, Scan, GetItem, and Query operations, and tested business data writes through the Backend.
A successful API Response does not automatically prove that data was stored on AWS. Direct DynamoDB item verification is necessary to confirm the integration.
Next: Verify data in the AWS Console

title: Worklog Week 3
content:
Week 3 Objectives: Begin developing the core Backend functionality of the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform in a local environment. Establish the Python and FastAPI project structure. Design REST APIs for activity management, student data, registration, and attendance. Understand how to organize Backend code using Routers, Services, Repositories, and Data Models. Implement the initial activity management functionality. Develop CSV/XLSX registration data reading, validation, and normalization. Build the foundation for Evidence Import. Develop real-time Check-in/Check-out APIs with registration and attendance status validation. Design reconciliation logic combining Registration, Attendance, and Evidence. Use synthetic datasets to test valid and invalid business scenarios. Prepare the Backend for future Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon S3 integrations. Tasks to Be Implemented This Week: Day Tasks Start Date Completion Date References Monday - Initialize the student-activity-platform project structure using Python and FastAPI. - Configure a Python Virtual Environment and install the required libraries. - Explore FastAPI application structure and module organization. - Separate Backend responsibilities into Router, Service, Repository, and Model components. - Establish the application entry point and Health Check API. - Learn how to run the local Backend using Uvicorn. 21/09/2026 21/09/2026 https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/ https://www.uvicorn.org/ Tuesday - Design REST APIs for Activity Management. - Define the Activity data structure, including Activity ID, title, time, location, and status. - Develop the initial activity creation, update, and retrieval operations. - Research approval, publication, and cancellation workflows. - Define request and response models using Pydantic. - Study HTTP error handling and input validation. - Test activity APIs using synthetic activity records. 22/09/2026 22/09/2026 https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/ https://docs.pydantic.dev/ Wednesday - Develop the Registration data processing module. - Read student registration records from CSV/XLSX files. - Validate required fields such as Student ID and student information. - Normalize data and detect duplicate records. - Design a Preview API that allows administrators to review data before importing. - Build the Import workflow and registration retrieval functionality. - Explore Evidence processing using CSV/XLSX files exported from Google Forms/Google Sheets. - Prepare synthetic datasets containing valid, incomplete, and duplicate records. 23/09/2026 23/09/2026 https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/ https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/request-files/ Thursday - Develop real-time Attendance APIs for Check-in/Check-out. - Define API inputs using Activity ID and Student ID. - Design registration verification before recording attendance. - Implement the logic for recording Check-in timestamps when API requests are processed. - Build Check-out handling based on the current attendance state. - Detect duplicate or invalid attendance operations. - Explore the rules for opening and closing Check-out periods. - Test Attendance APIs using synthetic student identifiers without relying on a physical QR camera. 24/09/2026 24/09/2026 https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/ Attendance business requirements Friday - Analyze and develop Reconciliation logic combining Registration, Attendance, and Evidence. - Define cases involving complete participation, missing Check-in, missing Check-out, missing Evidence, and missing attendance records. - Design participation statuses and scenarios requiring ADMIN review. - Build the initial APIs for reconciliation and result retrieval. - Explore the process for confirming or adjusting participation decisions. - Test the business workflow with synthetic student records. - Summarize completed modules and identify improvements for the following week. 25/09/2026 25/09/2026 Project Proposal, Business Rules, and FastAPI Documentation Week 3 Achievements: Established the FastAPI Backend foundation:
Initialized the Python project structure. Configured the local development environment and required dependencies. Learned how to run the Backend using Uvicorn. Organized Backend components using a separation-of-concerns approach. Established the REST API foundation for implementing business features. Developed the initial Backend code structure:

Developed the Activity Management module:

Defined activity lifecycle states for approval and publication workflows. Designed APIs for listing and retrieving activity details. Introduced input validation and business error handling. Studied CSV/XLSX reading and processing techniques. Identified required registration fields. Established Student ID normalization and missing-data validation. Designed duplicate and invalid record detection. Defined the workflow Preview → Validate → Import → View Registrations. Established the requirement to validate records before committing them to the official registration dataset. Explored Evidence processing:
Identified Google Forms/Google Sheets as sources of evidence data. Designed the process for importing exported CSV/XLSX files. Investigated Evidence validation using Student ID and Activity ID. Defined situations involving invalid evidence or records that do not match the registration dataset. Prepared the foundation for using Evidence during participation reconciliation. Developed real-time Attendance APIs:
Designed Check-in and Check-out APIs associated with Activity IDs. Used Student IDs to identify students during attendance processing. Established registration checks before accepting attendance events. Designed timestamp recording during Backend request processing. Introduced duplicate attendance prevention. Defined invalid attendance scenarios. Prepared the rules for opening and closing Check-out periods. Important principle: Check-in/Check-out data is recorded through APIs when attendance actions occur. Attendance is not primarily processed through batch Excel imports.
Designed the Reconciliation logic:
Combined three primary data sources: Registration. Attendance. Evidence. Defined participation situations: Registered students with complete attendance and evidence. Missing Check-in. Missing Check-out. Missing Evidence. No attendance records. Records requiring ADMIN review. Distinguished automatically evaluated results from cases requiring manual confirmation. Established the foundation for Finalize and Export operations. Tested business scenarios using synthetic datasets:
Registered students with valid Check-ins. Unregistered students attempting to Check in. Duplicate Check-in attempts. Invalid Check-out requests. Missing Check-in or Check-out information. Missing participation evidence. Duplicate or incomplete Student IDs in imported files. Records requiring manual reconciliation. Improved understanding of REST API development:
Studied HTTP methods such as GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE. Learned the roles of Request Bodies, Path Parameters, and Query Parameters. Explored HTTP status codes including 200, 400, 403, 404, 409, and 422. Used Pydantic concepts for input validation. Recognized the importance of consistent and informative API error responses. Prepared for AWS integration:
Identified Backend modules that could integrate with Amazon DynamoDB. Identified file categories suitable for Amazon S3 storage. Explored the Repository pattern to support future changes in persistence without rewriting core business logic. Continued prioritizing local testing and synthetic data before provisioning AWS resources. Challenges and Lessons Learned: Backend architecture: Separating Routers, Services, and Repositories improves maintainability but requires clearly defined responsibilities. Inconsistent imported data: Registration and Evidence files may contain missing columns, invalid Student IDs, and duplicate records, making Preview and Validation essential. Real-time attendance: Correct handling of repeated Check-in/Check-out attempts is necessary, and attendance events must be processed immediately. Multi-source reconciliation: Registration alone is insufficient to confirm participation; Attendance and Evidence must also be considered. Synthetic testing: Using artificial records helps identify business logic errors without exposing real student information. AWS preparation: Local-first Backend development reduces complexity and cloud costs during the initial implementation phase. Plan for Next Week: Continue improving core Backend functionality. Refine data persistence and business logic testing. Research and implement limited AWS Pilot integrations using Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon S3. Test AWS read/write operations using synthetic data. Check consistency between local application state and selected AWS Pilot workflows. Document test results and prepare technical materials for the next integration phase.

title: Blog 3 - From Amazon S3 to an Analytics Dashboard
content:
FROM S3 DATA FILES TO DASHBOARDS: BUILDING A DATA ANALYTICS PIPELINE WITH GLUE, ATHENA, AND QUICKSIGHT The Journey from Raw Data to Valuable Insights on AWS 1. When Data Goes Beyond Excel Files As a Data Science student, I frequently work with data cleaning, data analysis, and visualization.
However, while studying Cloud Computing at First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ), I encountered another important question:
How can a collection of data files stored in the Cloud be transformed into a Dashboard that supports decision-making?
In my Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform project, data is collected from multiple sources:
Registration data from the University Portal. Attendance data from Check-in and Check-out operations. Participation evidence from Google Forms or Google Sheets. Participation results from reconciliation and confirmation. After processing, the system can help answer questions such as:
How many students registered for an activity? How many students were confirmed as participants? What is the participation rate? How many students are missing Check-in or Check-out records? Which activities have the highest engagement? How does participation change across semesters? These questions helped me understand that the value of data is not limited to storage. It also depends on how effectively the data can be analyzed and used.
2. An AWS Data Analytics Architecture While researching the original project architecture, I studied an analytical model combining:
Amazon S3. AWS Glue. Amazon Athena. Amazon QuickSight. Each service has a different responsibility in transforming raw data into analytical insights.
This architecture represents research and a potential future enhancement. The current MVP uses an Analytics Dashboard developed directly with React/Vite and FastAPI.
3. Amazon S3: Where the Data Journey Begins Amazon S3 is an object storage service that supports different types of data, including CSV, JSON, images, documents, and analytical formats such as Parquet.
In an Analytics architecture, S3 can serve as the underlying data storage platform.
For example, student activity data could be organized using the following structure:
s3://student-activity-analytics-demo/ raw/ registrations/ attendance/ evidence/ curated/ participation/ year=2026/ semester=1/ activity_id=ACT001/ query-results/ The purpose of each area is:
raw/: Original data from different source systems. curated/: Validated, standardized, and processed data. query-results/: Amazon Athena query results. Organizing data into separate layers helps distinguish original data from datasets that are ready for analysis.
For larger datasets, Parquet and partitioning by year, semester, or Activity ID can help reduce the amount of data scanned during queries.
4. Data Cleaning: Why Raw Files Are Not Always Ready for Analysis Data collected from multiple sources often has different structures.
For example, a Registration file might contain:
student_id,full_name,activity_id 0818000001,Student A,ACT001 0818000002,Student B,ACT001 0818000003,Student C,ACT001 Attendance data might contain:
student_id,activity_id,check_in,check_out 0818000001,ACT001,08:05,11:30 0818000002,ACT001,08:10, Evidence data:
student_id,activity_id,evidence_submitted 0818000001,ACT001,true 0818000002,ACT001,true Simply uploading these files to S3 does not make them immediately suitable for analytics.
The following processing steps are required:
Standardize column names. Preserve student IDs as strings. Validate missing data. Detect duplicate records. Standardize timestamps. Match records using Student ID and Activity ID. Consolidate participation status. Create an analytical dataset. The processed dataset could look like this:
student_id,activity_id,registered,checked_in,checked_out,evidence_submitted,participation_status 0818000001,ACT001,true,true,true,true,CONFIRMED 0818000002,ACT001,true,true,false,true,PENDING 0818000003,ACT001,true,false,false,false,REJECTED This synthetic dataset illustrates possible reconciliation results.
PENDING represents a record awaiting confirmation in this example. CONFIRMED and REJECTED decisions must follow the applicable business rules and ADMIN review.
5. AWS Glue: Helping the System Understand Data Structures AWS Glue is a data integration service that supports data cataloging and Extract, Transform, Load (ETL) workloads.
In this architecture, the main component I studied was the AWS Glue Data Catalog.
The Data Catalog stores metadata such as:
Database names. Table names. Column definitions. Data types. S3 data locations. Partition information. Example:
Database: student_activity_analytics Table: student_participation Data Location: s3://student-activity-analytics-demo/curated/participation/ Columns: student_id string activity_id string registered boolean checked_in boolean checked_out boolean evidence_submitted boolean participation_status string An AWS Glue Crawler can scan data stored in Amazon S3 and create or update table definitions in the Data Catalog.
An important concept is:
The AWS Glue Data Catalog stores metadata describing the data, rather than all the actual records stored in S3.
For more complex ETL requirements, AWS Glue Jobs can be used to clean, transform, and convert data formats.
However, running a Crawler alone does not automatically clean the dataset.
6. Amazon Athena: Analyzing Data with SQL Amazon Athena is a service that allows SQL queries against data stored in Amazon S3 without requiring users to manage database servers directly.
Athena can use table definitions from the AWS Glue Data Catalog to identify data locations and structures.
After creating the student_participation table, I can study analytical queries such as the following.
6.1. Total Registrations SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_registrations FROM student_participation WHERE registered = TRUE; This query counts registered records.
The dataset should contain one record per student and activity to avoid duplicate counting.
6.2. Confirmed Participants SELECT COUNT(*) AS confirmed_participants FROM student_participation WHERE participation_status = 'CONFIRMED'; This metric represents the number of confirmed participation records.
6.3. Participation Rate by Activity SELECT activity_id, COUNT(*) AS total_registrations, SUM( CASE WHEN participation_status = 'CONFIRMED' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END ) AS confirmed_participants, ROUND( 100.0 * SUM( CASE WHEN participation_status = 'CONFIRMED' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END ) / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0), 2 ) AS participation_rate FROM student_participation WHERE registered = TRUE GROUP BY activity_id; The rate is calculated using confirmed participants among registered students.
6.4. Identifying Missing Check-out Records SELECT student_id, activity_id, checked_in, checked_out FROM student_participation WHERE checked_in = TRUE AND checked_out = FALSE; The results help organizers identify students requiring further review.
6.5. Identifying Missing Evidence SELECT student_id, activity_id FROM student_participation WHERE checked_in = TRUE AND evidence_submitted = FALSE; This query identifies students with attendance records but missing participation evidence.
These SQL queries are illustrative research examples. They do not represent Athena queries already deployed in my internship project.
7. Amazon QuickSight: Transforming Query Results into Dashboards Amazon QuickSight is an AWS Business Intelligence tool that supports data analysis and visualization.
In this architecture, QuickSight can connect to Athena and use analytical data to build Dashboards.
Instead of reviewing thousands of Excel rows, organizers can monitor important indicators through charts and summary tables.
The proposed Dashboard includes:
Component Purpose KPI Cards Total registrations, participation, and participation rate Bar Chart Compare engagement across different activities Line Chart Track participation trends over time Donut Chart Display the distribution of participation statuses Data Table Review records by Student ID or activity Filters Filter results by semester, activity, or data group Illustrative example:
Total Registrations: 1,200 Confirmed Registered Participants: 1,050 Participation Rate: 87.5% Participation Rate is calculated as:
Participation Rate = Confirmed Registered Participants / Total Registrations × 100 = 1,050 / 1,200 × 100 = 87.5% These are synthetic figures used to illustrate Dashboard metrics, not actual measurements from a university activity.
8. A Guide to Building an Experimental Analytics Pipeline The following walkthrough provides a reference exercise for AWS beginners.
Step 1: Prepare the Data Create a synthetic CSV dataset. Standardize column names. Validate student IDs and duplicate records. Add a Participation Status field. Avoid using personal information without authorization. Step 2: Create an Amazon S3 Bucket Create a private S3 Bucket. Maintain appropriate Block Public Access settings. Create a curated/participation/ prefix. Upload the standardized CSV file. Prepare an Athena query results location. Step 3: Configure the AWS Glue Data Catalog Create a Glue Database named student_activity_analytics. Create a Crawler using the curated/participation/ S3 location. Configure an IAM Role with the required S3 read permissions. Run the Crawler. Verify the generated Table and Data Types. Ensure that student_id and activity_id are recognized as strings to preserve identifier values correctly.
Step 4: Query Data with Amazon Athena Open the Athena Query Editor. Select the configured Database. Configure the Query Results location. Run an initial SELECT query. Verify the results and data types. Develop analytical SQL queries. Step 5: Build a Dashboard with Amazon QuickSight Configure QuickSight access to Athena and S3. Create an Athena Data Source. Select the Database and Table. Create a Dataset. Develop an Analysis. Add KPIs, charts, and Filters. Publish the Dashboard if sharing is required. QuickSight can use Direct Query or SPICE depending on analytical requirements and configuration.
Step 6: Review Costs and Clean Up Resources Review Glue Crawler executions. Review the amount of data scanned by Athena. Review S3 Storage usage. Review QuickSight subscriptions and SPICE usage where applicable. Remove unused experimental resources. Check AWS Billing. 9. Performance and Cost Optimization An important consideration when studying AWS Data Analytics is processing cost.
Potential optimization strategies include:
Use Parquet
Parquet is a columnar storage format that can allow Athena to read only the required columns rather than the entire dataset.
Partition Data
Partitioning data by year, semester, or Activity ID can reduce data scans when appropriate filters and table structures are used.
Avoid Unnecessary SELECT star Queries
Select only the columns required for analysis.
Control Glue Executions
Run Crawlers or ETL Jobs when metadata updates or data processing are required.
Manage QuickSight Resources
Choose suitable query modes, SPICE capacity, and subscription options according to actual analytical requirements.
These strategies help develop scalable analytics systems while maintaining cost awareness.
10. Data Security in Analytics Pipelines Student activity records may contain personal information such as student IDs, names, classes, and participation history.
An Analytics architecture should consider:
Keeping S3 Buckets containing student records private. Applying IAM Least Privilege permissions. Restricting access to authorized users. Using appropriate encryption. Excluding unnecessary personal information from Dashboards. Using synthetic data for learning and demonstrations. Controlling Dashboard sharing permissions. Not every user needs access to detailed student records.
A management Dashboard may only require aggregated statistics rather than access to the complete raw dataset.
11. Comparison with the Current Internship Project Component Current Project Researched Architecture Operational Database SQLite and DynamoDB Integration Data can be exported to analytical storage File Storage Amazon S3 in the Demo S3 Raw/Curated Data Data Processing FastAPI and Lambda CSV Demo Glue ETL or other processing tools Metadata Application data structures AWS Glue Data Catalog Query FastAPI business data processing Amazon Athena SQL Dashboard React/Vite Amazon QuickSight The current version of my project uses React/Vite and FastAPI to provide an Analytics Dashboard.
The Glue, Athena, and QuickSight architecture represents a potential enhancement for:
Long-term historical data analysis. Cross-activity and cross-semester analysis. Querying larger analytical datasets. Separating Analytics from daily operational workflows. Developing Business Intelligence reports. AWS Glue, Amazon Athena, and Amazon QuickSight have not been confirmed as implemented components of the current MVP.
12. Lessons Learned Through studying an AWS Data Analytics Pipeline, I developed a better understanding of different Data Engineering responsibilities:
Data Ingestion: Collecting and importing data. Data Storage: Storing data using Amazon S3. Data Processing: Cleaning and transforming data. Data Catalog: Managing metadata using AWS Glue. Data Query: Querying datasets using Amazon Athena. Data Visualization: Presenting insights using Amazon QuickSight. An attractive Dashboard is only the final stage of the workflow.
The quality of analytical results also depends on data accuracy, schema design, processing rules, and consistent definitions of business metrics.
13. Conclusion Starting with CSV files stored in Amazon S3, I can understand how an end-to-end Data Analytics workflow could be built on AWS.
AWS Glue manages metadata and supports data integration. Amazon Athena provides SQL querying capabilities. Amazon QuickSight transforms analytical results into charts and Dashboards.
I learned that Data Engineering is not limited to a single tool or service.
It involves connecting multiple components so that data can be collected, stored, standardized, processed, and analyzed effectively.
This knowledge helps me connect my Data Science background with Cloud Computing and provides a clearer direction for my future development in Cloud & Data Engineering.
14. References Amazon S3 Documentation AWS Glue Documentation AWS Glue Data Catalog Amazon Athena User Guide Amazon Athena Performance Tuning Amazon QuickSight User Guide AWS Analytics AWS Pricing Calculator
