title: Registration and Attendance Management
content:
Registration and Attendance Management This section documents the registration import and real-time Check-in/Check-out functions implemented in the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform.
University events often collect registrations through an external portal, while attendance is recorded at the venue. The objective of this module is to combine these records by activity and student, reduce manual spreadsheet processing, and prepare reliable data for subsequent reconciliation.
1. Data sources and implementation scope Data source Method used in the project Purpose University Portal ADMIN imports exported CSV/XLSX files Build the registration list Student card QR / Student ID (MSSV) ADMIN uses the attendance interface to submit an immediate API request Record Check-in and Check-out Activity configuration ADMIN manages the activity through the Web Application Apply the correct activity and attendance conditions The current version does not automatically synchronize with the University Portal API. Registration files are imported, whereas Check-in and Check-out events are sent to the FastAPI Backend when they occur. A scanner that provides the student ID as input may be used; complete camera-based QR scanning should not be assumed without device testing.
2. Technical implementation Frontend: React/Vite provides the ADMIN interfaces for activities, registration import and attendance. Backend: Python/FastAPI validates requests, enforces permissions and processes attendance rules. Local demo storage: SQLite stores application data for the locally running demonstration. AWS integration test: Amazon DynamoDB was used to test the SAP-Registrations and SAP-Attendance data groups. It is not presented as a fully migrated production database. Registration and attendance belong to the main FastAPI application, not the separate AWS Lambda CSV Processing Demo described in section 5.10.
3. Import student registration data ADMIN selects an activity, uploads the registration file exported from the University Portal and reviews the import result. The Backend checks the expected fields, student IDs, missing values and duplicate records according to the implemented import rules.
Figure 5.6.1. Registration import interface from the implemented Web Application.
4. Record Check-in and Check-out in real time During an event, the organizer selects the correct activity and identifies a student using their card information or MSSV. Each valid action is submitted immediately to the attendance REST API and stored as an attendance record.
The Backend checks whether the operation is allowed, including the activity, permitted time window and current attendance state. Check-out is recorded as a distinct operation; it is not inferred merely from a registration record.
Figure 5.6.2. Check-in operation in the Web Application.
Figure 5.6.3. Check-out operation in the Web Application.
5. Validation and verification The workshop verifies the following cases:
An eligible student is included in the correct activity’s registration data. A valid Check-in is recorded with its timestamp. A valid Check-out updates the corresponding attendance record. Duplicate or invalid requests are handled according to Backend rules. Student IDs remain associated with the correct Activity ID. ADMIN can review the recorded attendance data before reconciliation. The association of Activity ID and MSSV is essential: one student can participate in multiple activities, so attendance must not be matched using MSSV alone across the whole system.
6. Workshop contents Import registration data Prepare the activity and attendance conditions Perform Check-in and Check-out Verify attendance results 7. Expected learning outcomes After completing this section, learners can import and validate registration data, record real-time attendance through FastAPI, inspect the corresponding records and explain how these data become inputs to the reconciliation process in section 5.7.
Implementation note: The screenshots document the actual user interface and tests. The local FastAPI/SQLite workflow and the DynamoDB pilot have different scopes; the screenshots do not imply a fully cloud-hosted backend.

title: Self-Assessment
content:
Internship Self-Assessment During my participation in the First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) – AWS Study Group internship and learning program, I had the opportunity to explore the field of Cloud Computing, learn about Amazon Web Services (AWS), and apply the knowledge acquired at university to a practical project.
With an academic background in Data Science, I considered this internship an opportunity to expand my knowledge beyond data analysis and processing into system development, application deployment, and cloud resource management.
Throughout the internship, I focused on learning and practicing AWS services such as Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, AWS Amplify Hosting, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), and Amazon CloudWatch. I also strengthened my technical skills in Python, FastAPI, React/Vite, REST APIs, GitHub, and other software development tools.
One of my main responsibilities was developing the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform, a system designed to manage university activities and analyze student participation. Through this project, I gained practical experience in Backend development, Frontend development, registration and attendance processing, evidence reconciliation, analytics, and application deployment in a Demo environment.
In addition to technical knowledge, I improved my self-learning ability, documentation skills, requirements analysis, debugging techniques, and task management through weekly Worklogs.
Regarding my work ethic, I consistently tried to organize my tasks effectively, proactively research unfamiliar topics, and incorporate feedback to improve the quality of my work.
However, I also recognized areas that require further improvement, including practical system deployment experience, advanced problem-solving skills, technical communication, and time management.
To reflect objectively on my internship experience, I would like to assess myself using the following criteria:
Self-Assessment Table No. Criteria Description Good Fair Average 1 Professional knowledge and skills Applying Data Science, Python, FastAPI, React, and AWS knowledge to practical development ☐ ✅ ☐ 2 Learning ability Proactively researching AWS services, learning new technologies, and applying technical documentation ✅ ☐ ☐ 3 Proactiveness Independently researching solutions, planning tasks, and addressing project challenges ✅ ☐ ☐ 4 Sense of responsibility Completing assigned tasks carefully and monitoring progress ✅ ☐ ☐ 5 Discipline and time management Following schedules and managing time for learning, development, testing, and documentation ☐ ✅ ☐ 6 Willingness to improve Accepting feedback and continuously improving work quality ✅ ☐ ☐ 7 Communication skills Presenting ideas, discussing technical issues, and reporting work progress ☐ ✅ ☐ 8 Teamwork Sharing information, considering feedback, and collaborating in learning activities ☐ ✅ ☐ 9 Professional conduct Demonstrating responsibility, respecting processes, and maintaining work quality ✅ ☐ ☐ 10 Problem-solving skills Identifying root causes, researching solutions, and verifying fixes ☐ ✅ ☐ 11 Contribution to the project Developing activity management, data processing, analytics, and AWS integration features ✅ ☐ ☐ 12 Overall performance Technical progress, work attitude, and achievement of internship objectives ✅ ☐ ☐ 1. Strengths and Achievements Expanded Technical Knowledge
Through the internship, I gained valuable experience learning and practicing important AWS services. Previously, my academic knowledge mainly focused on Data Science, data processing, and specialized university subjects. After the internship, I developed a better understanding of how to organize a Web Application architecture integrated with Cloud services.
Developing the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform allowed me to combine programming, data management, API development, and application deployment within a practical system.
Self-Learning and Research Skills
I improved my ability to independently explore AWS Documentation, understand new services, and apply technical knowledge through hands-on exercises.
When encountering issues involving the Backend, Frontend, authentication, APIs, or AWS integration, I practiced identifying root causes, investigating individual components, and selecting appropriate solutions.
System Development Thinking
Working on the project helped me better understand the relationships between different application components.
I practiced workflows involving data collection, business processing, storage, reconciliation, analytics, and report generation. These experiences highlighted the importance of proper data structures and consistency across system features.
Testing and Debugging Skills
During development, I encountered and addressed various issues related to API connectivity, user authentication, authorization, data processing, and deployment configuration.
These experiences encouraged me to review actual results, interpret error messages, investigate causes, and perform verification after making changes.
Technical Documentation and Reporting
By preparing weekly Worklogs, writing bilingual Workshop documentation, and recording AWS exercises, I improved my ability to present technical information in a structured and understandable manner.
I also recognized that clear documentation supports project maintenance, testing, and future development.
2. Areas for Improvement Despite the progress I made, several areas still require further development.
Advanced Cloud Computing Knowledge: I need to deepen my understanding of Production architectures, Networking, Security, CI/CD, Monitoring, and AWS resource optimization. Although I have practiced integrating several services, I still need more experience with larger and more complex systems.
Problem-Solving Skills: Complex issues involving multiple application components sometimes require considerable investigation time. I need to improve my debugging methodology, develop more structured Test Cases, and strengthen my Log analysis skills.
Discipline and Time Management: I need to improve task estimation, prioritization, and time allocation between research, programming, testing, and documentation.
Technical Communication: I should become more confident when presenting technical solutions, sharing ideas, and explaining complex problems. I also need to continue improving my English communication skills in professional IT environments.
Practical Deployment Experience: The current project primarily serves educational and demonstration purposes. I need to gain more experience in scalability, security, performance optimization, Cloud Backend deployment, and Production system operations.
3. Personal Development Plan After the internship, I have identified several goals for continued professional development:
Strengthen AWS Knowledge: Continue studying AWS services, particularly Networking, Compute, Storage, Database, and Security.
Improve Python and Data Processing Skills: Develop stronger capabilities in data processing, API development, SQL, and tools relevant to Data Engineering.
Explore Cloud Architecture and Data Engineering: Study ETL/ELT workflows, Data Pipelines, Data Warehouses, and Cloud-based data processing architectures.
Continue Developing Practical Projects: Improve the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform, especially Cloud Backend deployment, system optimization, and advanced analytics functionality.
Enhance Soft Skills: Practice communication, teamwork, time management, and technical presentations in English.
4. Overall Assessment Overall, I would rate my internship performance as Good.
Although several areas still require improvement, I have gained valuable technical knowledge and practical experience, particularly in Cloud Computing, Web Application development, and data processing.
The internship helped me better understand how university knowledge can be applied to a structured development project, from requirements analysis and system design to implementation, testing, deployment, and documentation.
This experience provides an important foundation for my long-term career goal of becoming a Data Engineer / Cloud & Data Engineer.
I will continue learning proactively, addressing my weaknesses, and improving my ability to apply technical knowledge to practical projects.

title: Sharing and Feedback
content:
7.1. Overall Evaluation of the First Cloud AI Journey Experience 1. Learning and Working Environment During my participation in the First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) program, I had the opportunity to explore a learning environment focused on cloud computing technologies provided by Amazon Web Services (AWS). The program encouraged me to independently study technical documentation, explore new technologies, and apply theoretical knowledge to practical projects.
One of the aspects I appreciated most was the combination of theoretical learning and hands-on practice. Instead of only studying cloud computing concepts, I gradually designed, developed, and tested the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform, covering Backend development, Frontend implementation, data processing, and the deployment of selected components on AWS.
Throughout the development process, I encountered challenges involving environment configuration, component integration, debugging, and AWS service management. However, these challenges helped me improve my ability to research technical problems, identify root causes, and develop systematic solutions.
2. Support from Mentors and the FCAJ Community During my learning journey, the technical documentation, Workshop materials, and learning resources provided by the AWS Study Group community played an important role in helping me understand unfamiliar AWS services.
I particularly appreciated the program’s emphasis on independent learning, practical experimentation, and project-based development rather than passive theoretical study. Researching documentation, verifying configurations, and resolving technical issues helped me develop stronger self-learning habits.
I also found that practical examples and detailed, step-by-step instructions were especially valuable for students who were new to AWS.
For future programs, I hope more learning materials will cover real-world system architectures, security best practices, cloud deployment, monitoring, and cost optimization.
3. Relevance of the Project to My Academic Major As a student majoring in Data Science, I found that the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform was closely related to the knowledge and skills I had acquired at university.
The project focuses on student activity data management, registration processing, attendance tracking, evidence collection, data reconciliation, and participation analytics.
These functions allowed me to apply data processing concepts, database design principles, and analytical thinking to a practical management problem.
In addition to strengthening my academic knowledge, the project helped me explore software engineering technologies such as Python, FastAPI, React, JavaScript, and RESTful APIs.
More importantly, working with Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon CloudWatch, AWS IAM, and AWS Amplify helped me better understand the connection between Data Engineering, Software Engineering, and Cloud Computing.
4. Learning Opportunities and Technical Skill Development Throughout the project, I gained valuable experience in several technical areas.
Backend Development: I practiced building RESTful APIs using FastAPI, implementing authentication and role-based authorization, and managing student activities, registrations, and attendance records.
Frontend Development: I used React and Vite to develop a web interface, integrate APIs, and implement features for two user roles: ADMIN and STUDENT.
Data Processing: I worked with CSV/XLSX imports, registration data validation, real-time Check-in/Check-out records, participation evidence, data reconciliation, and analytical reporting.
AWS Cloud Services: I gained practical exposure to several AWS services:
Amazon S3 for object storage and data organization. AWS Lambda for experimenting with serverless CSV processing. Amazon DynamoDB for exploring NoSQL data storage. AWS IAM for access control and resource permissions. Amazon CloudWatch for monitoring application execution logs. AWS Amplify for deploying the Frontend application to the Cloud. Beyond technical skills, the project also helped me improve my planning, documentation, testing, troubleshooting, and technical English reading skills.
Maintaining Worklogs and Workshop documentation allowed me to track progress, review completed tasks, and better understand the overall development process.
5. Project Development Experience and Personal Initiative One of the most valuable parts of this experience was independently developing a system consisting of multiple interconnected components.
During the initial development stage, I faced challenges in database design, API organization, and Frontend implementation.
When integrating the Frontend with the Backend, I had to troubleshoot issues involving API configuration, authentication, authorization, and Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS).
Later, experimenting with AWS Lambda, Amazon S3, DynamoDB, and Amplify helped me understand the differences between developing an application locally and deploying selected components in a cloud environment.
These experiences showed me that software development involves much more than writing code. It also requires architecture design, testing, monitoring, security considerations, resource management, and technical documentation.
Although the project still has certain limitations, particularly because the Backend primarily operates in a local Demo environment and the full application has not been migrated to AWS, the development process gave me a more realistic understanding of the application lifecycle.
6. Learning Resources and AWS Cost Management I appreciated the availability of AWS services that allow students to explore cloud architectures and develop practical applications.
However, working with AWS also helped me recognize the importance of cloud cost management.
Students must understand which resources are running, monitor service usage, review configurations, and clean up unnecessary resources after completing their experiments.
During the project, I reviewed the AWS resources that had been used, examined CloudWatch logs, and planned the clean-up process following the completion of the system Demo.
I believe future FCAJ learning materials could place additional emphasis on AWS Free Tier, Cost Explorer, billing alerts, and practical cost management strategies to help students use cloud services more confidently and responsibly.
7.2. Most Satisfying Aspects of the Internship The most satisfying part of my experience was being able to transform theoretical knowledge into a functional software project.
Through the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform, I experienced multiple stages of application development, including requirements analysis, data modeling, Backend development, Frontend implementation, API integration, testing, deployment, and technical reporting.
In particular, implementing student activity management, attendance tracking, evidence processing, data reconciliation, and reporting functions helped me understand how data-driven systems can support real-world administrative processes.
I also found the troubleshooting process rewarding. Each technical issue I resolved contributed to a more stable application and strengthened my confidence in handling practical development challenges.
7.3. Areas for Improvement Despite the positive experience, I would like to offer several suggestions that could help improve future FCAJ programs.
First, the program could provide more end-to-end Workshops that guide students through the complete lifecycle of a project, from system design and development to deployment, monitoring, and optimization.
Second, more practical examples demonstrating how to integrate Frontend applications, Backend services, databases, and AWS resources would help students understand real-world cloud application architectures.
Third, security, AWS IAM best practices, cost monitoring, and resource clean-up should be emphasized throughout the learning process rather than being introduced only at the end.
Finally, additional sessions covering real-world engineering experiences, project case studies, and career opportunities in Cloud Engineering, Data Engineering, and Cloud & Data Engineering would be especially valuable for students preparing to enter the technology industry.
7.4. Would I Recommend FCAJ to Other Students? I would recommend the First Cloud AI Journey program to students who are interested in Cloud Computing, AWS, Software Development, or Data Engineering.
In my opinion, the program provides a valuable opportunity to explore technologies beyond traditional university coursework and gain practical experience with widely used cloud services.
However, students should be prepared to learn independently, read technical documentation, experiment with different solutions, and remain persistent when facing technical challenges.
These habits are essential for making meaningful progress throughout the program.
7.5. Suggestions and Future Expectations After completing the program and my project, I would like to continue developing my knowledge and skills in Cloud Computing and Data Engineering.
My future learning objectives include:
Improving my Backend development and system architecture skills. Exploring Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, DynamoDB, and other AWS data processing services in greater depth. Learning about ETL/ELT processes and data pipeline development. Deploying Backend applications to cloud infrastructure instead of relying primarily on local environments. Strengthening my knowledge of cloud security, monitoring, and cost optimization. Exploring Infrastructure as Code, CI/CD, and deployment automation. Continuing to improve the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform with a focus on scalability and practical deployment. If opportunities are available, I would be interested in participating in additional AWS-related Workshops, learning activities, or practical engineering projects.
7.6. Final Reflection The First Cloud AI Journey program provided me with a valuable opportunity to explore cloud computing and gradually apply technical knowledge to a practical software project.
By developing the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform, I strengthened my understanding of programming and data processing while learning how different AWS services can support application development.
Although there are still areas that require further study and improvement, the experience has helped me better understand my interests and long-term career direction in Cloud Computing and Data Engineering.
I sincerely appreciate the First Cloud AI Journey program and the AWS Study Group community for providing useful technical resources, learning opportunities, and practical guidance that have supported my professional development.

title: Evidence Import and Participation Reconciliation
content:
Evidence Import and Participation Reconciliation This section explains how the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform imports participation evidence, compares it with registration and real-time attendance records, and supports ADMIN confirmation of participation results.
An imported registration list does not prove attendance, and an attendance timestamp alone may not satisfy all requirements of an activity. Reconciliation helps organizers inspect data from multiple sources before making an authorized decision.
1. Data sources Dataset How it is collected Main information Registration CSV/XLSX imported from the University Portal Student ID and activity Attendance Real-time Check-in/Check-out through FastAPI Check-in and Check-out records Evidence CSV/XLSX exported from Google Forms or Google Sheets Submitted participation evidence The current application imports exported evidence files; it does not claim a direct Google Forms/Sheets API integration. Matching is performed using the corresponding Activity ID and MSSV, which prevents combining records from unrelated activities.
2. Import evidence data ADMIN selects the appropriate activity and imports evidence records exported from the external form or spreadsheet. The Backend checks the supported file format, required fields, student IDs and potential duplicates, then makes the data available for reconciliation.
Figure 5.7.1. Evidence import performed in the Web Application.
3. Reconcile registration, attendance and evidence The FastAPI Backend compares records for the selected activity and identifies whether registration, Check-in, Check-out and evidence information are present. The resulting view helps ADMIN recognize complete records and cases that need additional review.
Example condition What the organizer should check Registration, Check-in, Check-out and Evidence are available Verify the activity’s remaining eligibility rules Missing Check-out Review the incomplete attendance information Evidence exists without recorded attendance Verify the event requirements and source data Attendance exists but evidence is missing Determine whether evidence is required Records belong to another activity Correct the Activity ID association before proceeding These cases illustrate possible business conditions; they do not define new Backend status codes or mean that a student is automatically approved or rejected.
Figure 5.7.2. Reconciliation results in the implemented platform.
4. Confirm participation results After reviewing the consolidated data, an authorized ADMIN applies the rules of the activity and performs the supported participation-confirmation action. Records with missing or conflicting information should be investigated rather than altered merely to force a successful result.
Figure 5.7.3. ADMIN participation review and confirmation.
5. Architecture and scope Frontend: React/Vite displays import, reconciliation and confirmation interfaces. Backend: FastAPI performs matching and participation business logic. Local demo: SQLite stores the primary demo application data. AWS pilot: Amazon DynamoDB was used to test SAP-Evidence and SAP-Participation data groups. This functionality is handled by the current Web Application. AWS Glue, Amazon Athena and Amazon QuickSight are not components of the implemented reconciliation service.
6. Workshop contents Import evidence data Reconcile participation records Confirm participation results Verify final participation records 7. Expected learning outcomes After completing this section, learners can import evidence files, explain how the Backend matches data by Activity ID and MSSV, investigate incomplete records, understand the ADMIN confirmation step and prepare validated participation information for Analytics and Export in section 5.8.
Implementation note: Figures in this section are screenshots of the project. The tables describe scenarios for review, not results from a production-scale dataset or automatic approval rules.

title: Analytics Dashboard and Export
content:
Analytics Dashboard and Export In this section, we will explore data analytics, Dashboard visualization, and report export functionality in the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform.
After completing registration management, attendance recording, evidence imports, and reconciliation, the system contains the business datasets required to analyze student engagement.
University activity organizers need to understand registration totals, actual attendance, attendance completion, and confirmed participation results for each activity.
Manually aggregating multiple Excel files can be time-consuming and may introduce inconsistencies between reports.
The Analytics Dashboard helps ADMIN users monitor important indicators, review activity outcomes, and use data to support student activity management.
Analytics Data Sources The system uses the following business datasets:
Activities: Information about university activities. Registrations: Student registration records. Attendance: Real-time Check-in and Check-out records. Evidence: Participation evidence imported from CSV/XLSX files. Participation: Reconciliation and student participation confirmation results. These datasets are associated using Activity ID and Student ID to support accurate aggregation.
Analytics and Export Architecture Registration Data + Attendance Data + Evidence Data + Participation Results | v Python / FastAPI Backend | v Data Aggregation & Analytics | +----------------------+ | | v v REST API Response Report Generation | | v v React / Vite Dashboard CSV / XLSX | | v v ADMIN / STUDENT ADMIN Download The Python/FastAPI Backend retrieves, aggregates, and processes business data.
The React/Vite Frontend receives analytical results through REST APIs and displays indicators appropriate for the user’s permissions.
SQLite supports local Demo persistence and recovery. Amazon DynamoDB is integrated and tested for cloud-based business data storage.
Analytics Metrics The Analytics Dashboard may use indicators such as:
Total activities. Total registrations. Students with Check-in records. Students with Check-out records. Students with complete attendance records. Students with participation evidence. Confirmed participants. Rejected participants. Confirmed participation rate. The actual displayed indicators depend on the Analytics functionality available in the current project version.
Business Workflow Prepare Registration, Attendance, Evidence, and Participation data. Identify the activity scope for analysis. Aggregate data and calculate metrics through the Backend. Display analytical results on the React/Vite Dashboard. Review indicators and use supported filters. Export reports from business data. Verify consistency between the Dashboard, Backend, and exported reports. Contents Prepare analytics data and metrics Build the Analytics Dashboard Export CSV/XLSX reports Verify analytics and reports Objectives After completing this section, you will be able to:
Understand how business data supports an Analytics Dashboard. Distinguish registration, attendance, and confirmed participation data. Calculate analytical indicators using Python. Display analytics results using React/Vite. Inspect Dashboard data through REST APIs. Export reports for administrative use. Verify data accuracy across application components. Understand ADMIN/STUDENT authorization for analytics functionality. The project’s Analytics Dashboard is implemented using React/Vite and FastAPI. Amazon QuickSight, AWS Glue, and Amazon Athena are not used as the primary analytics components in this workshop.
Conclusion Through this section, learners will understand how to transform business records into meaningful analytical indicators that help organizers evaluate activity outcomes and student engagement.
This connects the platform’s data management capabilities with its analytics functionality, contributing to a more complete Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform.

Challenges and Lessons Learned: Multi-module testing: Systems with several components require both individual module tests and end-to-end workflow verification. title: AWS Amplify and Cloudflare Tunnel Deployment
content:
AWS Amplify and Cloudflare Tunnel Deployment In this section, we will deploy the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform to an Internet-accessible Demo environment using AWS Amplify Hosting and Cloudflare Quick Tunnel.
After developing the FastAPI Backend, React/Vite Frontend, DynamoDB integration, and business functionality, the next step is to deploy the Web interface to a Cloud environment for demonstration and testing.
Introduction to AWS Amplify Hosting AWS Amplify Hosting is a service for deploying and hosting Web Frontend applications on AWS.
The service supports:
GitHub Repository integration. Automated dependency installation and application builds. Deployment of built Frontend assets. HTTPS Website endpoints. Build-time environment variable management. Continuous Deployment when source code changes. The project uses AWS Amplify Hosting to deploy the React/Vite Frontend from the fcaj repository and main branch.
Introduction to Cloudflare Quick Tunnel Cloudflare Quick Tunnel provides a temporary HTTPS endpoint that forwards Internet requests to a service running on a local computer.
In the project’s Demo environment, the FastAPI Backend runs on Windows at:
http://127.0.0.1:8001 Cloudflare Quick Tunnel enables the Frontend deployed on AWS Amplify to send REST API requests to this Backend.
Deployment Architecture ADMIN / STUDENT | | HTTPS v Browser | | Load Frontend v AWS Amplify Hosting React / Vite Application Browser | | HTTPS REST API + Access Token v Cloudflare Quick Tunnel | v Local FastAPI Backend 127.0.0.1:8001 | +-- SQLite Demo Persistence | +-- Amazon DynamoDB Integration (when configured) In this architecture:
GitHub manages source code and provides the Frontend source to Amplify. AWS Amplify Hosting deploys the React/Vite Frontend. The browser loads the Frontend from Amplify. The Frontend sends REST API requests through Cloudflare Quick Tunnel. FastAPI processes authentication, authorization, and business operations. SQLite supports Demo data persistence. DynamoDB supports configured Cloud data integration workflows. AWS Amplify Hosting does not run the FastAPI Backend directly in the current architecture. The browser calls APIs through Cloudflare Quick Tunnel, which forwards requests to the local Backend.
Deployment Workflow Prepare the Frontend source code and GitHub Repository. Verify the React/Vite build process. Start the FastAPI Demo Backend on port 8001. Create a Cloudflare Quick Tunnel. Verify the HTTPS API Endpoint. Configure VITE_API_BASE_URL. Deploy the Frontend using AWS Amplify Hosting. Configure CORS for the Amplify Website origin. Verify authentication and business operations. Contents Prepare source code and deployment configuration Connect the Backend using Cloudflare Quick Tunnel Deploy the Frontend with AWS Amplify Hosting Verify the deployed application Objectives After completing this section, you will be able to:
Prepare a React/Vite application for AWS deployment. Understand Frontend builds and deployments from GitHub. Configure Vite environment variables for deployment. Create a Cloudflare Quick Tunnel for a local Backend. Deploy a Frontend using AWS Amplify Hosting. Verify CORS and HTTPS API connectivity. Test authentication and business operations after deployment. Distinguish between Demo and Production environments. Deployment Results During the deployment test on November 9, 2026, the project successfully deployed the Frontend using AWS Amplify Hosting, connected the local FastAPI Backend through Cloudflare Quick Tunnel, and verified ADMIN/STUDENT login and activity creation and persistence.
The current environment is a Demo rather than a fully cloud-hosted Production system.
Cloudflare Quick Tunnel is intended for temporary development and testing. Its URL may change after restarting the Tunnel. Use synthetic data and Demo accounts when exposing the Backend over the Internet.

title: Serverless Data Processing with Amazon S3 and AWS Lambda
content:
Serverless Data Processing with Amazon S3 and AWS Lambda This section documents an independent, actually tested CSV-processing experiment developed for the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform. It is not the primary FastAPI backend and is not described as a production, automatically triggered pipeline.
1. Objectives Store sample student registration records in a real Amazon S3 bucket. Configure the AWS IAM execution permissions required by Lambda. Write and test a Lambda function that reads and validates CSV data. Count valid, duplicate, and invalid records. Write the processing result as a JSON object back to S3. Review execution logs in Amazon CloudWatch. Capture and verify evidence for the FCAJ technical workshop. 2. Services Used AWS Service Role in the experiment Amazon S3 Input CSV and output JSON object storage AWS Lambda Process and validate registration records AWS IAM Lambda execution role and access permissions Amazon CloudWatch Lambda execution logs and metrics Region: Asia Pacific (Singapore), ap-southeast-1.
3. Actual System Architecture The following is the project’s actual architecture diagram. It distinguishes the main React/Vite–FastAPI–SQLite application, the DynamoDB storage pilot, and this independent S3/Lambda test. The demo was invoked through a Lambda Console Test Event, not by an S3 event notification.
4. AWS Resources Tested Resource Recorded identifier Amazon S3 bucket sap-data-project-2026-huflit01 Lambda function sap-csv-processor-demo IAM policy SAP-Lambda-S3-Demo-Access CSV input object lambda-demo/input/registrations.csv JSON output object lambda-demo/processed/registrations-result.json CloudWatch log group /aws/lambda/sap-csv-processor-demo These names describe resources used at the time of the exercise. They may no longer exist after the AWS cleanup documented in section 5.11.
5. Test Procedure and Real Evidence Step 1 – Prepare the S3 bucket and CSV input The input CSV contained four synthetic records, including one duplicate and one record with invalid data.
Step 2 – Configure IAM permissions The Lambda execution role was configured to permit the required S3 operations and CloudWatch logging.
Step 3 – Create and test AWS Lambda The function was invoked manually with a Test Event in the AWS Lambda Console. The execution returned a successful result for the recorded test.
Step 4 – Verify JSON output in S3 Lambda stored a JSON summary of the processed registration data in the configured S3 output location.
Step 5 – Review CloudWatch logs The CloudWatch records were used to inspect execution and troubleshooting information.
6. Recorded Test Results Metric Observed value Total CSV records 4 Valid 2 Duplicate 1 Invalid 1 Lambda response status code 200 The results relate only to the four-record experimental sample. They do not demonstrate a production-scale load test.
7. Detailed Workshop Guides Set up Amazon S3 and prepare CSV data Configure the IAM execution role Create the Lambda CSV processor Test the serverless processing workflow 8. Conclusion This exercise demonstrated how S3, Lambda, IAM, and CloudWatch work together in a focused serverless data-processing task. The core application’s normal CSV/XLSX import, attendance management, reconciliation, and analytics still run through FastAPI in the implemented demo.

React/Vite: Web user interface. AWS Amplify: Frontend hosting. Cloudflare Tunnel: Temporary HTTPS connectivity. FastAPI: REST APIs and business logic. SQLite: Demo data storage. DynamoDB/S3 Pilot: Selected AWS test integrations. The presentation should explain that the Backend has not been migrated to an entirely serverless AWS production architecture.
4. Explain the six AWS services:
AWS Service Actual Role AWS Amplify React/Vite Frontend hosting Amazon DynamoDB Business data storage experiments Amazon S3 File storage and processing results AWS IAM Lambda execution permissions AWS Lambda CSV processing demonstration Amazon CloudWatch Lambda logs and monitoring Distinguish Web Application services from Serverless Demo components. Explain each service’s purpose. Describe the budget-conscious deployment approach. Avoid presenting Cognito, API Gateway, Glue, Athena, or QuickSight as deployed services. 5. Demonstrate the primary application functions:
Authentication:
Sign in with ADMIN and STUDENT accounts. Verify role-based access. Sign out and check session behavior. Activity Management:
View the activity list. Create or update an activity. Review activity status. Registration Import:
Select a CSV/XLSX file. Preview and validate records. Import registration data. Real-time Attendance:
Submit a Check-in using a Student ID through FastAPI. Review results and timestamps. Perform Check-out. Test duplicate or invalid operations. Evidence Import:
Import evidence from a file. Validate records and match them with registered students. Reconciliation:
Combine Registration, Attendance, and Evidence. Review records requiring attention. Confirm or adjust participation results. Analytics and Export:
Display the Analytics Dashboard. Review registration and participation metrics. Export Excel reports. 6. Present the independent AWS Serverless Demo:
Amazon S3 (CSV Input) → AWS Lambda → Amazon S3 (JSON Output)
Supporting components:
AWS IAM provides S3 read/write permissions. Amazon CloudWatch records execution logs. Technical details:
Lambda Function: sap-csv-processor-demo. Runtime: Python 3.13. S3 Bucket: sap-data-project-2026-huflit01. Input: lambda-demo/input/registrations.csv. Output: lambda-demo/processed/registrations-result.json. IAM Inline Policy: SAP-Lambda-S3-Demo-Access. CloudWatch Log Group: /aws/lambda/sap-csv-processor-demo. Previously verified Week 10 result:
{ "total": 4, "valid": 2, "duplicates": 1, "invalid": 1 } This result will serve as evidence of Lambda, S3, IAM, and CloudWatch integration.
7. Collect and categorize feedback:
Functionality: Features that do not meet requirements. UI/UX: Layout, navigation, and user feedback. Data Processing: Import, Validation, and Reconciliation. Security: Authentication, Authorization, and data handling. Analytics: Accuracy of statistical indicators. Documentation: README, diagrams, and user instructions. Actual feedback will be documented after the demonstration.
8. Implement corrections and Regression Testing:
Investigate and address confirmed defects. Update Frontend or Backend components when necessary. Retest affected functions. Verify that account and activity changes do not affect unrelated records. Recheck Reconciliation and Analytics following modifications. Document unresolved issues and possible solutions. 9. Finalize project documentation:
Project README. AWS Architecture Diagram. API Documentation. User Guide. Test Report. Demo Script. Workshop Presentation. AWS Technical Evidence. Documentation should reflect the actual source code and deployed architecture.
10. Organize the GitHub Repository:
Verify the source code structure. Identify configuration files requiring protection. Review README and deployment instructions. Check Frontend and Backend paths. Preserve versions and supporting documents for reporting. Ensure that secrets are not committed to GitHub. 11. Evaluate MVP limitations:
The demo Backend depends on a local computer running FastAPI. Cloudflare Quick Tunnel uses a temporary URL that may change. SQLite is used for the demo environment rather than as a production database. DynamoDB integration remains limited to AWS Pilot scenarios. The Lambda CSV Processor is not connected to the main Registration Import workflow. Browser-based QR camera scanning has not been confirmed as complete. The application is not directly integrated with the University Portal. Large-scale production load testing has not been performed. 12. Propose future improvements:
Deploy the Backend on stable cloud infrastructure. Strengthen Authentication and security for production use. Expand DynamoDB or managed database integration. Consider S3 Event Notifications and Lambda for automatic file processing. Integrate a practical QR Scanner with real-time Attendance APIs. Connect registration data directly to the University Portal. Add Notifications and user support features. Enhance Dashboard analytics capabilities. Perform performance and load testing. Expected Challenges and Lessons to Review: Demo preparation: A clear script and reliable synthetic datasets reduce presentation risks. Local Backend dependency: If the computer or Cloudflare Tunnel stops, the public website may lose API access. AWS architecture: The six AWS services should be explained accurately without confusing AWS Pilot or Lambda Demo with production infrastructure. Feedback management: Suggestions should be prioritized based on impact and feasibility. Regression Testing: Changes to one module require checking related functions. Documentation consistency: README, Architecture Diagrams, and API Documentation must match the implementation. Cost management: AWS resources should be monitored throughout the Demo and handover phases. Data protection: Screenshots and test datasets should be reviewed before inclusion in public reports. Plan for Next Week: Complete Worklogs from Week 1 through Week 12. Verify consistency between Vietnamese and English versions. Finalize the Proposal, Workshop, Self-evaluation, and Sharing and Feedback sections. Review the internship report. Complete the final Architecture Diagram and technical documentation. Check the Hugo reporting website and GitHub Repository. Organize screenshots, test results, and AWS evidence. Review AWS Billing and active resources. Prepare final submission and project handover.

title: AWS Resource Clean-up
content:
AWS Resource Clean-up In the final workshop section, we will review, manage, and clean up resources used to build the Student Activity Management & Engagement Analytics Platform.
During AWS development, resources such as S3 Buckets, Lambda Functions, DynamoDB Tables, Amplify Apps, and CloudWatch Log Groups may remain active after an exercise is completed.
Effective resource lifecycle management helps reduce unnecessary costs and ensures resources are used appropriately.
Objectives After completing this section, you will be able to:
Inventory the AWS resources used in the project. Review costs using AWS Billing and Cost Explorer. Stop the FastAPI Backend and Cloudflare Quick Tunnel. Distinguish resources to retain from disposable test resources. Back up necessary data before deletion. Verify the environment after clean-up. Complete workshop documentation and evidence. Resources to Review Service Resource AWS Amplify React/Vite Frontend Hosting Amazon DynamoDB Five SAP business data tables Amazon S3 Project data storage bucket AWS Lambda sap-csv-processor-demo AWS IAM Execution Role and S3 Access Policy Amazon CloudWatch Lambda Logs and Metrics Cloudflare Quick Tunnel Local Environment FastAPI and SQLite Demo Clean-up Principles Before deleting any resource:
Identify whether the resource is still required. Inspect whether it contains important data. Review dependencies between services. Back up data that must be retained. Delete only resources confirmed to be unnecessary. Verify the result after clean-up. Do not delete SAP-Activities, SAP-Registrations, SAP-Attendance, SAP-Evidence, or SAP-Participation while they are still required for Demo or AWS integration testing.
Do not delete the project S3 Bucket without reviewing its contents.
Contents Review resources and costs Stop the Demo environment Clean up AWS test resources Verify clean-up and review the workshop Expected Results After completing this section, unnecessary Demo processes will be stopped, AWS resources will be reviewed, and important data will remain protected.
Resources required for future demonstrations, maintenance, or development should be explicitly marked for retention.
Clean-up does not require deleting the entire AWS environment. The main objective is safe and controlled resource management.

Understand how to design REST APIs, manage data, implement user authorization, and handle business workflows.
Gain experience in CSV/XLSX file processing, real-time Attendance data, reconciliation, and data analytics.
Develop the ability to perform testing, troubleshoot issues, and evaluate the limitations of an MVP system.
Complete the technical documentation, internship report, and supporting project evidence.
Improve independent research, GitHub usage, technical documentation, and project presentation skills.
Establish a solid foundation for further development in Cloud Computing, Data Engineering, and Cloud & Data Engineering.
